Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  110 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  11.2 × 10 9/l (mild lymphocytosis)  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  200 × 109/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  140 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.8 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  100 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  1200 U/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  420 U/l  30–130 IU/l  Bilirubin  230 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Hepatitis A  The fever, leukocytosis, history of recent travel abroad and transaminase >1000 U/l all point towards acute  hepatitis A infection. Hepatitis A has a similar course to non-pregnant patients and fulminant hepatic failure is  rare. In utero infection has been associated with postnatal complications, so if a pregnant patient is travelling to  an endemic area then vaccination is recommended.  A  Fatty liver of pregnancy  The patient is only in the 17th week of gestation. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare and potentially fatal  obstetric emergency that occurs in the third trimester. Presentation can be non-specific with nausea and  vomiting, abdominal pain or acute liver failure in the most severe cases. Bilirubin and transaminases tend to be  significantly raised with a rise in WCC and hypoglycaemia/hyperlactaemia (hallmarks of acute liver failure).  B  Cholestasis of pregnancy  With this answer, one would expect the patient to have pruritus. Bilirubin is normally not elevated. The  condition is characterised by pruritus (typically starting on the palms and soles of the feet) with raised fasting  and post-prandial serum bile acids. Total bilirubin is rarely raised. The condition occasionally presents with pale  stool and dark urine. It typically presents within the third trimester and resolves up to 6 weeks postpartum.  Treatment is for pruritus with ursodeoxycholic acid and rifampicin.  D  Budd Chiari syndrome  This clinical picture could resemble Budd–Chiari, however the travel history and lymphocytosis would favour an  alternative diagnosis of acute hepatitis A. One might also expect to see clinical features of portal hypertension.  Budd–Chiari is characterised by obstruction of the hepatic vein, sinusoidal congestion and portal hypertension.  Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state and the risk of Budd–Chiari is increased although it remains rare. Most  patients presenting with de novo occlusion tend to have an undiagnosed underlying thrombophilia and should  be investigated.  E  HELLP syndrome  The platelet count and blood pressure are normal and the patient is only in the 17th week gestation. HELLP  syndrome is an hepatic manifestation of pre-eclampsia. This occurs after the 20th week of gestation and tends  to occur in the presence of hypertension (>140/90 mmHg). Thrombocytopenia occurs as a result of a  microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. This takes place within the sinusoids leading to congestion, hepatic  ischaemia and a transaminitis.  A 38-year-old woman is referred to the clinic for abnormal liver function tests. She denies illicit drug or excess  alcohol use. Her general practitioner (GP) is concerned as her alanine aminotransferase is twice the normal limit  and alkaline phosphatase is also slightly elevated.  On examination, she is grossly obese with a body mass index (BMI) of 36; her BP is also elevated at 155/82  mmHg. No other significant findings are noted. Hepatitis B and C serology is negative.  Which of the following is the most useful initial investigation in this case?  A  Ferritin estimation  B  Autoimmune profile  C  Abdominal CT scan  D  Abdominal ultrasound scan  E  Liver biopsy  Explanation  D    Abdominal ultrasound scan  This patient is obese with abnormal liver function tests and the most likely diagnosis is non-alcoholic  steatohepatitis (NASH). Ultrasound will rule out significant other disease of the liver or biliary tract and is likely  to be hyperechogenic; fatty infiltration may be visualised when it is above 30% of the liver mass. Further  investigations for NASH include an MRI to provide more accurate estimation of liver fat, magnetic resonance  elastography (MRE) to estimate liver stiffness, and liver biopsy. Weight loss is the mainstay of treatment for this  condition. Orlistat has been shown to reduce hepatic fat, as has pioglitazone, although neither is licensed for the  treatment of hepatic steatosis.  A  Ferritin estimation  Although ferritin may be elevated, it is a non-specific finding in chronic liver disease and is therefore not useful  in further pinpointing the underlying diagnosis.  B  Autoimmune profile  Transaminases are elevated, which makes autoimmune hepatitis a possibility, although with the marked  elevation in BMI, NASH should be considered the most likely diagnosis.  C  Abdominal CT scan  CT scan is less useful with respect to elucidating liver architecture than MRI. The correct sequence of  investigations is therefore liver USS followed by MRI scanning later.  E  Liver biopsy  Liver biopsy is usually required to confirm the diagnosis of NASH and provide evidence on histological staging  of cirrhosis, although it is usually done after initial radiological investigations.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia. He initially  presented to his General Practitioner, as he had noticed significant weight loss and mild fatigue over several  months. There is no history of change in bowel habits. He has a history of hypertension, for which he takes  ramipril, but is on no regular medication apart from this. He has a vegetarian diet and takes over-the-counter  vitamins for iron, vitamin B 12 and folate.  On examination, his blood pressure is 142/82 mmHg. His body mass index is 20 kg/m 2, and abdominal and per  rectum (PR) examinations are unremarkable. He has no skin rashes, bruises or joint pain.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  78 g/l  135–175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  78 fl  76–98 fl  White cell count (WCC)  5.4 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets  180 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  49 mm/h  0–10 mm in the 1 sthour  Sodium (Na +)  140 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.4 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine  100 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
options: D. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody
E. One unit of blood transfusion
questions.explanation:   Endoscopy  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for colorectal cancer indicate referral via  the 2-week wait pathway should be completed for all adults aged over 60 who present with iron deficiency  anaemia or a change in bowel habit or a positive stool sample for occult blood. Both lower and upper  gastrointestinal endoscopy is recommended for these patients. The patient should have further investigations to  establish the cause of his anaemia if these tests are negative.  C  Haemolysis screen  A haemolysis screen is indicated in patients with a significant, unexplained drop in their Hb concentration. In the  presence of haemolysis, these patients may have signs of jaundice as well as fatigue. However, this patient’s  low Hb concentration can be explained by his iron deficiency and this, in itself, requires further investigation.  A  Bone marrow biopsy  Bone marrow biopsy may be indicated in cases of iron deficiency anaemia where there is a need to differentiate  iron deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease. However, in this case, the weight loss and patient’s  age mean that colorectal cancer should be suspected.  D  Immunoglobulin A (IgA) tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody  In this patient, TTG antibodies should be tested for. However, the next most appropriate step is to proceed to  further imaging to rule out the presence of colorectal cancer, as per the NICE guidelines which recommend that  given this patient’s age of over 60 and the presentation with weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia, colorectal  cancer should be ruled out with endoscopy.  E  One unit of blood transfusion  The NICE blood transfusion guidelines recommend a treatment threshold of a Hb concentration of 70 for  patients without acute coronary syndrome. Therefore, there is currently no indication to begin a blood  transfusion for this patient.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is referred by his general practitioner (GP) for an upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy. He  describes a 3-month history of worsening epigastric pain and anorexia. He suffers from chronic back pain  following a road traffic accident 5 years ago. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day and drinks 30 units of alcohol per  week.  Examination is unremarkable and all his blood tests are normal. You perform a gastroscopy, and there is no  blood in the stomach.  The oesophagus and duodenum look normal, but the appearance below is seen in the antral region of the  stomach (see below).  Which of the following is the most appropriate management step  
options: A. Refer back to the GP for smoking cessation advice
E. Adrenalin injection to the base of the lesion
questions.explanation:   Eradicate pylori if present  The endoscopic appearance is that of a large gastric ulcer with a white sloughy base. H. pylori, aspirin,  corticosteroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and smoking are aetiological factors for gastric  ulcer. Other less common causes include Crohn’s disease, tuberculosis and vasculitides. Biopsy for histological  analysis is important from the ulcer edge, to exclude malignancy. The association of H. pylori with gastric  ulceration is weaker (60–70%) than with duodenal ulceration (90%), but eradication therapy may prevent  recurrence.  C  Refer for partial gastrectomy  Partial gastrectomy was the mainstay of therapy for gastric ulcers, although the advent of modern medical  therapy (H2 antagonists and proton pump inhibitors) has massively reduced the need for surgery.  A  Refer back to the GP for smoking cessation advice  Clearly reducing smoking and alcohol consumption is important, but this alone won’t lead to resolution of the  ulcer without H. pylori eradication therapy.  D  Repeat endoscopy in 2 weeks  There is no indication for repeat endoscopy after only 2 weeks. H. pylori eradication should be attempted first,  with a follow-up endoscopy at least 4–6 weeks later.  E  Adrenalin injection to the base of the lesion  As the ulcer is covered in slough and there is no active bleeding, injection therapy is not indicated; disturbing the  overlying slough may actually increase the risk of further haemorrhage.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with a long-standing history of ulcerative colitis attends the clinic for review. He was also  diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) some years earlier and his LFTs have been monitored.  Recently, he has become severely jaundiced and requested an urgent hospital appointment.  Ultrasound demonstrated ductal dilatation with other areas of stricturing consistent with the PSC. MRI  cholangiography demonstrated marked ductal dilatation and a hilar lesion consistent with a  cholangiocarcinoma. There was evidence of local lymphatic invasion with enlarged lymph nodes around the  porta hepatis.  Which of the following represents the most appropriate management of this case?
questions.explanation:   Stenting of the lesion  There is evidence from the MRI scan that this patient has cholangiocarcinoma with local invasion. As such,  attempted surgical removal is likely to be unsuccessful. For this reason the treatment of choice is stenting via  ERCP. The procedure is successful at relieving symptoms of jaundice and may also relieve associated lethargy  and fatigue. Most patients with severe PSC are surveyed for the possible development of cholangiocarcinoma  and are recommended for liver transplantation before this occurs. Stent replacement may be required every 3–6  months, and adjuvant radiotherapy post stent placement may prolong survival for as long as 17 months.  Resectable lesions are associated with a 5-year survival as high as 40%.  E  Referral for Whipple’s procedure  Whipple’s procedure or pancreaticoduodenectomy is performed for resectable carcinomas of the head of the  pancreas. Only 10–20% of patients are actually suitable to undergo a Whipple’s procedure at the point of  diagnosis.  A  Referral for chemotherapy  5-FU and cisplatin are commonly used agents for cholangiocarcinoma, their effects are however limited,  meaning that chemotherapy isn’t the preferred option.  C  Referral for lobectomy  Local lymph node invasion has already occurred hence lobectomy isn’t an option for treatment here. In any case  lobectomy risks a new focus of cancer developing in the unresected portion of the liver.  D  Referral for liver transplantation  By the time local invasion has occurred, liver transplantation isn’t an option. Where lesions are resectable,  however, 5-year survival may be as high as 40%. Transplantation is the aim for severe disease before cancer  develops.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of diarrhoea and intermittent fresh rectal bleeding. She  works as a shopkeeper and smokes ten cigarettes per day. Her brother suffers from colitis. Blood tests show  microcytic anaemia and a raised C-reactive protein.  Colonoscopy shows inflammation in the recto-sigmoid colon and a normal terminal ileum. Histology suggests  indeterminate colitis. She turns up to clinic very keen to know the exact diagnosis.  Which of the following will favour a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease?
options: B. Detection of perinuclear anti-cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA)
C. Dilated colon on plain abdominal radiography
questions.explanation:   Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)  The diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease is based on clinical history, inflammatory markers, colonoscopy  and histology results. In around 10% of patients, it is impossible to distinguish ulcerative from Crohn’s colitis  and this is termed indeterminate colitis. Serological markers have been studied extensively in trials but are not  yet in everyday clinical use. Ulcerative colitis is strongly associated with perinuclear anti-cytoplasmic antibodies  (pANCA – detected in 60–70% of UC vs 10–15% of CD). The presence of anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae  antibodies favours Crohn’s disease (ASCA IgG + in 60–70% CD vs 10–15% of UC vs <5% in non-IBD colitis).  The two antibodies can be used in combination, and a serological profile of ASCA±pANCA– has an 80%  positive predictive value of progression to CD.  Reference: Mitsuyama K, et al. Antibody markers in the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. World Journal  of Gastroenterology. 2016;22(3):1304–1310. doi:10.3748/wjg.v22.i3.1304.  E  Arthritis  Although arthritis (including asymmetrical polyarthritis, spondylitis, sacroilitis and enthesopathy) is well  described as an extra-intestinal manifestation of Crohn’s disease, their presence or absence is not a good  predictive marker of underlying inflammatory bowel disease.  A  Anti-endomysial antibodies  Anti-endomysial antibodies are seen in coeliac disease. Although there is an overlap with inflammatory bowel  disease and coeliac disease, the positivity of these antibodies would not help clarify the diagnosis.  B  Detection of perinuclear anti-cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA)  pANCA positivity has been well described in inflammatory bowel disease but is more commonly seen in UC  rather than Crohn’s. In patients with indeterminate colitis (IC), pANCA and ASCA have been shown in studies to  provide a predictive value. ASCA-/pANCA+ serology in indeterminate colitis is 64% predictive for a diagnosis of  UC.  C  Dilated colon on plain abdominal radiography  This is a non-specific finding that could represent multiple pathologies: obstruction, volvulus, ileus or toxic  megacolon.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with intermittent episodes of diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal bloating and  flatulence. She has not lost weight over the course of the past year.  Clinical examination is unremarkable. Her BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 65/min and regular, BMI 24 and her  abdomen is soft and non-tender. Faecal occult bloods are negative and haematological and biochemical  investigations are unremarkable.  Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:   Irritable bowel syndrome  In the presence of a normal physical examination and a series of normal investigations, irritable bowel  syndrome is the most likely diagnosis here. Many patients with symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome also  have lactose intolerance. Hence, a trial of dairy-free diet may bring about significant improvement in symptoms,  as unmetabolised lactose contributes to large bowel symptoms of bloating and flatulence because lactose  provides a substrate for metabolism by colonic bacteria. Other components of the diet may be excluded on a  trial basis to assess the impact on symptoms.  C  Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease is usually a consideration when these symptoms present in association with iron deficiency  anaemia, rather than the normal blood work up seen here.  A  Colonic carcinoma  Given that there is no weight loss and investigations are normal, and the fact that this patient is only 28 years  of age, a diagnosis of colonic carcinoma is very unlikely.  B  Crohn’s disease  Crohn’s disease is associated with the development of chronic abdominal pain, weight loss and anaemia, rather  than the picture seen here.  D  Ulcerative colitis  UC is associated with distal bowel symptoms, which result in bloody diarrhoea with mucus and raised  inflammatory markers, rather than the benign picture with normal investigations.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman is admitted comatose to the resuscitation room. Her husband describes a few days of  increasing confusion.  Past medical history is of diabetes, primary biliary cholangitis and one episode of variceal haemorrhage. Drug  therapy includes ursodeoxycholic acid, metformin and aspirin. She does not consume alcohol or any illicit drugs.  On examination, she is drowsy and unable to converse. There is no meningism, and pupils are equal and  reactive. She has assumed a decorticate position, plantars are upgoing. Bedside blood glucose is 6.1 mmol/l.  The remainder of systemic examination is unremarkable. As well as extensive investigations reported below, a  full sepsis screen is sent to the lab. She was intubated for airway protection.  Initial blood tests reveal:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin  89 g/l  115–165 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  13 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets  60 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.2 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine  66 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Prothrombin Test (PT)  19 s  10.6–14.9 s  Urea  16 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  45 mg/l  0–10 mg/l  Bilirubin  12 µmol/l  2–17 μmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase  10 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Aspartate aminotransferase  (AST)  36 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  38 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Albumin  28 g/l  35–55 g/l  CT brain  Mild atrophy  EEG  Diffuse symmetrical triphasic sharp waves  How should this patient be further managed?
questions.explanation:   Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy  Although the patient has relatively normal transaminases (aminotransferases), we know from the history of  varices that she has cirrhotic liver disease. We can also deduce from her low albumin and prolonged  prothrombin time that her synthetic liver function is severely compromised. Thus a likely diagnosis of grade III–  IV hepatic encephalopathy can be made. The electroencephalogram (EEG) picture is classical for hepatic  encephalopathy. Her serum ammonia ought to be measured. The next stage of management is to identify any  possible precipitants and reverse them.  In this patient, the likely precipitants are sepsis and gastrointestinal bleed; note the raised inflammatory  markers, anaemia and disproportionate rise in urea. Therefore, an upper GI endoscopy is the best option  presented here. Although commonly used, interventions such as non-absorbable disaccharides (lactulose),  antibiotics and protein restriction have little evidence base.  A  Lorazepam boluses intravenously  The diagnosis is hepatic encephalopathy, and drugs such as benzodiazepines ought to be avoided where  possible.  B  Intravenous aciclovir  It is sensible to consider viral encephalitis in patients with confusion, but in this case the features suggest  hepatic encephalopathy and serum ammonia should be checked to confirm this.  C  Magnetic resonance image (MRI) brain  Obtaining an MRI brain is likely only to delay treating the underlying problem – a probable upper GI bleed. In  hepatic encephalopathy, basal ganglia high signal on T1-weighted images can be seen. In severe hepatic  encephalopathy such as this, diffuse brain swelling may be seen.  E  Plasma exchange  Plasma exchange is not helpful in treating hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.question: A 52-year-old Russian immigrant with a background of haemophilia A is admitted after a road traffic accident.  He is transfused with four units of blood and given recombinant factor VIII concentrate. He otherwise appears  well. He drinks 10 units of alcohol per week and denies and previous intravenous (iv) drug use. He underwent  surgery as a child whilst in Russia.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  140 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)  88 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  120 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Bilirubin  25 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  You suspect he has viral hepatitis.  What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:   Hepatitis C  Unfortunately, due to inadequate screening of donated blood and the pooling of multiple samples, significant  numbers of haemophilia patients have been infected with hepatitis C virus following blood transfusions, so  option C is correct. The picture seen here is most typical of hepatitis C infection, and around 50% of patients are  diagnosed on routine liver function testing with an isolated rise in alanine transferase (ALT). Diagnosis is made  by confirming the presence of hepatitis C antibodies using ELISA.  D  Hepatitis D  This is a less common virus that requires patients already infected with hepatitis B virus for its existence and  replication.  A  Hepatitis A  This is spread by the faecal oral route, and is usually a prodromal illness of jaundice, fever, nausea, vomiting or  abdominal pain - but you are told this patient is fit and well.  B  Hepatitis B  Although a good option here, it is not the best answer as hepatitis B screening was introduced some years  before screening for hepatitis C, which came later, including in Russia. Given we are told the operation took  place when he was a child, he’s more likely to have been exposed to hepatitis C  E  Hepatitis E  This is spread by faecal oral transmission and the history of ingesting contaminated water or food. Hepatitis E is  more common in pregnancy, but is usually self-limiting.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man is seen in the clinic with a 6-month history of abdominal pain, 6 kg weight loss and  intermittently he has noticed dark urine which lasted for a few days. He also has noticed night sweats, which  soak his nightclothes. There is a history of ulcerative colitis which is currently well controlled; he does not  smoke and drinks a couple of pints of beer at the weekend.  On examination, he looks well and has no jaundice, clubbing or lymphadenopathy. He has a 4 cm non-tender  hepatomegaly and the rest of his examination is normal.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  White cell count (WCC)  6.7 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Haemoglobin (Hb)  135 g/l  135–175 g/l  Platelets (PLT)  379 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  61 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Bilirubin  21 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  245 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)  256 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Albumin  36 g/l  35–55 g/l  Serum electrophoresis  Polyclonal increase in immunoglobulins  Auto-antibodies (ANA)  1 : 64  c-ANCA  Negative  p-ANCA  1 : 320  Abdominal ultrasound (US)  Hepatomegaly but no bile duct dilation  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Primary sclerosing cholangitis  Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease of unknown aetiology. The diagnosis is  based a combination of clinical features which often come on insidiously, including hepatomegaly, intermittent  jaundice, fevers of unknown origin, pruritus, abdominal pain and weight loss. This, together with a cholestatic  biochemical profile and typical cholangiographic abnormalities of generalized beading and stenosis of the  intrahepatic and extra-hepatic biliary tree, characterise PSC. PSC is usually progressive, leading to cirrhosis,  portal hypertension and liver failure. Ultrasound is normal in 50% of patients at an early stage of the disease.  Pathognomonic histology shows a concentric obliterative fibrosis of interlobular bile ducts, with the presence of  intrahepatic cholangiectasis and ductal obliteration.  Therapeutic interventions, such as dilation of strictures or placement of an endoprosthesis, can be performed  during endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Many pharmacological therapies have been  tried, without great success. Dietary replacement of vitamins A, D, E and K should be commenced. Liver  transplantation is an option in terminal liver failure.  A  Primary biliary cholangitis  Primary biliary cholangitis is interlobular bile duct damage caused by granulomatous autoimmune  inflammation. This can result in fibrosis, cirrhosis and portal hypertension. It is associated with antimitochondrial  antibodies and is far more common in females, typically at 50 years of age. Presentation is typically  asymptomatic with incidental biochemical cholestasis but can cause lethargy and pruritus progressing to  ascites. The presence of night sweats and absence of pruritis, as well as the demographics, makes this an  unlikely diagnosis.  C  Chronic active hepatitis  Viral hepatitis causes fever, malaise, anorexia and nausea, which can progress to jaundice. In patients with  chronic infection this may progress to cirrhosis, which may lead to episodes of acute decompensation of liver  disease. The blood tests suggest a primarily cholestatic injury as opposed to a hepatic cause, and there is no  clear history of risk factors.  D  Polyarteritis nodosa  Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotising vasculitis that causes thrombosis, and can also cause aneurysms, in  medium-diameter arteries, which can lead to organ infarction. It is more common in men and with hepatitis B.  The absence of systemic features and rash makes this an unlikely diagnosis, and the demographics of the  patient are not supportive.  E  Hydatid disease  Cystic hydatid disease occurs following transmission of ingesting the eggs of parasites such as Echinococcus. It  is common in China, Russia, Japan, India, Pakistan and Wales. Clinically the organs most commonly affected are  the liver and lungs. In the liver it can cause obstructive jaundice whilst in the lungs it can cause haemoptysis  and dyspnoea, and rupture can lead to anaphylaxis. The absence of travel history and of potential exposure  makes this very unlikely, as does the weight loss.

questions.question: A 19-year-old student presents to the university health service complaining of flu-like symptoms, lethargy and  jaundiced sclerae and an inability to eat due to a sore throat. He remembered that his father may have suffered  from a liver condition.  On examination, he is pyrexial 38.2 °C, BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular. He has signs of  pharyngitis on examination of his throat.  Investigations reveal:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  23 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  28 u/l  10 - 40 u/l  Bilirubin  78 μmol/l  1 - 22 μmol/l  Albumin  41 g/l  35 - 55 g/l  Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention in this case given the most likely  diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Observation    The clinical picture is highly suggestive of Gilbert’s syndrome, and as such, observation and supportive therapy  for the acute flu-like illness is the management of choice. When jaundice is severe (as occurs only rarely in  Gilbert's), phenobarbitone can rapidly decrease unconjugated serum bilirubin levels. This condition is autosomal  recessive and is characterised by unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia caused by impaired glucuronyl transferase  activity. Jaundice may be precipitated by fasting, excessive alcohol consumption or acute illness. Other liver  function tests apart from bilirubin level are generally normal. It is likely that a viral illness has led to a period of  fasting and the symptoms seen here.  E  Hepatitis screen  Isolated elevated bilirubin in the context of an inherited liver condition is consistent with Gilbert’s syndrome, not  with hepatitis. In hepatitis a marked elevation in transaminases would be expected.  A  Phenobarbitone  Phenobarbitone is usually only considered for severe jaundice. At this stage it’s more appropriate to manage  this patient conservatively.  B  Diazepam  Phenobarbitone, rather than diazepam is used as an enzyme inducer in the treatment of acute Gilbert’s  syndrome.  D  Hepatic ultrasound scan  Given transaminases are normal, and this patient has evidence of an inherited liver problem, Gilbert’s is much  more likely than obstructive liver disease.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man is seen in neurology outpatients after being referred with disinhibited behaviour of 2  months’ duration. His family tells you that he passes urine in public and the police have brought him home on  two occasions recently. He has been losing weight for the last year and was previously 110 kg, now weighing  92 kg. He has diarrhoea and his family tell you it smells bad and is difficult to flush. The patient complains of  pain in his right knee, left ankle and lower back.  On examination, he looks pale and has angular cheilitis. He has a distended abdomen with some shifting  dullness but no palpable organomegaly. His palmo-mental reflex is positive. The right knee and left ankle are  both swollen with minimal tenderness and a good range of movement.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Sodium (Na +)  134 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.1 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  4.8 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  45 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Corrected calcium (Ca 2+)  1.74 mmol/l  2.20–2.60 mmol/l  Albumin  27 g/l  35–55 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  6.5 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Haemoglobin (Hb)  92 g/l  135–175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  78.2 fl  76–98 fl  Platelets (PLT)  512 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.4  < 1.1  Computed tomography (CT) brain  Normal  Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD) is performed and duodenal biopsy demonstrates expanded villi  containing macrophages staining positive with periodic acid–Schiff stain.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Whipple's disease  Whipple disease is a systemic disease caused by Tropheryma whippeli, a Gram-positive, non-acid-fast rod. It is  usually found in white, middle-aged males, most commonly in Europe. The classic presentation, believed to be  caused by organism infiltration of the body tissue, is that of a wasting illness characterised by four cardinal  features: migratory arthralgia of the large joints, arthritis, intermittent diarrhoea and colicky abdominal pain. The  disease can affect the central nervous system (CNS) and produce frontal signs (such as in our patient),  meningoencephalitis or dementia.  The organism is taken up by the macrophages, and diagnosis is established by identifying ‘foamy’ macrophages  that stain positive with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain on jejunal biopsy. PCR testing is also used for  confirmation. Other infections, such as with endemic fungi (e.g. Histoplasma spp.), Rhodococcus and HIVinfected mycobacterial disease, can be histologically similar to Whipple’s disease, but many can be ruled in or  out by additional testing (i.e. staining for organisms, culture, antigen testing). Antibiotics are the mainstay of  treatment - usually co-trimoxazole or tetracycline is given for 1 year. Clinical failure is suggested by a positive  PCR in the relevant specimen from patients who fail to respond clinically to adequate therapy or have  recurrence of symptoms after initial improvement. One third of patients relapse.  B  Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease could explain the gastrointestinal symptoms and malabsoption picture and, on rare occasions,  has been associated with neuropsychiatric disease. However, the PAS positivity on the small bowel histology is  not consistent.  A  Hartnup disease  Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by impaired amino acid transport in the apical brush  border membrane of the small intestine and the proximal tubule of the kidney. If symptomatic, it usually  presents in childhood with pellagra-like skin eruptions, cerebellar ataxia and gross aminoaciduria.  C  HIV enteropathy and dementia  HIV infection can lead to scarring of the lymphoid structures within the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in chronic  malabsorption and weight loss. In addition, the gastrointestinal symptoms of Mycobacterium avium  intracellulare (MAI) enteropathy (almost exclusively seen in patients with AIDS, or those who are severely  immunosuppressed) and Whipple’s disease are similar. Neurocognitive disorders can be seen in advanced or  untreated HIV infection. However, there is no history of cough, which would be the usual first presentation of  MAI infection. And while M. avium-positive duodenal biopsies are also PAS positive, contrary to Whipple’s  disease, they also stain positive with Ziehl-Neelson. Whipple’s disease is more likely to explain the overall  clinical picture.  D  Tropical sprue  The gastrointestinal symptoms of tropical sprue and Whipple’s disease are indistinguishable. However, the  cognitive changes as seen in this case would be more difficult to attribute to tropical sprue. Furthermore,  histology of the duodenum would reveal flattened villi and inflammatory cell infiltrates, but no PAS-positive  macrophages.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents to the Neurology Outpatient Clinic due to memory loss and ataxia. He reports  recent weight loss of 10 kg over six months, associated with fatigue, change in bowel habits with watery  diarrhoea and abdominal pain. He has a past medical history of osteoarthritis and hypertension.  On examination, he appears tanned, with loose clothing. A systolic murmur over the left fifth intercostal space is  appreciated on cardiovascular examination. His abdomen is soft but distended, and there is palpable pelvic  lymphadenopathy. Neurological examination reveals that cranial nerves are intact and peripheral power and  sensation are normal in the upper and lower limbs, but there is clonus in the ankles bilaterally. When his gait is  assessed, he has a broad-based stance and sways while mobilising from one end of the room to the other.  Cognitive testing reveals an Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS) of 8 out of 10.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Whipple’s disease  This patient has Whipple’s disease, an infection caused by the pathogen Tropheryma whipplei. Classical  symptoms include gastrointestinal symptoms that resemble other malabsorption syndromes, migratory  arthralgia and fever. Sacroiliitis is common and the HLA-B27 antigen is more commonly found among affected  individuals. One-third of patients have cardiac involvement with pericarditis or endocarditis, which rarely causes  significant symptoms. Neurological features include ataxia, confusion, seizures, delirium and cognitive  impairment. Diagnosis is made by intestinal biopsy and identification of the organism. Periodic acid–Schiff  staining shows foamy macrophages, and polymerase chain reaction will detect the bacterium. Treatment  involves antibiotic therapy, with an initial phase of parenteral treatment, followed by 12 months of oral  antibiotics. Relapse is common, often presenting with central nervous system (CNS) symptoms.  A  Coeliac disease  This patient has Whipple’s disease which classically presents with migratory arthritis, intermittent diarrhoea  and colicky abdominal pain. The main differential here would be coeliac disease, due to weight loss and  diarrhoea. However, Whipple’s disease is the correct answer here because of the presence of systemic disease  patterns (cardiac murmur indicating endocarditis, ataxia due to neurological involvement), due to the spread of  the causative organism T. whipplei to other tissues. Coeliac disease may cause symptoms of malabsorption and  other complications; however, it does not present with the typical features of endocarditis and neurological  involvement seen here.  B  Friedreich’s ataxia  Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive disease, which usually presents in the teenage years with  deafness, progressive spinocerebellar ataxia, optic atrophy and progressive muscle wasting. Patients may also  present with cardiomyopathy; however, it is not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, as in the case here.  C  Small bowel adenocarcinoma  Small bowel adenocarcinoma may present with changes in bowel habit, anaemia, weight loss, abdominal pain  and bowel obstruction but is now relevant here.  E  Wilson’s disease  Wilson’s disease is an inherited disorder characterised by accumulation of copper in the body, which results in  chronic liver disease, CNS abnormalities, including tremors, muscle stiffness, dysarthria, dysphagia and  incoordination, and psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depression and psychosis. It is not associated with  gastrointestinal symptoms, as seen in Whipple’s disease.

questions.question: A 72-year-old female is admitted with a 2-month history of diarrhoea. She has loose motions with no blood,  four times per day. Her stool cultures are negative and her examination is normal. She has a background of  rheumatoid arthritis for which she is in remission; hypertension, chronic renal impairment with a creatinine of  151 μmol/l and depression.  Colonoscopy demonstrates mild diverticular disease. Biopsy shows evidence of colitis with lymphocytic  infiltration. Her daughter finds a list of her medications that she is taking and shows them to you.  Which one of the following medications is most likely to be causing her diarrhoea?
questions.explanation:   Lansoprazole  Many drugs contribute to causing diarrhoea and it is very important to get a good drug history when evaluating  a patient with chronic diarrhoea. The list is endless and one must use the BNF to check whenever one is not  sure. Drugs causing diarrhoea include broad-spectrum antibiotics, antihypertensives such as diuretics, digoxin,  some cholesterol-lowering drugs, sodium valproate, thyroxine, levodopa, antacids, theophylline, colchicines,  non-steroidals and oral hypoglycaemic drugs. Mechanisms leading to diarrhoea are diverse, including effects on  transit time, alterations in bowel flora, and impact on colonic inflammation, such as the development of  lymphocytic colitis seen with non-steroidals. With respect to lansoprazole it appears to result in the  development of microscopic colitis.  E  Spironolactone  Mild diarrhoea is a rare side effect of spironolactone therapy, although it isn’t as a result of microscopic colitis.  A  Ramipril  Ramipril is associated with gastritis and pancreatitis, and in some cases diarrhoea, although this isn’t manifest  as lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis.  B  Amlodipine  Abdominal pain and intermittent nausea are the commonest associations with amlodipine use, and diarrhoea is  uncommonly reported, although it isn’t thought to be due to microscopic colitis.  C  Furosemide  Although loop diuretics have a recognised association with diarrhoea, this isn’t due to lymphocytic colitis. The  changes in bowel habit are potentially due to an alteration in GI motility.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic due to abnormal liver function tests which were  a finding on a battery of blood tests checked by her GP. She attended the general practitioner (GP) because of  increased fatigue and symptoms of itching. She was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome several years  ago, but this has since become quiescent. She has no other significant past medical history except for hormone  replacement therapy and takes no regular medication. She is a non-smoker and drinks 6 units of alcohol per  week. She has no risk factors for hepatitis.  On examination she looked well, her BMI is 22. Some xanthelasmata were noted, but there was no jaundice,  clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender and the liver edge was palpable 1 cm  below the costal margin. Cardiorespiratory and neurological examination was unremarkable.  Investigation results are below:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  130 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  6.0 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  220 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume  (MCV)  82 fl  80 - 100 fl  International normalised ratio  (INR)  1.1  < 1.1  Erythrocyte sedimentation  rate (ESR)  4 mm/h  1 - 20 mm/h  Sodium (Na +)  140 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.8 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Urea  5.2 mmol/l  2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  100 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Fasting glucose  4.1 mmol/l  < 5.9 mmol/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  < 4 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Cholesterol  7.8 mmol/l  < 5.2 mmol/  Bilirubin  16 µmol/l  1 - 22 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  850 u/l  30 - 150 u/l  Gamma-glutamyl transferase  (GGT)  52 u/l  < 50 u/l  Alanine aminotransferase  (ALT)  48 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Albumin  38 g/dl  35 - 55 g/dl  Abdominal ultrasound  Slight hepatomegaly, no other focal abnormality, no  biliary obstruction  Which further investigation would be most specific in making the diagnosis?
options: B. Computed tomography (CT) scan of abdomen
questions.explanation: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies  Clinical features are pointing towards a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), which is a chronic  progressive disorder with the gradual destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to fibrosis and  cholestasis and ultimately hepatic cirrhosis. PBC is usually presented in middle-aged females with early  symptoms of pruritis, fatigue, which can progress to the development of obstructive jaundice and portal  hypertension. 50% of patients may be asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis and are detected by abnormal  liver function tests especially elevated alkaline phosphatase. Anti-mitochondrial antibody has a sensitivity of  95% with a specificity of 98%. Treatment options include colestyramine for pruritis (naltrexone and rifampicin  may also help), ursodeoxycholic acid and liver transplantation for end staged disease (e.g. bilirubin > 100  µmol/L). Once jaundice develops, the survival rate is < 2 years without liver transplantation.  B  Computed tomography (CT) scan of abdomen  CT scan of abdomen can be helpful in differentiating PBC from other biliary conditions e.g. carcinoma of bile  duct, but not specific for PBC. There is a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with PBC.    A  Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)  MRCP can help to exclude chronic biliary obstruction (stone or stricture), however, it is not specific for PBC.  D  Hepatitis serology  PBC must be differentiated from chronic hepatitis (due to viral infections) by performing hepatic serology tests.  Hepatic serology is not specific for underlying possible diagnosis of PBC.  E  Anti-nuclear antibodies  Patients with clinical and histological picture of PBC but negative anti-mitochondrial antibodies are referred to  as antibody –negative PBC or autoimmune cholangitis, which is associated with high levels of anti-nuclear  antibodies and smooth muscle antibodies. Almost all cases of SLE show a positive serum ANA.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl is sent to you for assessment, as she is profoundly depressed. She has features of anhedonia  and anorexia over the last 6 months. Before this, she had always been an excellent student and has many  friends.  She has no known medical problems, but her mother has a history of schizophrenia. She does not smoke or  drink, and both she and her parents deny that she has used drugs.  On examination, she is well-dressed but does not keep eye contact. She tells you that she is hearing secondperson auditory hallucinations and has done so for 3 months. She has an expressionless face and when writing  a sentence she has small, cramped handwriting. Her gait is slow and there is some increased tone in her right  arm.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Albumin  36 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  201 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  121 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Bilirubin  28 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Wilson’s disease  Wilson’s disease is an inherited disorder of hepatic copper disposition caused by mutations in the gene ATP7B  on chromosome 13. The average prevalence is 30/million. It can present as either psychiatric  (depression/neurotic behaviour), neurological (extrapyramidal signs) or with liver disease (asymptomatic  hepatomegaly, elevated transaminase).  Biochemical findings include low serum ceruloplasmin and copper and elevated 24 h urinary excretion of  copper. There is an increased copper concentration in the liver parenchyma. Kayser–Fleischer rings need to be  looked for with a slit lamp and are present in 60% of cases. The mainstay of treatment is chelation therapy, with  penicillamine. Second-line treatment involves trientine, and occasionally zinc. With effective and early  treatment, most patients are well and live normally.  A  Abuse of clozapine  The atypical antipsychotics carry a lower risk of extrapyramidal symptoms than typical antipsychotics. The more  common signs and symptoms such as lethargy and sedation (histamine blockade), miosis, tachycardia,  orthostatic hypotension (alpha-adrenergic blockade) and confusion (muscarinic blockade). Clozapine abuse is  not the best explanation for this patient’s presentation with extrapyramidal signs and deranged liver function  tests.  B  Chronic abuse of LSD  Lysergic acid use can cause a wide variety of neuropsychiatric symptoms, including visual illusions and  distortion of time perception. Chronic use can lead to persistent psychosis, but is unlikely to account for the  neurological signs and raised ALT.  C  Ganser syndrome  Ganser syndrome is a dissociative disorder characterised by absurd or approximate answers to questions  (paralogias), clouding of consciousness, somatic conversion symptoms, hallucinations and amnesia. The  syndrome is associated with a history of head injury, Munchausen syndrome, solitary confinement or extreme  stress. This diagnosis would not explain the extrapyramidal signs and abnormal liver function tests.  D  Othello syndrome  Othello syndrome is a term used to describe morbid jealousy, which may involve delusions, obsessions and  overvalued ideas. It would not explain this patient’s neurological signs or deranged liver function tests.  A 50-year-old Asian male, presents with a 3-week history of jaundice and pruritus. He has a 1-year history of  diarrhoea which had been diagnosed as irritable bowel syndrome by his general practitioner. There is no history  of foreign travel and he denies any illicit drug use or recent blood transfusion. On examination he appears  jaundiced and has scratch marks on his trunk, but the liver is not enlarged and there is no evidence of ascites.  A liver biopsy is performed and the histology shows typical onion skin-type periductal concentric ﬁbrosis.  What is the most likely diagnosis?  A  Primary biliary cholangitis  B  Haemochromatosis  C  Autoimmune hepatitis  D  Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)  E  Alcoholic liver disease  Explanation  D  Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)  Periductal concentric fibrosis (‘onion skin’) is a classic histopathologic finding of PSC on liver biopsy. The long  history of diarrhoea should make you consider a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a condition  strongly associated with PSC. In fact approximately 60-80% of patients with PSC have concomitant IBD.  E  Alcoholic liver disease  There is no history of alcohol excess, and liver biopsy would usually show fatty change, cell necrosis and  Mallory bodies.  A  Primary biliary cholangitis    This typically shows a dense lymphocytic infiltrate in the portal tracts with granulomatous destruction and loss  of medium-sized interlobular bile ducts, focal and variable within the liver.  B  Haemochromatosis  When a liver biopsy is performed in this setting, Perls' Prussian blue stain would be performed to evaluate the  degree and cellular distribution of hepatic iron stores.  C  Autoimmune hepatitis  The findings on liver biopsy are described as interface hepatitis, formerly referred to as piecemeal necrosis. This  is because portal inflammation is seen eroding through the limiting plate between the portal tract and liver  parenchyma.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man presents with a 10-month history of pain in his lower back, hips, ankles and feet. He has  tried osteopathy, acupuncture and diclofenac, but had no relief. He has also been feeling increasingly tired and  breathless on walking up steep inclines. He had lost 10 kg in the last 6 months despite eating reasonable  meals. He had no dysphagia or night sweats, but does report intermittent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. He  smokes 30 cigarettes/day and drinks two pints of beer 3 times per week. His past history includes  hypothyroidism for which he takes thyroxine, and his mother is a tablet-controlled diabetic.  On examination, his clothes fit loosely and he looks pale. He has no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. He had  normal cardiac, chest and abdominal examinations.  On joint examination, there was pain when moving each joint but no obvious focus of the pain. Chest X-ray is  normal, faecal immunochemical test (FIT) is negative.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  71 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  6.5 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  512 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  136 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.8 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  71 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Urea  4.6 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Corrected calcium (Ca 2+)  1.82 mmol/l  2.20–2.60 mmol/l  Albumin  26 g/l  35–55 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  71.2 fl  76–98 fl  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.5  < 1.1  Parathyroid hormone (PTH)  15 pmol/l  0.9–5.4 pmol/l  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease is common, with a prevalence of 1: 100 and as much as 1: 30 in the west of Ireland. Only onethird of patients present with chronic diarrhoea and steatorrhoea. Malabsorption in this case has caused vitamin  D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism, low albumin, impaired clotting, iron deficiency anaemia and  weight loss. The vitamin D deficiency has led to osteomalacia, causing the presenting feature of lower back and  leg pain. Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common presentation of coeliac disease. Having other autoimmune  conditions in coeliac patients is common, such as hypo/hyperthyroidism and type 1 diabetes mellitus (7%).  B  Metastatic caecal carcinoma  Caecal carcinoma can present with anaemia, although it is much less likely to present with osteomalacia than  coeliac disease.  A  Crohn’s disease  Crohn’s disease is less likely to have an insidious presentation like this with predominant symptoms of  osteomalacia, and is more likely to present with significant diarrhoea and abdominal pain.  D  Whipple disease  Whipple’s disease is associated with diarrhoea and malabsorption, but it is also associated with small joint  polyarthritis and is significantly rarer than coeliac disease.  E  Intestinal lymphangiectasis  Intestinal lymphangiectasia is a protein-losing enteropathy and presents in childhood with symptoms of  malabsorption and peripheral oedema.  A 23-year-old man presents to the Colorectal Clinic with two discrete episodes of haematochezia. He has had  no fresh bleeding per rectum, nor has he been experiencing abdominal pain. He has a healthy lifestyle recently  and denies unintentional weight loss. He has no medical history of note. His father died of colorectal cancer at  the age of 54 and his paternal aunt has a current diagnosis of thyroid cancer.  On examination, his observations are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and a digital  rectal examination reveals no visible cause of his haematochezia.  He is referred for a colonoscopy that shows 15 adenomatous polyps ranging from 3 mm to 1.5 mm.  What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?  A  Adenomatous polyposis coli genetic testing  B  Carcinoembryonic antigen testing  C  CT abdomen  D  Faecal calprotectin  E  Faecal immunochemical testing  Explanation  A    Adenomatous polyposis coli genetic testing  This patient has a likely diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), given the young presentation of  haematochezia and adenomatous polyps on colonoscopy. FAP is an autosomal-dominant condition caused by  mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene causing hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps  throughout the colon. It comes with almost a 100% risk of colorectal cancer if not treated with a prophylactic  pan-colectomy.  The family history of colorectal cancer and associated malignancies with FAP (eg thyroid cancer) makes FAP an  even more likely diagnosis. Colonoscopy and biopsy form the mainstay of investigation for the condition.  However, genetic testing is recommended for patients with ten or more adenomatous polyps on a single  colonoscopy, as it helps to aid the diagnosis and decision for surgical intervention.  E  Faecal immunochemical testing  Faecal immunochemical testing is used in the investigation of colorectal cancer. It detects the presence of blood  within the stool by using antibodies specific for haemoglobin. As this patient is presenting with haematochezia,  this result is likely to be positive. However, it is much more likely that this patient has FAP rather than colorectal  cancer or FAP that has already malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer.  B  Carcinoembryonic antigen testing  Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although  FAP has a very high risk of becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore,  it would not aid in the specific diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal  cancer.  C  CT abdomen  Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although  FAP has a very high risk for becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore,  it would not aid in the specific diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal  cancer.  D  Faecal calprotectin  Faecal calprotectin is used in the investigation of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which is a useful  differential diagnosis to consider given the onset of rectal bleeding at a young age. However, this typically  presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss, and the absence of these features plus the family  history of malignancy makes IBD less likely.

questions.question: A 32-year-old white bar owner returns from Spain and requires emergency consultation in the General  Medicine Clinic. He feels lethargic and has not been able to maintain an adequate erection during intercourse or  masturbation during the past few months. This is causing some marital difficulties. He also complains of  swelling of his ankles and swelling around the abdomen.  On examination, he appears tanned. There is a paucity of underarm and genital hair, and he has evidence of  chronic liver disease and testicular atrophy. Past history of note includes arthritis and joint pain. He admits to  drinking 12 units of alcohol per week (a glass of wine or half a pint of beer).  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Fasting glucose  8.2 mmol/l  < 5.6 mmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  183 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Bilirubin  125 μmol/l  1 - 22 μmol/l  What would be the next best investigation to lead to this patient’s diagnosis?
options: D. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver
E. Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation
questions.explanation:   Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation  Symptoms of haemochromatosis usually begin in men aged between 30 and 50 years and include increased  skin pigmentation (due to iron deposition and melanin), cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, arthropathy, impotence in  men and heart failure. First-line screening involves measuring patients’ serum transferrin saturation and ferritin  levels. Previously, liver biopsy with total hepatic iron estimation was considered the gold standard test for  haemochromatosis. Now, however, genetic screening for the two identified mutations is seen as the next  investigation of choice after transferrin saturation estimation. Around 10% of the Northern European population  are heterozygous for each mutation (so-called compound heterozygotes), and this may account for the  accelerated deterioration of liver function in patients with moderate alcohol intake corresponding to 15–30  standard drinks (units) per week.  C  Liver ultrasound scan  A liver ultrasound scan is not indicated to diagnose haemochromatosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver  is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for the measurement of liver iron deposition in  haemochromatosis.  A  Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c)  This patient has a raised fasting glucose level, which is common in patients with haemochromatosis. Diabetes  occurs in these patients due to iron deposition within the pancreas, affecting endocrine function, and/or liver  cirrhosis. Although diagnosis and treatment of diabetes in these patients are important, HbA1c is not as  accurate due to the increased turnover of red blood cells. Furthermore, HbA1c measurement will not lead to the  diagnosis, making this an incorrect option.  B  Liver FibroScan  Liver FibroScan is used to assess the degree of fibrosis in fatty liver disease, hepatitis and cholestatic disease. It  can be used in haemochromatosis but is not the next best step in confirming this patient’s diagnosis.  D  Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver  This patient likely has haemochromatosis, based on his symptoms, examination and investigation findings.  Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver is a good, non-invasive investigation for measuring liver iron content in  cases of haemochromatosis. However, the first-line investigations which can point toward the diagnosis of  haemochromatosis are ferritin levels and serum transferrin saturations, which are both raised in cases of  haemochromatosis.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man is seen in clinic with a 3-month history of chronic epigastric discomfort. The pain comes and  goes and radiates to his back and his right shoulder tip at times. It is worse after meals but there is no relieving  factor. He feels nauseous most of the time and has foul-smelling stools. He has lost 2 stones in weight. He also  complains of intermittent light-headedness. He drinks a bottle of wine on most nights and smokes 20  cigarettes/day.  On examination, he is thin and looks neglected. His abdomen is soft, but tender on deep palpation in the  epigastric area. He has a 2 cm non-tender liver edge. He also has decreased sensation to light touch on both  feet.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  102 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  12.1 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  462 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  131 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.2 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  64 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Amylase  35 U/l  < 200 U/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  104 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  121 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Bilirubin  24 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Corrected calcium (Ca 2+)  2.01 mmol/l  2.20–2.60 mmol/l  Abdominal X-ray (AXR)  Normal  Oesophago-gastro duodenoscopy  (OGD)  Mild gastritis  Campylobacter-like organisms (CLOs)  -  Ultrasound abdomen  Mildly enlarged liver with fatty  change  Spleen & kidneys  Normal  Pancreas  Partially obscured by overlying bowel  gas  Faecal elastase  110 µg E1/g of stool  200 to > 500 µg E1/g of  stool  He is referred for a secretin test, which reveals the following:  Investigation  Result  Volume collected  110 ml  Bicarbonate  52 mEq/l  What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. Bacterial overgrowth of the gut
questions.explanation:   Chronic pancreatitis  This patient has a history of excess ethanol consumption and chronic abdominal pain. In early disease there  may be no X-ray calcification of the pancreas, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatogram (ERCP) and  computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen can also be normal. Faecal elastase is in the mild-to-moderate  pancreatic insufficiency range, and the most likely diagnosis therefore is chronic pancreatitis. Treatment acutely  is as for acute pancreatitis, but chronic pain control is often difficult and patients become opiate dependent.  Pancreatic enzyme replacement is used. These patients also usually become diabetic and should be monitored  for symptoms of hyperglycaemia such as polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy and dehydration.  B  Bacterial overgrowth of the gut  Bacterial overgrowth syndrome presents with bloating, eructation and intermittent diarrhoea, weight loss is not  as severe as that seen here, and faecal elastase remains in the normal range.  C  Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease is associated with symptoms of malabsorption, positive anti-TTG antibodies, and faecal  elastase remains in the normal range.  D  Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide-secreting tumour (VIPoma)  VIPomas are vanishingly rare and are associated with large-volume diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and dehydration.  The chronic excess alcohol consumption counts towards an alternative diagnosis here.  E  Caecal carcinoma  Caecal carcinoma is often symptomless in the early stages, and presents late with iron deficiency anaemia or  ultimately obstruction, rather than the chronic diarrhoea seen here.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman is referred to the Cardiology Department with intermittent palpitations. She describes  episodes of ‘feeling flushed’ associated with a fluttering feeling in the chest. She denies any chest pain or  breathlessness. There are no risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or any history or rheumatic fever. She is  also suffering from paroxysms of diarrhoea.  On examination she appears well in herself. There are prominent v-waves noted on inspection of the jugular  venous pulse. A pansystolic murmur is audible at the left sternal edge. The chest is clear on auscultation. A  pulsatile liver is felt 2 cm below the costal margin on palpation of the abdomen.  Which of the following investigations is most likely to yield the underlying diagnosis?
options: A. 24 h urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
questions.explanation: 24 h urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)  This patient presents with features of carcinoid syndrome. This is a paraneoplastic syndrome secondary to a  carcinoid tumour. The most common locations for a carcinoid tumour are in gut and arise from the  enterochromaffin cells. Carcinoid tumours secrete serotonin, which is metabolised by the liver. If the carcinoid  tumour metastasises to the liver, serotonin enters the systemic circulation. Release of circulation is associated  with flushing, diarrhoea and bronchoconstriction. Continued serotonin exposure can result in restrictive  cardiomyopathy secondary to fibrosis. This can lead to valvular pathology (in this case the tricuspid valve). 5HIAA is a degradation product of serotonin, which is excreted in the urine. A level of >25 mg per 24 is  diagnostic.  D  Chest X-ray    Carcinoid syndrome can occur secondary to a carcinoid tumour in the lungs (a common extra-GI site for primary  carcinoid tumours). However, the features supporting tricuspid regurgitation point towards a liver metastasis as  the serotonin source. A chest X-ray in this patient may only show non-specific changes or appear normal.  B  Echocardiogram  This patient likely has tricuspid regurgitation secondary to the carcinoid plaques on the tricuspid valvular  apparatus,seen in 50% of cases of serotonin syndrome. The echocardiogram would likely demonstrate these  cardiac abnormalities. However, it is not the investigation of choice to reveal the underlying cause.  C  24 h electrocardiogram (ECG)  Although this patient reports symptoms suggestive of palpitations (‘fluttering feeling in the chest’), there are no  features suggestive of a sinister arrhythmic event. This patient likely has carcinoid syndrome, which does not  commonly affect cardiac conduction.  E  Abdominal ultrasound  This patient has an enlarged liver on clinical examination. This may be due to hepatic metastatic spread of a GI  carcinoid tumour or secondary to the apparent tricuspid regurgitation. An abdominal ultrasound may show a  hepatic tumour, but it is unlikely to be able to differentiate between a carcinoid tumour and a metastatic  adenocarcinoma. Although it is an important investigation, it is unlikely to be the key to the underlying  diagnosis.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man from Bangladesh comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a 6-week history of  weight loss, fever, night sweats and dull abdominal pain. He lives in a rural community in Bangladesh that is  mostly farmland and has been visiting his daughter for the past week. He has a past history of hypertension, for  which he takes nifedipine, but is otherwise well.  On examination, his BP is 105/60 mmHg; his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Marked hepatosplenomegaly is  noted on abdominal palpation. His BMI is 22 kg/m 2.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  89 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  5.4 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  89 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  102 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  188 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  320 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Bilirubin  14 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Albumin  32 g/l  35–55 g/l  Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)  121 IU/l  100–190 IU/l  Prothrombin time (PT)  12.1 s  10.6–14.9 s  Which of the following is the most useful next step with respect to confirming the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Direct agglutination testing  The most likely diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis, typically presenting with the syndrome ‘kala-azar’, which  causes insidious progressive fatigue, weight loss and night sweats, along with splenomegaly and fever.  Anaemia and liver dysfunction are common on baseline blood testing. This travel history from a rural area of  Bangladesh increases the likelihood of sandfly bites that transmit the disease. Direct agglutination testing and  recombinant kinesin antigen (rK39) testing have high levels of sensitivity and specificity. They should be  considered as non-invasive investigative options before moving towards more invasive testing, such as bone  marrow aspiration.  B  Dental scrapings  The most likely diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis. Dental scrapings are usually considered for the diagnosis of  mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, which is not indicated here. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis presents with nasal  symptoms, mucosal bleeding and increased secretions.  A  Bone marrow aspiration  Bone marrow aspiration could be considered in myeloproliferative conditions. However, the normal LDH level  and travel history are pointers against this. There is the added risk of complications of bone marrow aspiration  that should not be taken lightly.  D  Liver biopsy  Liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis but is not the most useful next step. It should be considered in  cases where clinical suspicion is high and direct agglutination testing has not been suggestive of the diagnosis.  There is the added risk of bleeding associated with this procedure and this should not be taken lightly.  E  Splenic aspiration  Splenic aspiration biopsy, although it would provide a definitive diagnosis, is not the most useful next step in  the management of this patient. It should be considered in cases where clinical suspicion is high and direct  agglutination testing has not been suggestive of a diagnosis. There is the added risk of bleeding associated  A 32-year-old nurse presents with iron deficiency anaemia. She prefers mainly white meat and fish but claims  that her diet is sufficiently varied. She also reports frequent diarrhoea and weight loss of 6 kg in the past year.  On examination, her BMI is 22, but no other abnormalities are found.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  104 g/l  115–155 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  80 fl  76–98 fl  Serum ferritin  14 µg/l  10–120 µg/l  Serum folate  1.4 µg/l  2.0–11.0 µg/l  Albumin  34 g/l  35–55 g/l  Immunoglobulin G (IgG)  15 g/l  5–16 g/l  IgA  3.8 g/l  1.0–4.0 g/l  IgM  2.6 g/l  0.5–2.0 g/l  An OGD is performed, which shows some mild duodenitis. Small bowel biopsies are taken and are reported as  showing subtotal villous atrophy.  What is the most likely diagnosis?  A  Coeliac disease  B  Crohn’s disease  C  Small bowel lymphoma  D  Whipple’s disease  E  Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth  Explanation  A    Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease is characterised by diarrhoea and malabsorption precipitated by sensitivity to gliadin, a protein  fraction of gluten found in wheat, rye, barley and oats. Peaks of incidence occur in the third and seventh  decades, there is a slight female preponderance and incidence is increased in Caucasian populations. Diagnosis  is made by testing for tissue transglutaminase antibody (TTG) or small bowel biopsy, which shows the classical  appearance of subtotal villous atrophy. Coeliac is also an important cause of iron deficiency anaemia caused by  malabsorption of iron, as seen in this patient. Therefore, Option A is correct as it best fits the clinical picture and  biopsy findings. Note that this patient has a normocytic anaemia, as she is both iron deficient (microcytic) and  folate deficient (macrocytic) giving an overall normocytic picture. Treatment for coeliac is avoidance of glutencontaining foods.  C  Small bowel lymphoma  This is extremely rare, and usually occurs in older individuals and one would expect to see abnormal plasma  cells on biopsy such as abnormal T-cell proliferation.  B  Crohn’s disease  Although this can cause villous atrophy of the small bowel, the classical biopsy findings are non-caseating  granulomas and transmural inflammation. This may also be associated with aphthous ulcers in the mouth.  D  Whipple’s disease  This is a rare malabsorptive disease caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei and occurs in conjunction  with neurological, cardiac or rheumatological sequelae. This patient did not elicit any of these symptoms.  E  Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth  This usually gives a high folate as a result of bacterial synthesis, and is more commonly associated with  patients who have diabetes or other autoimmune conditions such as scleroderma.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman was admitted via the Emergency Department complaining of intermittent epigastric pain.  She had had a cholecystectomy 1 year ago for these symptoms but continued to have pain after the procedure.  The pain was severe, typically coming on when she was eating, radiating to the back and was accompanied by  nausea and sometimes vomiting. It tended to last for several hours and did not vary in intensity. She has had  five such attacks over the last year.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal Values  Bilirubin  21 µmol/l  1 - 22 µmol/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  100 u/l  10 - 40 u/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  110 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  176 u/l  30 - 150 u/l  Amylase  220 u/l  23 - 65 u/l  An ultrasound scan showed a moderately dilated common bile duct (12 mm) but no stones were seen.  Consequently, she underwent an endoscopic retrograde cholangiogram which, again showed mildly dilated  ducts. A sphincterotomy was performed along with trawling of the bile duct, again revealing no cause. Postprocedure she developed acute pancreatitis from which she recovered with conservative management.  Subsequently, her symptoms resolved.  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction  The symptoms described by this woman and her response to sphincterotomy are characteristic of sphincter of  Oddi dysfunction (SOD), which causes non-calculous obstruction of flow of biliary and/or pancreatic fluid.  In SOD, the sphincter is hypertonic (>40 mmHg on manometry) and may also be dyskinetic. SOD typically  occurs in middle-aged women, but may present in any age group, including children. The usual presenting  symptoms are those of biliary-type pain, i.e. epigastric or right hypochondrial pain that is severe, steady and  may radiate to the back or shoulder.  Since the symptoms of SOD are usually so similar to that of gallstone disease, the diagnosis of SOD is often  only made after cholecystectomy. SOD may also manifest as recurrent episodes of apparently idiopathic  pancreatitis, but jaundice is rare.  There are three categories of SOD:  Type I: People with typical biliary pain, abnormal liver enzymes and radiological evidence of impaired  biliary drainage  Type II: People with typical biliary pain, with either abnormal liver enzymes or radiological evidence of  impaired biliary drainage  Type III: People with typical biliary pain, but no other abnormalities.  Definitive diagnosis of SOD is made by manometry, although delayed drainage of contrast at ERCP is also a  classic sign (>45 min). Rates of post-ERCP pancreatitis are increased five-fold in people with SOD.  Treatment of SOD with smooth muscle relaxants (such as nifedipine) improves symptoms in a proportion of  affected people, but at rates similar to placebo overall. Endoscopic sphincterotomy is often effective in treating  people with type I SOD, and may help people with type II SOD, but is usually of no benefit in people with type  III SOD. Botulinum toxin injection into the sphincter of Oddi may have a role in treatment, particularly for people  with type III SOD.  E  Primary sclerosing cholangitis  Primary sclerosing cholangitis only typically causes biliary pain in the presence of cholangitis, and is associated  with a beaded pattern to the biliary tree on cholangiography.  A  Recurrent biliary stones  Recurrent biliary stones may be ruled out given that none were seen on her ERCP.  B  Non-ulcer dyspepsia  Non-ulcer dyspepsia does not explain this woman’s abnormal liver enzymes and imaging findings.  C  Chronic pancreatitis  No typical risk factors for chronic pancreatitis are given, and it is unusual for chronic pancreatitis to cause such  marked biliary dilatation.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man visited his general practitioner (GP) some 10 days after returning from holiday with his  friends in Turkey. He admitted to drinking up to 10 pints of lager per day during his 2-week holiday and  frequently bought food from street sellers.  Since his holiday, he has given up smoking as he said he did not enjoy it any more. There was a history of  paracetamol use in the past few days for a sprained ankle sustained when slipping in the street, and there was  some concern that he may have taken a couple of extra tablets while on holiday. Most recently, he has been  suffering from fever and anorexia.  On examination, he was jaundiced.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Bilirubin  345 μmol/l  1 - 22 μmol/l  Aspartate aminotransaminase (AST)  400 u/l  10 - 40 u/l  Which of the following investigations is most likely to give the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Hepatitis serology  It seems likely that this man has an acute hepatitis. This is unlikely to be an acute alcohol-related phenomenon  as he has taken some 10 days to present. The clue is in his visit to Turkey, where he is likely to have been  exposed to hepatitis A. This is the commonest cause of viral hepatitis worldwide, transmitted via the faeco-oral  route, and is associated with non-specific symptoms such as nausea, anorexia and distaste for cigarettes.  Hepatitis A is not associated with progression to chronic liver disease. During the convalescent period, 5–15%  of patients may have relapses of their hepatitis but these resolve spontaneously. Occasionally a more severe  jaundice with prolonged cholestasis may occur over the course of 7–20 weeks. Mortality (due to fulminant  hepatic necrosis) is rare at around 0.1%, but increases with age.  C  Paracetamol level  In a patient presenting 10 days after his holiday, paracetamol levels are not of value in determining whether  excess paracetamol during the trip contributed to his symptoms.  A  Conjugated bilirubin  Given that transaminases are elevated, Gilbert’s disease can be ruled out as a cause of his symptoms.  B  Clotting screen  Although this man has acute hepatitis, synthetic liver function is highly unlikely to be affected and clotting won’t  reveal an underlying cause of liver disease.  E  Serum ammonia  Serum ammonia is most useful in the evaluation of hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.question: A 40-year-old farmer is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward with a 3-week history of intermittent  abdominal pain, nausea, reduced appetite and 5 kg weight loss. He had no past medical history of note and has  no allergies.  On examination, his temperature is 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 99 bpm and a BP of 119/60 mmHg. There is  tenderness in the right upper quadrant with palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
