Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  140 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.7 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Neutrophils  4.6 × 10 9/l  1.8–7.5 × 10 9/l  Lymphocytes  4.5 × 10 9/l  1.0–4.0× 10 9/l  Eosinophils  1.6 × 10 9/l  0.1–0.4× 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  140 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.5 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  6.5 mmol/l  1.8–7.1 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  109 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  An ultrasound scan (USS) liver is requested:    What is the recommended management of this patient?
questions.explanation:   Albendazole and surgical resection  This patient likely has hydatid disease, given the symptoms of abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia and weight  loss, in addition to findings of eosinophilia and multiple liver cysts on ultrasound imaging. Hydatid disease is a  zoonotic infection caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus which is commonly transmitted by infected  dogs and foxes. Contact with animals is a risk factor for the infection and the occupational history of being a  farmer is significant in this instance. Importantly, unlike other causes of hepatic cysts (eg amoebic liver abscess),  hydatid disease can remain asymptomatic for some time before being diagnosed. Treatment of hydatid disease  involves a combination of albendazole, corticosteroids and surgical resection to ensure complete clearance of  the infection.  Image source: By R. Badea and Simona Ioanitescu, (CC BY 3.0), CC BY 3.0,  https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=65099337  A  Amphotericin B  Amphotericin B is a potent antifungal agent used in the treatment of invasive Candida albicans and  Cryptococcus neoformans. Fungal infections do not typically cause eosinophilia as seen in this patient. Rather, it  is much more likely that the patient is suffering from a parasitic infection (eg helminth) for which amphotericin B  has no efficacy.  B  Mebendazole  Mebendazole is used in the management of parasitic infections, particularly threadworm, hookworm and  roundworm. In contrast, albendazole is more commonly used in the management of hydatid disease with  mebendazole reserved as the second line. Nevertheless, surgical cyst removal is generally necessary, making  an antiparasitic agent used in isolation less likely to achieve complete clearance.  C  Metronidazole  Metronidazole is an antibacterial agent with good activity against anaerobic bacteria. Therefore, it is generally a  useful antibiotic to treat intra-abdominal infections. Metronidazole is also used to treat amoebic liver abscesses  which can present very similarly to hydatid disease. However, some distinguishing factors include eosinophilia  and the presence of multiple cystic liver lesions (representing daughter cysts) which are more common in  hydatid disease. In contrast, an amoebic liver abscess is a smooth cystic mass without numerous daughter  cysts.  D  Praziquantel  Praziquantel is used in the treatment of helminthic infections including intestinal tapeworm infection. However,  hepatic disease requires alternative forms of treatment including albendazole and surgical resection.

questions.question: A 45-year-old banker is referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver function tests. He had a heart  attack 2 years ago and is regularly seen in the Diabetic Clinic for poor glycaemic control. He currently takes  metformin, atenolol and atorvastatin. He drinks socially and smokes 10 cigarettes per day. There is no history of  blood transfusion or drug abuse.  On examination, he is overweight and there is an enlarged, non-tender liver. Ultrasound scan of the liver is  reported as showing a generalised, hyper-echogenic appearance with no focal lesions.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  130 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  8.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  240 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  83 fl  76–98 fl  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.1  < 1.1  Sodium (Na +)  136 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.7 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  9.0 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  90 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  39 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  96 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  70 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  135 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Hepatitis and autoimmune serology  Negative  Ferritin  Normal  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis  Most patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) are asymptomatic. The condition is usually discovered  incidentally after abnormal liver tests. Diffuse fatty change can be detected on ultrasonography as a hyperechogenic appearance. It is part of a metabolic syndrome and is commonly associated with obesity, diabetes  mellitus, hypercholesterolaemia and drugs. In patients with NASH, the ratio of aspartate aminotransferase  (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is usually <1, whereas in alcoholic liver disease the ratio is usually >2.  Liver biopsy reveals macrovesicular steatosis. Treatment is that of underlying cause, encouraging moderate  weight loss, exercise, improved diabetic control, treatment of hyperlipidaemia and avoidance of alcohol.  Bariatric surgery is perhaps the best therapeutic modality in the presence of severe obesity.  A  Drug-induced hepatitis  While statins can cause abnormal liver function tests, the history does not suggest that this has been recently  commenced. Furthermore, a true drug-induced hepatitis would likely result in a more marked rise in liver  enzymes. Given the risk factors, and ultrasound findings suggestive of fatty change, non-alcoholic  steatohepatitis is a better answer.  C  Alcoholic-induced hepatitis  The history does not suggest that the patient drinks alcohol to excess, and the ratio of aspartate  aminotransferase (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is <1, suggestive more of NASH than alcoholic liver  disease, where the ratio is usually >2.  D  Chronic active hepatitis  There are no particular risk factors given in the history, and viral serology is negative.  E  Amyloidosis  Hepatic amyloidosis occurs in the setting of primary (AL) or secondary (AA) amyloidosis. Hepatomegaly is  present in 80% of patients, but one would expect the presentation to include other signs and symptoms of  systemic illness such as weight loss, abdominal pain, anorexia, ascites, peripheral oedema and splenomegaly.  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is frequently raised. Ultrasonographic findings of hepatic amyloidosis include  heterogeneous echogenicity. The diagnosis of gastrointestinal amyloid requires a tissue biopsy with positive  staining of amyloid by Congo red or the presence of amyloid fibrils on electron microscopy.

questions.question: A concerned 29-year-old woman attends her general practitioner (GP) practice complaining of two days of  painless rectal bleeding. There has been no change in her bowel habit. She denies any other constitutive  symptoms and has no significant travel history. She is particularly concerned since her mother, who is 48 years  old, has recently been diagnosed with cancer of the bowel. On further questioning, it appears that her maternal  grandfather also died after suffering from bowel cancer.  The GP suspects that there may be an inherited tendency towards this disease and is especially concerned  about familial adenomatous polyposis.  What physical feature is most commonly found in this condition?
options: A. Hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:   Hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium  Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by the presence of  hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. There is a wide phenotypic spectrum of FAP, with all  phenotypes having an underlying germ-line mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene. The average age  of the polyposis is 16 years, with all patients having this syndrome developing colon cancer if left untreated.  The average age of onset of colorectal cancer is 39 years. Physical features associated with this condition  include congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, dental abnormalities including supernumerary  teeth and dentigerous cysts, osteomas of the skull and mandible, and fibromas and epidermoid cysts in  prepubescent patients.  D  Cutaneous lipomas  Lipomas per se are not associated with increased risk of cancer, although weight gain is associated with a range  of cancers including colon and breast cancer, which are linked to increased insulin resistance.  B  Early onset cataracts  Early onset cataracts may be associated with decreased antioxidative activity, and have been shown in  epidemiological studies to be associated with increased risk of head and neck cancer and hepatoma.  C  Axillary freckling  Axillary freckling is identified in hereditary non-polyposis cancer, rather than FAP.  E  Pre-auricular skin tags  Abnormalities of the ear cartilage are more commonly associated with renal and cardiac abnormalities. They are  not thought to be associated with increased risk of colonic polyps.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with known rheumatoid arthritis complains of generalised pruritis.  On examination, she is mildly jaundiced and has periorbital xanthelasmata. Abdominal palpation reveals  hepatomegaly 2 cm below the right costal margin. She has no lymphadenopathy.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  112 g/l  115–155 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  89 fl  76–98 fl  White cell count (WCC)  4.6 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  310 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  34 mm/hour  1–20 mm/hour  Albumin  30 g/l  35–55 g/l  Bilirubin  30 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  260 IU/l  30–130 IU/  Which of the following tests would be most useful?
questions.explanation:   M 2 subtype anti-mitochondrial antibody  Primary biliary cholangitis is a slowly progressive inflammation and destruction of the intrahepatic ducts  leading to eventual cirrhosis. The cause is unknown but it is thought to be an autoimmune disease, and there is  a strong association with other autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome and  CREST syndrome. Most patients are diagnosed between the ages of 40 and 70 years, and 90% of patients are  female.  D  M 5 subtype anti-mitochondrial antibody  Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are found in over 90% of patients, the M 2 subtype being specific. Therefore M 5 is  not the most specific for primary biliary cholangitis.  B  Anti-smooth muscle antibody  Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic hepatitis characterised by immunologic and auto-immunologic features,  generally including the presence of circulating auto-antibodies and a high total serum gamma globulin, usually  confined to the IgG fraction. The main circulating auto-antibodies, although not specific for the disease, are  antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) in type 1 disease and, in type 2  autoimmune hepatitis, anti-liver-kidney microsome-1 antibodies (ALKM-1) and anti-liver cytosol antibody-1  (ALC-1). In this case, it is primary biliary cholangitis that we are wanting to diagnose so anti-smooth muscle  antibody is not particularly useful.  C  Hepatitis serology  Hepatitis serology is negative in primary biliary cholangitis and there is no association.  E  Serum electrophoresis  Serum electrophoresis is abnormal in disorders such as multiple myeloma, but not in primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman is being investigated for intermittent dysphagia and has had a normal upper  gastrointestinal endoscopy. She undergoes oesophageal manometry and some of the results are outlined  below. She has symptoms of Raynaud’s, and some skin thickening over her hands, but no other significant  medical problems.  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure  8 mmHg  17 - 36 mmHg  Residual lower oesophageal sphincter relaxing pressure  7 mmHg  < 8 mmHg  Peristalsis:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Proximal amplitude  80 mmHg  33 - 91 mmHg  Distal amplitude  25 mmHg  64 - 154 mmHg  Which one of the following is the most likely diagnoses?
questions.explanation: Scleroderma    The finding of a low resting lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure is a requirement for a diagnosis of  scleroderma-associated dysmotility. It may also be found in the hypocontractile oesophagus associated with  reflux disease. However, in the presence of skin thickening and symptoms of Raynaud’s, the most likely  diagnosis is systemic sclerosis.  D  Achalasia  Absent distal peristalsis, high resting LOS pressures and failure of LOS relaxation would be expected in cases  of achalasia.  B  Diffuse oesophageal spasm  This is a condition characterised by uncoordinated oesophageal contractions, which can lead to pain on eating,  dysphagia and regurgitation in some cases.  C  Globus  Globus is a psychological condition which would only be diagnosed in the absence of abnormal finding on  investigation.  E  Non-specific oesophageal dysmotility  This is a disorder of peristalsis but would not be associated with the other features of systemic sclerosis  (thickened skin and Raynaud’s) that are present in this case.

questions.question: A 46-year-old Malaysian woman with hepatitis C-related liver cirrhosis is seen in clinic for her 6-monthly  follow-up. She remains well and a surveillance ultrasound shows two small focal lesions in the liver. Her  alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is 78 ng/ml (10–20). It was 30 ng/ml six months ago. Spiral computed tomography scan  of the liver and thorax confirms two liver lesions, both measuring 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm and no pulmonary lesions.  What is the most definitive way to manage these two liver lesions?
options: C. Percutaneous ethanol injection of the lesions
D. Trans-catheter embolization of the lesions
questions.explanation:   Liver transplantation  The only proven potentially curative therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains surgical, either hepatic  resection or liver transplantation. Liver transplantation should be considered in any patient with cirrhosis and a  single small HCC (<5 cm) or up to three lesions (<3 cm). Hepatic resection should be considered as a primary  therapy in any patient with HCC and non-cirrhotic liver. A rising alpha-fetoprotein indicative of a hepatoma and  biopsy is not always necessary to avoid seeding of tumour.  D  Trans-catheter embolization of the lesions  Chemo-embolisation can produce tumour necrosis and has been shown to affect survival in highly selected  patients with good liver reserve, although in this case it would only be considered if liver transplantation was  not an option.  A  Partial hepatic resection  This is not advised because of the potential to generate new areas of dysplasia within the remaining abnormal  liver.  C  Percutaneous ethanol injection of the lesions  Percutaneous ethanol injection has been shown to produce necrosis of small HCC and is best suited for  peripheral lesions. Given the two lesions here are small, liver transplantation if possible is the preferred  intervention.  E  Intravenous interferon  Systemic therapies including interferon have a poor response rate in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma  and would not be curative. Transplant is therefore preferred.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man presents to accident and emergency complaining of a 4-day history of upper abdominal  pain which radiates to his back, along with nausea and diarrhoea. He has been admitted to hospital twice in the  past 8 months with similar symptoms and has lost approximately 5 kg in weight over this time.  His past medical history includes hypertension, gastric ulceration and a partial gastrectomy 12 years ago. His  current medication includes atenolol 50 mg once daily and omeprazole 20 mg once daily.  The following blood results were obtained:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  White cell count (WCC)  12.6 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Haemoglobin (Hb)  124 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  112 fl  80 - 100 fl  Platelets (PLT)  110 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  135 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.2 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Urea  2.4 mmol/l  2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  64 mmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Corrected calcium (Ca 2+)  2.24 mmol/l  2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  64 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  250 u/l  30 - 150 u/l  Bilirubin  26 μmol/l  1 - 22 μmol/l  Albumin  30 g/l  35 - 55 g/l  Random glucose  18 mmol/l  3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l  3-day faecal fat excretion 21 g/day = 63 g total (normal < 30 g/3 days)  Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:   Alcohol abuse  In view of this man’s history, the most likely diagnosis is recurrent pancreatitis secondary to alcohol abuse or  gallstones. Alcohol is a cause of chronic pancreatitis, whereas gallstones may be associated with recurrent  acute pancreatitis. Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis and sclerosing  cholangitis. Chronic pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition which is characterised by irreversible damage to  both the exocrine and endocrine pancreas. This patient’s faecal fat excretion is high (> 30 g/3 days) indicating  pancreatic enzyme insufficiency. This is further supported by an elevated random glucose consistent with a  diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Initial further investigations in this patient should include abdominal ultrasound  and, if indicated, abdominal CT or MRCP.. Chronic pancreatitis is treated with pancreatic enzyme  supplementation and complete abstention from alcohol. Approximately 60% of patients survive two years.  B  Haemochromatosis  There is an absence of other symptoms of haemochromatosis including increased pigmentation, endocrine  dysfunction and costochondritis, and presentation at an age earlier than 64 years would be expected.  C  Sclerosing cholangitis  Primary sclerosing cholangitis is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and usually presents at  an earlier age than 64 years.  D  Gastric carcinoma  Gastric carcinoma is less likely as the underlying diagnosis, given very gradual weight loss over the past 8  months, and no symptoms suggestive of gastric obstruction.  E  Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease is a possible differential, but given the duration of symptoms, more pronounced anaemia and  associated conditions such as dermatitis herpetiformis would be expected.

questions.question: A 31-year-old previously fit and healthy woman is knocked over by a cyclist on the pedestrian crossing. She is  admitted to hospital and has an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan. This shows that the spleen and  liver are normal except for a cyst in the pancreas. The cyst shows features of a 1 cm serous cystadenoma.  Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: D. Resection of tail of pancreas
questions.explanation:   Do nothing  Serous cystadenomas (SCAs) are benign tumours of the pancreas commonly picked up on imaging. They are  rarely >2 cm and usually remain benign, and therefore do not require follow-up. The differential in this case  would be a mucinous cystadenoma, which has malignant potential (in about 25% of cases). CT and MRCP can  differentiate between the two but occasionally EUS with FNA of serous fluid may be required. High levels of  CEA are typically observed in a mucinous cystadenoma (but are normal in a serous cystadenoma). The  international consensus guidelines (2012) recommend all mucinous cystadenomas should be resected.  Other cystic lesions of the pancreas that may be noted incidentally include intraductal papillary mucinous  neoplasm (IPMN), which also has a malignant potential and requires MRCP surveillance; pancreatic  pseudocysts (in a patient with a history of pancreatitis); retention cysts (simple cysts, seen in association with  Von Hippel–Lindau disease and polycystic kidney disease); and papillary cystic neoplasm (typically seen in  young females, in the tail or body of the pancreas).  Reference: Tanaka et al. Pancreatology 12 (2012): 183–197.  E  Resection of whole pancreas  There is no malignant potential of SCAs. Pancreatectomy would be considered in mucinous cytadenoma or in  IPMN with high-risk radiological features (see consensus guidelines mentioned above).  B  Annual follow-up  As there is no malignant potential of SCAs, this is not recommended. Annual follow-up is recommended for  patients with low-risk or stable IPMNs with MRCP and clinical examination.  C  Resection of cyst alone  This is not recommended as there is no malignant potential for SCAs. A mucinous cystadenoma would be  resected, but pancreatectomy with lymph node dissection remains the standard of care in these cases.  D  Resection of tail of pancreas  There is no malignant potential for SCAs. This option could be considered in a patient with a papillary cystic  adenoma, as this tends to occur in the pancreatic tail and metastasis is rare.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive intermittent dysphagia to both solids and  liquids, and a persistent productive cough. He is a long-term smoker but otherwise is fit and well; he reports no  significant weight loss.  Clinical examination is unremarkable and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy report from another hospital is  normal.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Bilirubin  19 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  22 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  31 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Albumin  42 g/l  35–55 g/l  Haemoglobin (Hb)  148 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  9.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  258 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure  60mmHg  17–36 mmHg  Residual lower oesophageal sphincter relaxing pressure  12mmHg  < 8 mmHg  Peristalsis reveals the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Proximal amplitude  80 mmHg  33–91 mmHg  Proximal duration  3s  2.0–3.6 s  Distal amplitude  0 mmHg  64–154mmHg  Distal duration  Absent  2.9–5.1 s  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Achalasia  Achalasia describes a failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, and affects an estimated 10 in  10,000 people. Endoscopy is often normal but can show lower oesophageal dilatation and failure of the lower  oesophageal sphincter (LOS) to relax. The hallmark feature of manometry is absence of peristalsis in the distal  oesophagus, accompanied by failure of the LOS to relax during swallowing (i.e. a high residual relaxing  pressure). These features may be accompanied by a high resting LOS pressure, but this is not necessary for a  diagnosis. Achalasia often causes intermittent symptoms, with residual food and liquid in the distal oesophagus  causing halitosis and recurrent chest sepsis due to nocturnal aspiration.  B  Nutcracker oesophagus  Nutcracker oesophagus is an oesophageal dysmotility disorder characterised by dysphagia of both liquids and  solids, with chest pain. In nutcracker oesophagus, there is oesophageal pressure exceeding 180 mmHg, which  this patient does not have.  A  Scleroderma  Scleroderma is an autoimmune connective tissue disorder which causes fibrosis of organs. It can cause fibrosis  of the oesophagus leading to dysphagia, but is unlikely without other features such as calcinosis, Raynaud’s,  sclerodactyly and telangiectasis. Scleroderma can also lead to reduced or occasionally absent distal peristalsis,  but this is accompanied by low resting LOS pressures.  C  Diffuse oesophageal spasm  Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes intermittent dysphagia and chest pain. A barium swallow can differentiate  from achalasia by demonstrating abnormal oesophageal contractions such as a corkscrew pattern. In this  patient there is interruption of peristalsis, which does not fit.  D  Carcinoma of the oesophagus  Oesophageal cancer is associated with male gender, smoking history, oesophageal reflux, Barrett’s oesophagus  and achalasia. Management is via an MDT approach. The presence of intermittent rather than progressive  dysphagia makes this unlikely, as does the abnormal manometry.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of chronic diarrhoea. She underwent an extensive small  bowel resection for Crohn’s disease 2 years earlier and has not been well since.  On examination, she has a BMI of 17, with multiple scars on the abdomen. Additionally she is suffering from  dermatitis, glossitis and angular stomatitis.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  104 g/l  115–155 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  106 fl  76–98 fl  White cell count (WCC)  5.6 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  232 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  12 mm/hour  < 10 mm/hour  Sodium (Na +)  139 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.9 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  100 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  29 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  52 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Short bowel syndrome  Short bowel syndrome has many causes, but in adult patients it is usually the result of extensive surgery  undertaken for either Crohn’s disease or mesenteric infarction. We can see from the patient’s blood results that  she has a macrocytic anaemia, likely indicating a failure to absorb B 12. Her low albumin of 29 also suggests  significant malabsorption. Dermatitis is a feature of failure to absorb essential fatty acids (linoleic acid and  linolenic acid). These patients also commonly exhibit dehydration and signs of hypovolaemia due to extensive  gastrointestinal fluid losses. In some individuals adequate oral intake may be impossible; parenteral nutrition  may be the only option, but is associated with significant long-term morbidity and mortality.  A  Reactivated Crohn’s disease  The fact that the patient has a low ESR level makes a diagnosis of active inflammation unlikely. The chronicity  of her symptoms going back 2 years also makes an exacerbation of her Crohn’s less likely as the answer here.  B  Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease more often presents with generalised symptoms of tiredness, weight loss and iron deficiency  anaemia, though it can present with features of florid malabsorption in severe cases. However, given that we  already know that this patient has had an extensive small bowel resection, that represents a far more likely  explanation for her clinical picture.  D  Bacterial overgrowth  Bacterial overgrowth tends to present with chronic diarrhoea and/or steatorrhoea with anaemia. Given that both  Crohn’s disease and extensive small bowel resection can predispose to the condition, it should certainly be  considered in this case. However, the fact that the patient has evidence of chronic malabsorption is more easily  explained by a loss of surface area for digestion and absorption caused by short bowel syndrome.  E  Cryptosporidium infection  Cryptosporidium is a protozoal parasite and generally causes a short illness with voluminous watery diarrhoea  and abdominal cramps. The exception is in severely immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS,  where it can develop into a serious chronic condition with persistent severe diarrhoea and weight loss. We are  given nothing in the history to suggest that degree of severe immunocompromise in this patient.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of lower abdominal pain for the  past day that has worsened over the past few hours. He had two episodes of vomiting on his way to the  hospital.  On examination, his blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 108 bpm. Abdominal palpation  revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa. There was no guarding or rigidity. After further radiological  examination, the patient was taken up for surgery and the surgical specimen is shown below.    Which of the following is the most likely pathology in this patient?
options: A. Infection of the terminal ileum resulting in granuloma formation
B. Inflammation of a congenital outpouching of the small intestine
D. Inflammatory bowel disease with stricture formation
E. Salmonella enteritis resulting in perforation
questions.explanation: Inflammation of a congenital outpouching of the small intestine  This is descriptive of Meckel’s diverticulitis. The surgical specimen shows the presence of a Meckel’s  diverticulum, which is the most common congenital abnormality of the small intestine. The most common  presentation is with bleeding, followed by diverticulitis which can be confused with appendicitis. In a large    majority of cases, Meckel’s diverticulum may be incidentally found during surgery. A computed tomography (CT)  abdomen may be helpful in the diagnosis, whereas a Meckel scan with technetium-99m pertechnetate may be  more accurate in identifying it.  Image Source: Milliways, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons  D  Inflammatory bowel disease with stricture formation  This is descriptive of Crohn’s disease, which presents with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, rather than with  the acute presentation seen here. Besides, there are no strictures observed in the gross specimen presented  here.  A  Infection of the terminal ileum resulting in granuloma formation  This is descriptive of ileocaecal tuberculosis, which usually does not have such an acute presentation. Besides,  an outpouching of the small intestine is suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum.  C  Inflammation of the appendix  This is descriptive of acute appendicitis. However, the gross specimen shows an outpouching of the small  intestine in the anti-mesenteric border, suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum.  E  Salmonella enteritis resulting in perforation  Typhoid due to Salmonella infection can cause longitudinal ulcers which may result in intestinal perforation.  However, intestinal perforation usually occurs after more than two weeks of illness. Besides, there is no  evidence of perforation in the gross specimen shown here.

questions.question: A 35-year-old Iraqi student was admitted to the Emergency Department on a number of occasions with  abdominal pain associated with arthralgia and fever.  Previous medical history included appendicectomy and cholecystitis. Pain was often associated with  constipation that became diarrhoea when the pain resolved.  Clinical examination revealed a pyrexia of 38.5 °C, with generalised rebound tenderness in the abdomen and  diminished bowel sounds. Bilateral swollen knees were noted and clear fluid was aspirated from each joint.  Computed tomography (CT) examination was unremarkable.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  135 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  300 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Bilirubin  10 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  16 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  21 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Albumin  40 g/l  35–55 g/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  72 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  50 mm/hour  1–20 mm/hour  Synovial fluid  No organisms  Urinalysis  Protein+++  Urinary porphyrins  Normal  Males: 135–175 g/l  What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Familial Mediterranean fever Females: 115–155 g/l
questions.explanation:   Familial Mediterranean fever  Familial Mediterranean fever is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by sporadic paroxysmal attacks of  fever and serosal inflammation. Patients are recurrently admitted to hospital and undergo extensive  investigation and often abdominal surgery, but no specific pathology is found. Constipation accompanying the  fever is common and diarrhoea may follow its resolution. Synovitis has been reported in up to 75% of patients.  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are elevated, and serosal (peritoneal or pleural) or  synovial fluid may show large numbers of neoutrophils with no organisms. Amyloidosis manifesting as  proteinuria can occur, particularly in Sephardic (Middle Eastern and North African) Jews. Therefore, Option A is  the best answer here. A specific genetic test is now available to aid diagnosis, and the treatment of choice is  colchicine.  B  Crohn’s disease  It could explain many of these symptoms, including the abdominal pain with associated joint pains, as Crohn’s is  associated with extra-intestinal manifestations such as arthritis. However, this patient has a fever and, in the  context of Crohn’s disease, you would be concerned about an abscess or another complication of Crohn’s such  as a perforation, which would usually be apparent on a CT scan.  C  Acute intermittent porphyria  Normal urinary porphyrins effectively rule out acute intermittent porphyria.  D  Adult Still’s disease  This condition is usually associated with a classic salmon-coloured rash and a raised ferritin. Splenomegaly can  also be present.  E  Irritable bowel syndrome  A 62-year-old man presents to the Colorectal Clinic for a review of his test results. He had presented earlier  that year with a 6-month history of lower abdominal pain and constipation. An urgent CT scan of the abdomen  and pelvis shows an ill-defined mass in the lower rectum measuring 30 mm × 28 mm × 16 mm. A diagnosis of  stage 2a colorectal adenocarcinoma is made.  He has no significant past medical history of note and is normally fit and active. In the clinic today, the patient is  keen to explore treatment options.  What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?  A  Adjuvant chemotherapy following surgery  B  Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery  C  Observation with close surveillance  D  Palliative chemotherapy without surgery  E  Surgical resection alone  Explanation  E    Surgical resection alone  Surgical resection is the mainstay of treatment for stage 2a colorectal cancer, aiming for complete removal of  the tumour with clear margins. Adjuvant chemotherapy is not routinely indicated in stage 2a disease, unless  specific high-risk features are present. However, chemotherapy would be considered in stages 2b and 2c.  D  Palliative chemotherapy without surgery  This would not be suitable for stage 2a colorectal cancer, which is potentially curable with surgery. Palliative  chemotherapy is typically reserved for advanced or metastatic disease where surgery is not a curative option.  Given that this patient is relatively young with a good performance status, surgery should most definitively be  considered as an option for managing his cancer.  A  Adjuvant chemotherapy following surgery  This is not the most appropriate initial management for stage 2a colorectal cancer. Adjuvant chemotherapy is  generally not recommended for stage 2a disease, unless there are high-risk features such as poor histological  differentiation or lymphovascular invasion. It would be considered in later stages of the disease such as stages  2b, 2c and 3.  B  Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery  This would not be appropriate for stage 2a colorectal cancer, as neoadjuvant chemotherapy is typically reserved  for locally advanced (stage 3) or metastatic (stage 4) disease. Stage 2a patients usually undergo surgery as  primary treatment without neoadjuvant therapy.  C  Observation with close surveillance  While surveillance is important following treatment for colorectal cancer, including stage 2a disease,  observation alone without surgical intervention is not appropriate as it does not address the primary tumour.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a long history of diabetes and previous cerebrovascular accident is admitted with early  satiety, postprandial vomiting and abdominal distension. There is no history of haematemesis or abdominal  pain. He opens his bowels regularly. He is on insulin therapy, digoxin and aspirin.  On examination, he is overweight and he is in atrial fibrillation. His abdomen is distended and tympanic, but is  otherwise soft and non-tender with active bowel sounds. Rectal examination reveals soft brown stool.  Neurology examination reveals a residual right-sided paralysis.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  134 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  12.7 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  319 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  133 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.1 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  117 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  81 fl  80 - 100 fl  International normalized ratio (INR)  1.2  < 1.1  Urea  10.4 mmol/l  2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l  Albumin  36 g/l  35 - 55 g/l  Corrected calcium (Ca 2+)  2.06 mmol/l  2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l  Glucose  11.2 mmol/l  3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l  Chest X-ray  Normal  Abdominal X-ray  Dilated stomach  Upper GI endoscopy is normal.  Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
options: D. Trial of a gastric pacemaker
questions.explanation:   Trial of domperidone  Gastric motility is frequently affected in diabetes mellitus, with a reported prevalence of gastroparesis of 10%,  although in reality this is probably significantly higher. Patients should initially be investigated with an  endoscopy to exclude anatomical lesions such as pyloric stenosis. Gastric emptying scans using solid-phase  meals are usually necessary. Treatment is often difficult and improving diabetic control can be beneficial, but a  prokinetic drug has the added effects of increasing locally released acetylcholine at the myenteric plexus.  Domperidone is now the initial intervention of choice, with metoclopramide having fallen out of favour because  of long-term neurological sequelae associated with its use.  B  Trial of high-fibre diet  High-fibre diets may result in significant residual solid material remaining within the stomach, exacerbating  symptoms of gastroparesis.  A  Recommend less frequent meals  Patients should be encouraged to eat smaller, more frequent meals with a lower potential residual solid  component, to minimise solid food retention in the stomach.  C  Trial of nifedipine  Nifedipine is a potential intervention for the treatment of oesophageal spasm in achalasia, but it has no role in  the treatment of diabetic gastroparesis.  D  Trial of a gastric pacemaker  Gastric pacemakers are viewed by NICE as a research intervention for patients with gastroparesis resistant to  other interventions.  An 18-year-old woman is seen to take a large quantity of paracetamol tablets following an argument with her  boyfriend. At 72 h later, she presents to the Emergency Department with jaundice and vomiting.  On examination, her BP is 105/72, pulse is 85 and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and tells you she is  passing only small amounts of dark urine.  Which of the following would be the best indicator of her overall prognosis?  A  Prothrombin time  B  Liver transaminases  C  Serum paracetamol levels  D  Bilirubin  E  Urea  Explanation  A    Prothrombin time  Paracetamol can cause liver failure even at relatively low doses (>7 g). The transplant criteria published by  King’s College Hospital are based on prognostic factors from a large retrospective cohort of patients. In these  criteria, coagulopathy (prolonged prothrombin time/increased international normalised ration (INR)) is an  important prognostic indicator along with encephalopathy, development of kidney disease and acidosis not  corrected by fluid resuscitation.  Maximal liver damage will occur approximately 72 h after ingestion when prothrombin time will be maximally  prolonged – it will then either return to normal (recovery with no sequelae) or remain prolonged (acute liver  failure – recovery unlikely).  E  Urea  Creatinine, not urea is used as an indicator of impending acute kidney disease in paracetamol overdose.  Measurement of urea is confounded as a measure of renal failure because of it’s absorption as part of a 'blood  meal'.  B  Liver transaminases  Transaminases are released by damaged hepatocytes and are always raised in significant paracetamol  poisoning, reaching levels of >10 000 IU/l. Transaminase levels are, however, not good indications of whether  progression to acute liver failure will occur.  C  Serum paracetamol levels  Although raised serum paracetamol levels at >48 h would suggest a large or staggered overdose, both more at  risk of progressing to acute liver failure, the value has no prognostic role.  D  Bilirubin  Although serum bilirubin is included in some prognostic indices in paracetamol poisoning, it is nowhere near as  reliable as prothrombin time. Transaminases, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGt), albumin and alkaline  phosphatase are of no benefit.

questions.question: You are asked to review a 42-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis who is an inpatient on the Gastroenterology  Ward. His spironolactone has been withdrawn, but the nurses are concerned as his creatinine has risen to 180  µmol/l. He has received albumin infusions.  On examination, his BP is 110/70 mmHg, with pulse 75/min and regular. He has marked ascites consistent with  cirrhosis. You suspect hepatorenal syndrome.  Which of the following is the most effective intervention with respect to his renal function?
questions.explanation:   Terlipressin  The class of drugs known as splanchnic vasoconstrictors has been studied regarding treatment of individuals  with hepatorenal syndrome. One of the drugs terlipressin, has a positive impact on both blood pressure and  glomerular filtration rate (GFR), when used in combination with albumin. Terlipressin is a non-selective V1  vasopressin agonist, with lower incidence of ischemic complications as compared to ornipressin. Also,  terlipressin can be given as a bolus. Albumin is useful in expanding the plasma volume and maintenance of  cardiac output. Liver transplantation is the ultimate definitive treatment of hepatorenal syndrome. Over the  longer term, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be of value, although ultimately liver  transplantation is the most effective option. In a study by Sarwar et al. (see below), complete response to  terlipressin–albumin therapy was seen in 58.3% patients, 29.2% achieved partial response with > 25%  creatinine reduction, while 12.5% showed no response.  Reference: Sarwar, S., Khan, A.A. (2016). Hepatorenal syndrome: Response to terlipressin and albumin and its  determinants. Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences 32(2):274–8.  E  Midodrine  Midodrine (an alpha-agonist) is used the treatment of postural hypotension and is non-selective in constricting  splanchnic vessels, and thus cannot be used in this case. Where terlipressin therapy is not available, initial  treatment with a combination of midodrine, octreotide and albumin is suggested. Investigations of midodrine  alone or in combination have shown conflicting results for systemic and renal haemodynamics and renal  function in patients with cirrhosis-related complications.  B  Lactulose  Lactulose is used in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It reduces ammonia production in the  intestine. Lactulose is the mainstay of treatment and results in improvement in approximately 70–80% of  patients with overt hepatic encephalopathy. It would not be effective in this particular scenario.  C  Furosemide  Furosemide, a diuretic, is not indicated as the patient is already on spironolactone and his blood pressure needs  to be maintained at an optimal level.  D  Dobutamine  Dobutamine is less selective in vasoconstriction of the splanchnic vasculature as compared to terlipressin, and  would be ineffective in maintaining blood pressure in this situation.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with shortness of breath. He is a known alcoholic and has a past history of  ischaemic heart disease.  On examination, he looks jaundiced but his abdomen is soft and non-tender. His blood pressure is 109/82  mmHg, pulse is 80 and regular and his chest sounds clear with good breath sounds bilaterally.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  70 g/l (elevated reticulocytes)  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  8.2 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  92 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.9 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  85 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Bilirubin  35 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)  400 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Cholesterol  10 mmol/l  < 5.2 mmol/l  Which of the following diagnoses do you think he has?
questions.explanation:   Zieve syndrome  Zieve syndrome occurs in patients with excessive alcohol consumption, with haemolysis and severe  hyperlipidaemia, abdominal pain and transient mildly raised bilirubin. It usually occurs in males and resolves  once alcohol consumption is stopped.  D  Gilbert syndrome  Gilbert syndrome is a benign cause of isolated hyperbilirubinaemia episodes of jaundice can be triggered by  illness, surgery or dehydration.  B  Whipple’s disease  Whipple’s disease is a cause of gastrointestinal (GI) malabsorption, and is caused by the Gram-positive  bacterium Tropheryma whippelii. It is also associated with joint pains.  C  Crigler Najjar syndrome  Crigler–Najjar syndrome is a rare congenital disorder of bilirubin conjugation. It has two distinct forms, type 1  and type 2: type 2 patients can survive to adulthood without any neurological impairment, whereas this  impairment is seen in neonates in type 1 cases.  E  Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis syndrome (NASH)  NASH is fatty liver disease unrelated to alcohol exposure and is seen in obese patients with insulin resistance,  including those with type 2 diabetes.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. For the past four weeks, he has had  increasingly frequent diarrhoea, opening his bowels up to eight times per day. Over the past few days, the  diarrhoea has become increasingly mixed with blood. He has no past medical history of note and takes no  regular medication. He tells you he has lost 5 kg in weight over the past few months and has suffered from  intermittent night sweats.  On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg while his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. His abdomen is  soft and he has mild left-sided tenderness. Bowel sounds are normal and PR reveals no masses. Repeated  stool cultures taken by his General Practitioner are negative.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  133 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.1 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  421 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.8 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  100 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  189 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  42 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  75 mm/1 st h  < 10 mm/1 st h  Albumin  31 g/l  35–55 g/l  Bilirubin  17 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Which of the following is the most useful investigation to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Flexible sigmoidoscopy  Given the history of chronic bloody diarrhoea, coupled with multiple negative stool cultures, ulcerative colitis is  the main diagnosis to exclude. Bearing in mind that distal disease is always present, a flexible sigmoidoscopy  coupled with biopsy is the most useful step in establishing the diagnosis. Oral and rectal corticosteroids are the  key to achieving remission, coupled with a 5-ASA compound.  B  Barium enema  While a barium enema can show evidence of colonic pathology in ulcerative colitis, it is contraindicated in  patients with acute severe colitis due to the risk of perforation and should not be performed here.  A  Abdominal X-ray  An abdominal X-ray would not lead to a confirmed diagnosis of the underlying condition (ulcerative colitis)  which is the question here. It would, however, be useful in the work-up of patients presenting with an acute  severe flare of colitis, as is the case here, in order to investigate for toxic megacolon. Truelove and Witt’s criteria  define acute severe colitis as more than six bloody stools per day along with any one of the following:  tachycardia > 90 bpm  fever > 37.8 °C  Hb < 105 g/l  Raised inflammatory markers.  D  Hydrogen breath test  Hydrogen breath testing is useful in confirming a diagnosis of bacterial overgrowth syndrome. Patients with  bacterial overgrowth typically present with bloating and abdominal pain along with diarrhoea and flatulence.  E  Ultrasound scan (USS) abdomen  While a USS abdomen can be useful in the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease it cannot differentiate  between ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease. It is a more useful in the investigation the of the hepatobiliary  disorders which are complications in these patients. Ulcerative colitis is an important risk factor for primary  sclerosing cholangitis and gallstone disease.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man who recently emigrated from China had some routine blood work by his general practitioner  (GP).  His hepatitis-B screen came back showing positive HBs and hepatitis-B IgG core antibodies. Anti-HBe was  positive, but he is e-antigen negative and s-antigen negative.  The GP immediately referred the patient to your clinic, but before doing this sent some liver function tests.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Bilirubin  12 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  42 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  67 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Albumin  36 g/l  35–55 g/l  HBV DNA  Negative  The patient seems to be in good health.  What is the most appropriate management of this patient?
options: B. Discharge back to the GP
D. Start combined lamivudine and interferon therapy
E. Offer an HIV, Hep-C test and discharge the patient back to the GP if negative
questions.explanation: Offer an HIV, Hep-C test and discharge the patient back to the GP if negative    A patient who is HBs antibody positive indicates previous infection unless they have been vaccinated against  Hep-B. The phenomenon of loss of HbeAg and seroconversion to anti-Hbe-positive status indicates a reduction  of inflammation accompanied by histological change from active to inactive hepatitis. E-antigen negativity  implies that he no longer has active infection. Guidance suggests that in this case it is worth offering an HIV  test, as exposure to hepatitis B may well indicate exposure to other blood-borne viruses.  For indications for treatment, refer to NICE guidance CG165.  D  Start combined lamivudine and interferon therapy  Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated for a man over 30 years old, with LFTs and negative HBV DNA.  Antiviral treatments for HBe-Ag-negative chronic hepatitis-B include PEGinterferon alfa-2a (first line), entacavir  and tenofivir.  A  Elective liver biopsy  In patients with HBe-negative chronic hepatitis and mildly raised ALT, liver biopsy is usually only considered in  those patients who have serum HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/ml, to determine whether treatment is warranted.  This patient has nearly normal LFTs and negative HBV DNA.  B  Discharge back to the GP  He should be tested for other blood borne viruses, and offered transient elastography testing.  C  Start interferon therapy  Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated for a man over 30 years old, with normal LFTs and negative HBV  DNA.

questions.question: A 50-year-old bar owner comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. He has suffered from chronic  diarrhoea for many years, accompanied by intermittent abdominal pain, and is finding it impossible to maintain  his weight. He admits to drinking excess alcohol in the past, although now he claims to have reduced his intake  to one glass of whisky per day. He also smokes 20 cigarettes per day.  On examination, his blood pressure is 135/75 mmHg and pulse 80 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft,  although he complains of vague tenderness in the epigastrium. His body mass index (BMI) is 21 kg/m 2.  Investigations:  Investigations  Results  Normal Values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  108 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  7.1 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  151 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine  90 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  29 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  121 U/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  172 U/l  30–130 IU/l  Bilirubin  17 µmol/l  < 17 µmol/l  You suspect him to be suffering from chronic pancreatitis.  Which of the following is the best way to confirm functional pancreatic insufficiency?
questions.explanation:   Faecal elastase  Faecal elastase measurement is the preferred approach to evaluating chronic pancreatitis because it requires a  single random stool sample, with values of elastase of < 200 ug/g being suggestive of pancreatic insufficiency.  D  Lipase  Like amylase, random lipase measurement is not useful in the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis. It is only useful  in diagnosing acute pancreatitis where patients usually present with acute epigastric pain and vomiting.  A  Amylase  Random measurement of amylase and lipase is of no value in detecting either chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic  insufficiency. Minor elevations may be seen in patients with obesity and diabetes, but this has no prognostic  value with respect to pancreatic disease.  B  Faecal fat estimation  Faecal fat estimation is both time-consuming and unpleasant in terms of collection and analysis. Qualitative  staining for fat with sudan staining is not recommended. A quantitative approach looking at thresholds of > 7  g/fat excretion per day (possible pancreatic insufficiency) and > 10 g/fat excretion per day (likely pancreatic  insufficiency) is therefore required.  E  SeHCAT test  The SeHCAT test is used for determining bile acid malabsorption. It uses a radiolabelled taurine-conjugated bile  acid analogue, and retention is measured at seven days using a gamma camera.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease at the age of 17 years. He has been admitted to  hospital on a yearly basis since his diagnosis with acute flare-ups requiring courses of systemic corticosteroids.  He has no extra-enteric manifestations of Crohn’s disease, but has had a problematic perianal fistula requiring  frequent courses of antibiotics. He is finding it difficult to maintain attendance at work because of ill health.  Which of the following steps is recommended next to maintain remission in this patient?
questions.explanation:   6-Mercaptopurine  Thiopurines (azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine) are the most effective agents in maintaining remission in  Crohn’s disease long term. If not tolerated, methotrexate could be used as an alternative. Thiopurines are  thought to be particularly effective in patients with fistulating disease. Infliximab is of value in long-term  remission in fistulating Crohn’s disease (and possibly in non-fistulating disease) but is generally used alongside  a thiopurine. Over the long term, it may prove a superior option to methotrexate, but currently it is still  considered only after a traditional second line therapy has failed to gain control.  E  Sulphasalazine  ASA (5-Aminosalycilic acid) compounds such as balsalazide and sulphasalazine have a role in maintaining  remission and are generally well tolerated but are not as effective as thiopurines.  B  Polymeric diet  This has most value in reducing the severity of acute flares and their frequency, rather than resolving fistulae.  C  Budesonide  Steroids do not have a role in maintaining remission, their main value is in treating acute flares of Crohn’s  disease.  D  Ciclosporin  Cyclosporine is of most use in the treatment of severe ulcerative colitis which is unresponsive to high dose  corticosteroids and 5-ASA compounds.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of jaundice, nausea and right  upper quadrant abdominal pain. There is no history of fevers or recent travel. He has a past medical history of  rheumatoid arthritis, for which he has been taking methotrexate for the past four months. He drinks two glasses  of wine three times a week and denies smoking or recreational drug use.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  White cell count (WCC)  10.2 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  135 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.2 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  90 µm/l  50–90 µmol/l  Bilirubin  60 μmol/l  1–21 μmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  150 U/l  1–40 U/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  180 U/l  1–40 U/l  Albumin  40 g/l  35–50 g/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  80 U/l  30–130 U/l  Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)  50 U/l  1–54 U/l  What is the most likely cause of this patient's liver injury?
questions.explanation:   Drug-induced hepatitis  The most likely cause of the patient’s liver injury is drug-induced hepatitis, given the recent history of  methotrexate use. The patient’s blood results demonstrate evidence of acute hepatitis with raised AST and ALT  levels, with a normal ratio, and raised bilirubin levels. Methotrexate, a commonly used medication for  rheumatoid arthritis, is known to cause hepatotoxicity. It is important to promptly recognise and discontinue the  offending medication in cases of drug-induced hepatitis to prevent further liver damage and facilitate recovery.  Bilirubin levels of more than twice the upper limit of normal are indicative of severe hepatotoxicity and are  associated with a 10–15% mortality rate.  A  Alcoholic hepatitis  This patient’s history does not suggest significant alcohol consumption, with six standard glasses of wine  totalling 12 units across the week. This makes a diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis less likely. Additionally,  alcoholic hepatitis would typically cause a raised AST : ALT ratio of more than 2 and elevated GGT levels, which  are not seen here.  B  Autoimmune hepatitis  While autoimmune hepatitis is a consideration in patients with elevated liver enzyme levels and jaundice, the  onset of symptoms within a short time frame from starting methotrexate makes drug-induced hepatitis a more  likely diagnosis in this case.  D  Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease  Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) typically presents with elevated liver enzyme levels and may  progress to liver fibrosis and cirrhosis. LFTs tend to show an AST : ALT ratio of less than one. Bilirubin levels are  typically normal and are only elevated with decompensated disease. Adding to this, the patient’s history of  methotrexate use makes drug-induced hepatitis a more likely explanation for the liver injury in this case.  E  Viral hepatitis  The absence of fever or recent travel and a normal WCC make viral hepatitis unlikely. The history of recent  methotrexate use with the LFT results seen above makes a drug-induced cause more plausible.

questions.question: A 35-year-old patient with a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) has suffered a number of episodes of pan-colitis  over the last 11 years. He is currently managed with infliximab and has stable disease.  He has read on the Internet that people with UC have an increased risk of cancer and liver disease and wishes  to discuss this. He has not had any weight loss or additional bloody diarrhoea.  The general practitioner (GP) measures his carcino-embryonic antigen level (CEA) and alpha fetoprotein, and a  surveillance colonoscopy is arranged.  Which of the following is the correct advice to give him?
options: A. CEA is a useful screening test for bowel cancer
B. Faecal calprotectin elevation indicates a possible neoplasm
C. Cancers tend to present earlier in patients with UC and are therefore easier to treat
D. Alpha-fetoprotein is a good marker for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in this case
E. He is at risk of PSC despite good control of his UC at the current time
questions.explanation:   He is at risk of PSC despite good control of his UC at the current time  Although this patient’s UC is currently well controlled, it won’t significantly impact on future risk of PSC, which  is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease.  C  Cancers tend to present earlier in patients with UC and are therefore easier to treat  Due to the fact that symptoms may be confused with active inflammatory bowel disease, diagnosis is often  made late.  A  CEA is a useful screening test for bowel cancer  CEA is not reliable as a test for diagnosing early colon cancer, but is considered as a test for cancer recurrence in  those who have undergone a surgical resection.  B  Faecal calprotectin elevation indicates a possible neoplasm  Faecal calprotectin is a measure of active inflammatory bowel disease.  D  Alpha-fetoprotein is a good marker for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in this case  Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, not for PSC.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and an upper GI  haemorrhage. She admits that she went foraging for mushrooms some 3 days earlier and cooked some that she  found in the forest, but no one else in the family wanted to take the risk of eating them. A sample of leftover  mushrooms suggests they were Death Cap.  On examination, her BP is 110/72 mmHg, with pulse 92/min and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and  right upper quadrant of her abdomen. There is dried blood around her lips and evidence of bruising on her arms  and legs.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  91 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.5 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  121 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  138 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  5.2 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  255 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Which of the following would be an indicator for transplant according to the King’s College Hospital  criteria (non-paracetamol induced liver failure)?
questions.explanation:   Bilirubin 320 µmol/l  Bilirubin levels of >300 µmol/l is one of the prognostic indicators that determines referral for liver  transplantation.  Several factors are important in the prognosis of patients with acute liver failure. Several criteria have been  developed to predict when liver transplantation is indicated, the most widely accepted being the King's College  Hospital criteria:  INR >6.5; or,  Three of the following five criteria:  Patient age <11 or >40;  Serum bilirubin >300 micromoles per litre;  Time from onset of jaundice to the development of coma >7 days;  INR >3.5; or  Drug toxicity, regardless of whether it was the cause of the acute liver failure.  C  Alkaline phosphatase 430 U/l  ALP levels are not included in the King’s College Hospital criteria for predicting when to refer the patient for  liver transplantation.  A  Age 34  Age of less than 11 years or more than 40 years is considered to be one of the prognostic indicator criteria for  liver transplantation.  B  ALT 2300 U/l  ALT level is not included in the King’s College Hospital criteria of prognostic indictors for liver transplantation.  E  INR 3.2  INR of >6.5 is considered one of the positive indicators that determines referral for liver transplantation.  A 24-year-old woman comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She complains of weight loss,  intermittent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea which has increased over the past few months. She also has a  history of type I diabetes, for which she takes a basal bolus insulin regimen.  Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/75 mmHg; pulse is 85 bpm and regular. She looks pale and has a  body mass index (BMI) of 20 kg/m 2.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  101 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  9.7 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  178 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  138 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  95 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  26 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  85 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Bilirubin  17 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  183 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Calcium (Ca)  2.15 mmol/l  2.2–2.6 mmol/l  Anti-endomysial antibody (IgA)  Negative  Which of the following is the most useful next step given the negative anti-endomysial antibody result?  A  Duodenal biopsy  B  Gluten-free diet  C  Immunoglobulin electrophoresis  D  SeCHAT testing  E  24hr fecal fat collection  Explanation  C    Immunoglobulin electrophoresis  Insufficient levels of IgA lead to falsey negative coeliac serology (both IgA tTG and IgA endomysial antibodies).  As IgA deficiency can coexist in up to around 5% of patients with coeliac disease. It is therefore necessary here,  given the suspicious clinical scenario and concurrent autoimmune disease, to rule out IgA deficiency before  excluding coeliac disease based on negative serology alone. Duodenal biopsy would be appropriate after IgA  testing.  A  Duodenal biopsy  Although anti-endomysial antibody is negative, this test requires sufficient levels of IgA which has not been  tested for. It raises the possibility of IgA deficiency and would be required for testing before a duodenal biopsy  is clinically indicated.  B  Gluten-free diet  Although this is a treatment option for coeliac disease, it may obscure the diagnosis if further requiring  duodenal biopsy after IgA testing. A gluten-free diet is a significant undertaking for which coeliac patients must  strictly adhere to lifelong. It should not, therefore, be advised to be started without a diagnosis first.  D  SeCHAT testing  SeCHAT testing is not clinically indicated. This is a test of bile acid malabsorption which is common in  inflammatory bowel disease. The clinical scenario would indicate she may have coeliac disease.  E  24hr fecal fat collection  24-hour faecal fat collection is a test for fat malabsorption which is not currently indicated by the clinical  scenario.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man complains of acute epigastric pain radiating to his back. This is associated with vomiting.  The pain is improved when he sits forward. He drinks half a bottle of whisky per day.  On examination, he is mildly pyrexial. He looks jaundiced and unwell. He is tachycardic and slightly  hypotensive. There is generalised tenderness of the abdomen. There is no guarding or rebound rigidity. Bowel  sounds are normal.  Electrocardiography, erect chest and abdominal radiography are normal. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a  small liver, normal bile ducts and minimal fluid around the pancreas.  Which of the following is an indicator of poor prognosis for his condition?
questions.explanation:   Serum calcium = 1.91 mmol/l  The patient has acute pancreatitis secondary to alcohol (95% of acute pancreatitis is attributable to gallstones  and alcohol). The pain in pancreatitis can be very severe and is relieved by leaning forward. In severe cases,  patients are shocked.  There are several severity scoring systems used to assess prognosis/predict mortality. The Ranson criteria use  the following parameters (assessed at admission and 48h) to predict mortality in alcoholic pancreatitis: age >  55, WCC > 16.0 × 10 9/l, fasting blood glucose > 11 mmol/l, LDH > 350 IU/l, serum AST >250 IU/l; within 48 h  of admission: haematocrit decrease by >10%, arterial Pa0 2 <8 kPa, serum calcium < 2.0 mmol/l, blood urea  nitrogen increase > 1.8 mmol/l, base deficit > 4 mmol/l, fluid sequestration > 6 l. Mortality ranges from 1% for  those with <3 criteria to 90% for those with >6 criteria.  Other assessment systems include the Glasgow score and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation  (APACHE) II scoring system.  There are limitations to most scoring systems (as most require 48 h to determine predicted outcome) and the  patient needs to be aggressively fluid resuscitated early to reduce the chance of progression to end organ  dysfunction (250–500 ml/h isotonic crystalloid during first 12–24 h). The most recent British Society of  Gastroenterology guidelines are from 2005. For more recent guidelines see American College of  Gastroenterology: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2013), Am J Gastroenterol 2013; 108:1400–1415.  E  Serum creatinine = 150 mmol/l  This creatinine may be indicative of early kidney disease, which is a marker of severe pancreatitis, but serum  creatinine in isolation is not in the recognised severity criteria.  A  PaO 2 = 9.5 kPa  In the Glasgow prognostic criteria for alcoholic and gallstone pancreatitis, a Pa O 2 of <8kPa in room air is a  marker of poor prognosis. Other criteria include:  Age  >55  Serum albumin  <32g/l  Serum Ca  <2 mmol/l  Blood glucose  >10 mmol/l  Serum LDH  >600 units/l  Serum urea nitrogen  >16.1 mmol/l  WBC  >15  With a score <3, severe pancreatitis (defined as the presence of persistent organ failure >48 h) is unlikely to  occur.  B  Serum albumin = 34 g/l  In the Glasgow prognostic criteria for alcoholic and gallstone pancreatitis, an albumin of <32 g/l is a poor  prognostic indicator.  D  Aspartate aminotransferase = 98 IU/l  An AST >250 would be predictive of severity in the Ranson criteria.  A 55-year-old man was found on the street by the police. He complains of right upper quadrant pain and  anorexia. He works at a building site but has recently lost his job.  On examination, he smells very strongly of alcohol. He has icteric sclera. His temperature is 37.6 °C. There is  spider naevi and palmar erythema. Heart sounds and chest examination are unremarkable. Abdominal  examination reveals dull flanks and a tender liver edge. There is no focal neurology but a hepatic flap is present.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  121 g/l  135–175 g/l  White blood count (WBC)  17.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  80 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Mean cell volume (MCV)  103 fl  76–98 fl  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.6  < 1.1  Sodium (Na +)  132 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  1.7 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  70 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  35 g/l  35–55 g/l  Bilirubin  102 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  45 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  100 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  156 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Ferritin  987 µg/l  20–250 µg/l  Hepatitis and autoimmune serology  Negative  What is the most likely diagnosis?  A  Hepatoma  B  Alcoholic hepatitis  C  Choledocholithiasis  D  Viral hepatitis  E  Haemochromatosis  Explanation  B    Alcoholic hepatitis  Alcoholic hepatitis commonly occurs after a prolonged period of alcohol abuse or return to alcohol after period  of abstinence. It often presents with malaise, anorexia, mild fever, tender hepatolomegaly, and (if severe)  jaundice. Investigations usually reveal mildly increased serum transaminases, macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia,  poor hepatic synthetic function, leukocytosis irrespective of infection and increased acute phase reactants.  Usually the AST : ALT > 2.  The prognosis depends on its severity. Malnutrition, jaundice, fluid retention and encephalopathy are associated  with poor outlook. Histology can help to confirm diagnosis.  The mainstay of treatment is supportive in nature:  Alcohol abstinence  Prevention and treatment of alcohol withdrawal  Fluid management  Nutritional support  Infection surveillance  Prophylaxis against gastric mucosal bleeding  The discriminant function (DF) can be used to identify patients for treatment. Those who have a value > 32 may  benefit from corticosteroids. If there is a contraindication to steroids, pentoxifylline is an alternative.  A  Hepatoma  The development of a hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with liver cirrhosis is a possible cause of  decompensation. However, the history of alcohol, low-grade fever and high WCC, make alcoholic hepatitis a  more likely cause.  C  Choledocholithiasis  Acute gallstone impaction in the common bile duct is likely to present with right upper quadrant pain, with  possible complicating cholangitis causing a fever. But this would not account for the macrocytosis, signs of  chronic liver disease, and decompensation with jaundice, ascites and asterixis.  D  Viral hepatitis  This could be the cause of chronic liver disease, which has now decompensated, but we are told that viral  serology is negative.  E  Haemochromatosis  There is no suggestion of other organ involvement, and haemochromatosis is less likely to explain the tender  hepatomegaly, raised WCC, and mild fever. The raised ferritin in this case is likely due to alcoholic liver disease  and not haemochromatosis.

questions.question: You are seeing a 25-year-old woman in clinic with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC). She had extensive colitis  10 years ago, which has improved with medical treatment.  Last year, she had been diagnosed with early primary sclerosing cholangitis after an MRCP and liver biopsy. Her  last colonoscopy was 6 months ago, which detected no active disease, and random biopsies were normal. She  is remaining well and asymptomatic.  Physical examination is unremarkable, with a normal BMI of 23.  When should colonic screening be performed on this patient?
options: A. Colonoscopy should be performed only when there are symptoms of colitis
B. Colonoscopy should be performed in 10 years’ time
C. Colonoscopy should be performed annually
D. Colonoscopy should be performed in 3 years’ time
E. Flexible sigmoidoscopy should be used 2-yearly
questions.explanation:   Colonoscopy should be performed annually  This patient has had ulcerative colitis (UC) for 10 years and has developed associated primary sclerosing  cholangitis (PSC) of the liver. Patients with concomitant UC and PSC are at a higher risk of developing colonic  cancer, and it is recommended that they be screened annually with colonoscopy. Those with history of colon  cancer in a first-degree relative under 50 years of age should also be subject to annual surveillance.  D  Colonoscopy should be performed in 3 years’ time  Those with intermediate-risk disease, extensive colitis with mild active endoscopic/histological inflammation or  post-inflammatory polyps or family history of colorectal cancer in a first-degree relative aged 50+, should be  surveyed 3-yearly.  A  Colonoscopy should be performed only when there are symptoms of colitis  Given there is significant risk of colonic dysplasia and subsequent carcinoma, expectant colonoscopy only when  there are symptoms runs the risk of missing a lesion that could be advanced at the point of diagnosis.  B  Colonoscopy should be performed in 10 years’ time  Even those patients with low-risk disease (those with previous extensive colitis with no active  endoscopic/histological inflammation or left-sided colitis or Crohn's colitis of <50% colon) should be surveyed  5-yearly.  E  Flexible sigmoidoscopy should be used 2-yearly  Flexible sigmoidoscopy is inappropriate because it would fail to detect right-sided colonic lesions.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man complains of lethargy and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He has a long  history of intermittent heartburn and has occasionally passed some dark red blood mixed with his stools.  Other past medical history includes hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has not lost  any weight recently, is an ex-smoker and drinks only occasional alcohol.  Physical examination confirms hypertension, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, but is otherwise unremarkable.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  84 g/l  135–175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  70 fl  76–98 fl  White cell count (WCC)  9.5 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Neutrophils  5.4 × 10 9/l  2.5–7.58 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  258 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Renal and hepatic function are normal.  Gastroscopy and barium enema are normal.  Mesenteric angiography showed an abnormal vascular blush in the ascending colon.  What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.explanation:   Angiodysplasia  This patient has a microcytic anaemia and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding. The findings on mesenteric  angiography, combined with a normal barium enema, suggest a diagnosis of angiodysplasia. Angiodysplasia  may be found throughout the gastrointestinal tract, although it most commonly occurs in the caecum and  ascending colon. It is a significant cause of chronic anaemia and can also cause acute haemorrhage. Treatment  is either by heat coagulation at endoscopy or by embolisation of the bleeding vessel during angiography.  C  Colonic varices  Colonic varices would produce distension of the veins in the colon and would not appear as an abnormal  vascular blush on mesenteric angiography.  A  Colonic carcinoma  Barium enema would not be normal in colonic carcinoma – we would expect a colonic mass in carcinoma. The  mesenteric angiography would be normal.  D  Meckel’s diverticulum  Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It results from  incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct leading to the formation of a true diverticulum of the small intestine.  Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the small bowel wall. It arises from the antimesenteric surface of the middle-to-distal ileum. The diverticulum represents a persistent remnant of the  omphalo-mesenteric duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac in the foetus. Meckel's diverticulum is  uncommon and often clinically silent, particularly in adults. Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum may be  discovered during abdominal exploration for the evaluation of unrelated pathology. Less commonly, it is found  incidentally on diagnostic imaging. When symptomatic, Meckel's diverticulum may present with abdominal pain  or symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction. Mesenteric angiography is not abnormal as in  this case.  E  Ulcerative colitis  Ulcerative colitis is characterised by recurring episodes of inflammation limited to the mucosal layer of the  colon. It commonly involves the rectum and may extend in a proximal and continuous fashion to involve other  parts of the colon. Patients with ulcerative colitis usually present with diarrhoea, which may be associated with  blood. Bowel movements are frequent and small in volume as a result of rectal inflammation. Associated  symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, urgency, tenesmus and incontinence. Patients with mainly distal  disease may have constipation accompanied by frequent discharge of blood and mucus. The endoscopic  findings in patients with ulcerative colitis include loss of vascular markings due to engorgement of the mucosa,  giving it an erythematous appearance.
