In some cases progression to ERCP may be required to  confirm the diagnosis for example by obtaining biopsy specimens. Symptomatic patients with papillary stenosis  have responded symptomatically to endoscopic sphincterotomy. Antibiotics have not been shown to be useful.  Some clinicians use ursodeoxycholic acid in patients with intrahepatic disease, with an observed improvement  in liver enzymes.  C  Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)  In this case, given that the CT has not revealed the underlying diagnosis, MRCP is a logical next step before  progressing to ERCP.  A  Blood culture  This would not particularly contribute to diagnosis - imaging of the biliary tree is required to explore this  patient’s symptoms pattern of liver enzyme derangement.  B  Liver biopsy  Liver biopsy has little value in the diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy; diagnosis is informed by imaging of the  biliary tree.  E  CT abdomen  CT is more useful than ultrasound in identifying intrahepatic strictures, and can be effective in identifying  intrahepatic masses, abdominal adenopathy, and pancreatic disease in jaundiced patients. But CT is inferior to  ERCP in its ability to display the necessarily precise biliary anatomical details for the definitive diagnosis of  AIDS cholangiopathy.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man with a 12-year history of recurrent peptic ulceration presents to his General Practitioner  with a further relapse.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Fasting serum gastrin  480 pmol/l  < 55 pmol/l  Serum gastrin following injection of secretin (2 U/kg)  720 pmol/l  Which of the following is associated with the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nephrolithiasis  This patient has Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, a rare condition in which a gastrin-secreting adenoma results in  severe and recurrent gastric and duodenal ulceration. The condition may be diagnosed by detecting a raised  serum gastrin level, or if there is doubt as to the diagnosis with only a mild elevation in gastrin level, the  secretin test leads to a marked elevation in gastrin levels. The level of gastrin seen here is markedly elevated.  Treatment is with high-dose proton pump inhibitors and, if possible, surgical resection of the adenoma.  Approximately 50% of adenomas are malignant, with a 5-year survival rate of 80% for a single tumour.  Zollinger–Ellison syndrome may arise as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1). Nephrolithiasis  may occur in association with Zollinger–Ellison syndrome in MEN-1 due to the presence of hypercalcaemia.    D  Renal cysts  Renal cysts are not a recognised complication of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome or MEN-1. Recognised risk factors  for renal cysts are age, male gender, renal dysfunction and hypertension. Examples of renal cystic disease  include polycystic kidney disease, medullary cystic disease and medullary sponge kidney.  A  Marfanoid body habitus  This patient has Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, which may occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1  (MEN-1). Marfanoid body habitus is associated with MEN-2.  C  Medullary thyroid cancer  This patient has Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, which may occur as part of MEN-1. Medullary thyroid cancer is  associated with MEN-2.  E  Small bowel cancer  Small bowel cancer is not a recognised complication of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome or MEN-1. This is a  complication seen in coeliac disease and Crohn’s disease.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with no previous significant medical history presents for review.  Medication history includes the oral contraceptive pill and she smokes 15 cigarettes per day and drinks 15 units  per week. She complains of vague upper abdominal pain, worse on the right-hand side.  On examination, there is a palpable non-tender mass in the right hypochondrium. Investigations reveal mild  elevations in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT); alpha-fetoprotein is within  the normal range. Hepatic ultrasound scan reveals a solitary mass in the left lobe of the liver, which is  hypoechoic and subcapsular.  Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:   Hepatic adenoma  This woman has a history of use of the oral contraceptive pill, with an asymptomatic liver mass. It is hypoechoic  and subcapsular, appearing uniform in texture. The presence of a normal alpha-fetoprotein makes  hepatocellular carcinoma unlikely; therefore, the most likely diagnosis is hepatic adenoma. Stopping the oral  contraceptive pill often causes tumour regression, although complete regression is very atypical. Any tumour  regression reduces risks associated with elective surgical resection; although mortality associated with  resection is very rare, surgery results in significant morbidity in around 13% of patients. In patients who  experience some regression after stopping the pill, there is still a risk of malignant transformation, and such  patients should be monitored with alpha-fetoprotein measurement if they are unwilling or unable to undergo  elective tumour resection.  D  Hydatid cyst  Hydatid disease appears as a multi-loculated cyst on ultrasound scan rather than the hypoechoic mass which  isn’t multi-loculated here.  B  Hepatocellular carcinoma  Hepatocellular carcinoma is usually seen against a background of chronic liver disease with cirrhosis, and is  associated with rapid worsening of ascites with elevation in alpha-fetoprotein.  C  Liver metastasis  Liver metastases are usually characterised by more than one lesion, and the absence of other symptoms of  cancer, makes this a much less likely diagnosis.  E  Focal nodular hyperplasia  The echogenicity of both FNH and its scar is variable, which makes it difficult to detect on ultrasound. Some  lesions are well demarcated and easily seen whereas others are isoechoic with surrounding liver. Detectable  lesions characteristically will demonstrate a central scar with the displacement of peripheral vasculature on  colour doppler examination, rather than the well demarcated hypoechoic lesion seen here.

questions.question: A 53-year-old woman is referred to the clinic by her general practitioner (GP) for fatigue, lethargy, mild itching,  muscle and joint pains. She has a history of hypothyroidism which is treated with 100 mcg of thyroxine daily.  Her TSH has been stable for the past 5 years.  On examination, there is jaundice, with mild hepatomegaly and more than five spider naevi on the upper body.  Investigations reveal:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Bilirubin  125 μmol/l  1 - 22 μmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  230 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  185 u/l  30 - 150 u/l  Albumin  28 g/l  35 - 55 g/l  Hypergammaglobulinaemia  polyclonal  Anti-smooth muscle antibodies  positive  Anti-nuclear antibody  positive  Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis    Autoantibodies associated with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis include anti-smooth muscle antibodies,  antinuclear antibodies and anti-actin antibodies. Autoimmune hepatitis is much more common in women.  Diagnosis and prognostic assessment is best informed via liver biopsy. After an initial period of high-dose  prednisolone, azathioprine is often added as a steroid-sparing agent. A number of physicians employ a  maintenance regime of prednisolone 10 mg and azathioprine 50 mg per day as maintenance therapy. Initial  remission is possible in around 80% of patients, though relapse often occurs if therapy is withdrawn. Liver  transplant is successful in patients who fail medical therapy.  B  Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)  PBC is associated with an obstructive liver function test picture, and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies.  A  Primary sclerosing cholangitis  Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, an obstructive LFT picture, and a  range of positive autoantibodies which may include pANCA.  D  Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis  Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis occurs predominantly in children and is associated with anti-liver kidney  microsomal antibodies.  E  Type 3 autoimmune hepatitis  Type 3 autoimmune hepatitis is associated with soluble liver or liver-kidney antigens.

questions.question: An 18-year-old female student is being investigated in the clinic for weight loss and diarrhoea. The symptoms  started about one year ago and she has been progressively losing weight. She is in the clinic with her parents,  who are extremely concerned for their daughter.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  112 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  4.2 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  160 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  132 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.1 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  55 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate  (ESR)  6.0 mm/hour  1–20 mm/hour  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  83 fl  76–98 fl  C-reactive protein (CRP)  4.0 mg/l  < 0 mg/l  Urea  2.5 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Upper gastrointestinal (GI)  endoscopy  Normal appearances with normal duodenal  biopsies  Colonoscopy  Melanosis coli  What is the most likely cause of the symptoms?
questions.explanation:   Senna abuse  Anthraquinone laxative derivatives such as senna are absorbed in the large intestine, where they lead to  cellular apoptosis, resulting in brown pigmentation of the colonic mucosa, so-called melanosis coli.  B  Lactulose abuse  Lactulose is an osmotic laxative which increases intraluminal/stool water, resulting in softening; it does not lead  to colonic pigmentation.  C  Sodium docusate abuse  Sodium docusate, like lactulose, is primarily a stool softener and does not lead to colonic mucosal cell apoptosis  and melanosis coli.  D  Methylcellulose abuse  Methylcellulose is a bulk-forming laxative and must be taken with large amounts of fluids to achieve its laxative  effect.  E  Colchicine use  Colchicine is rarely used, normally for the treatment of gout in patients where other interventions are  unsuitable. It is therefore doubtful as to how this patient would have gained access to the medication. It does  not cause melanosis coli.

questions.question: A 54-year-old businessman is brought in by ambulance from the airport with sudden-onset, excruciating upper  abdominal pain radiating to his back following a flight. He has had recurrent vomiting during the whole of his  flight. He has a history of hiatus hernia but no history of cardiac problems. He drinks 10 units of alcohol per  week.  On examination, he is dyspnoeic and cyanosed. Blood pressure is equal on both arms and there is no radial–  radial delay. His saturation is 88% on high-flow oxygen. Heart sounds are normal.  On chest examination, there is reduced air entry and dullness to percussion on the left side. There is marked  epigastric tenderness and rigidity. His pain fails to improve with morphine or pethidine. Amylase and cardiac  enzymes are within normal range.  Electrocardiography demonstrates sinus tachycardia but no other abnormalities.  Chest X-ray shows a left pleural effusion.  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Boerhaave’s syndrome  Repeated vomiting followed by epigastric pain and pleural effusion should lead one to consider the diagnosis of  spontaneous rupture of the oesophagus, also known as Boerhaave syndrome. It is relatively uncommon but  serious and potentially fatal. It is complete transmural laceration of the lower part of the oesophagus, with  gastric contents entering the mediastinum and pleural cavity. If one were to perform a pleural fluid aspirate, one  is likely to aspirate gastric contents. It is usually caused by vomiting against a closed glottis.  Other clinical features that may suggest the diagnosis include odynophagia and surgical emphysema in the  neck. It is more common in men than women and typically present in those between 50–70 years old. Early  operation after appropriate resuscitation offers the best chance of survival.  C  Acute pancreatitis  A rise in amylase >3× the upper limit of normal is one of the diagnostic criteria for pancreatitis, and therefore  the normal amylase level precludes this. See AGA guidelines on management of acute pancreatitis. Reference:  American Journal of Gastroenterology 108, 1400–1415 (September 2013).  A  Dissecting thoracic aneurysm  Patients presenting with dissection classically have a history of hypertension. One would also expect a disparity  in the blood pressure and pulse in acute dissections. Patients may also present with a neurological deficit due to  involvement of the spinal and carotid arteries.  B  Aspiration pneumonia  Although the recurrent vomiting and hiatus hernia would certainly be a risk factor, the persistent, excruciating  pain would be uncharacteristic for an aspiration pneumonia as would such a rapid onset of a pleural effusion.  D  Perforated duodenal ulcer  One would expect to see pneumoperitoneum with a perforated duodenal ulcer, and the presence of a unilateral  effusion is not characteristic.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is found to have the following blood results on routine preoperative blood tests. She  presented due to yellowing of her skin following a short bout of flu, from which she has now recovered.  She has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medications. Examination reveals jaundice, but no  other abnormalities.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Bilirubin  36 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  108 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  20 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Urine dipstick  Normal  Given the likely diagnosis, which is the best course of action?
options: A. Complete viral screen for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), infectious hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus
E. Ultrasound scan of the liver, including portal Doppler
questions.explanation:   Complete full blood count  This patient has asymptomatic jaundice following a recent viral infection. Gilbert syndrome is a common cause  of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia following fasting or physiological stress and is often diagnosed  incidentally. It is characterised by mildly elevated bilirubin levels. In this patient who reveals no prior history of  jaundice, it is important to rule out haemolysis as a cause of jaundice by also checking the patient’s full blood  count. If this is abnormal, a blood film, reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase level and direct antigen test  may also be requested. If these tests are negative, a presumptive diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome can be made.  The diagnosis can be confirmed by either an increase in bilirubin level provoked by fasting or by a slow rise in  bilirubin level following administration of intravenous nicotinic acid. No treatment is necessary and the  prognosis is excellent.  A  Complete viral screen for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), infectious hepatitis, Epstein–Barr  virus and cytomegalovirus  Although this patient has had a recent viral illness, she has completely recovered and her liver function tests  only reveal an abnormality in her bilirubin levels, pointing towards a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome, which  causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Viral screening for the above viruses would be necessary if she  had evidence of acute liver disease on examination or her liver function tests.  C  Liver biopsy  Liver biopsy is an invasive test and is not necessary to make a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome in this patient who  is otherwise well. A liver biopsy may be indicated if there is evidence of concomitant liver disease.  D  No further investigations necessary  This patient likely has Gilbert syndrome which is a common cause of isolated unconjugated bilirubinaemia.  However, given that this young patient reports no history of previous presentations with jaundice, it would be  pertinent to rule out haemolysis (eg due to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma) as the cause of her bilirubinaemia and  therefore, a full blood count of at least should be completed. If this reveals a low haemoglobin level, then  further testing of reticulocyte count, blood film, lactate dehydrogenase level and direct antigen test should be  completed.  E  Ultrasound scan of the liver, including portal Doppler  Although ultrasound scanning is a safe and non-invasive test, it is not necessary to make a diagnosis of Gilbert  syndrome, especially in the absence of any evidence of liver disease on examination and normal transaminase  levels on liver function testing.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with mild haemophilia B is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic by his General  Practitioner who has noted deranged liver function tests. The patient’s blood tests were checked when he  moved back to the United Kingdom after having worked abroad for many years. He had attended for a routine  prescription of his antihypertensive medication and statin therapy. He has not had any significant bleeding  episodes for ten years and informs you his haemophilia was diagnosed when he was eight years old when he  had significant bleeding after surgery for appendicitis. The haemorrhage required treatment and an admission  to intensive care. He does not smoke and has never injected drugs.  On examination, he is well, with no organomegaly. He reports no symptoms of jaundice or discolouration of his  urine.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  130 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  4.2 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  200 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  85 fl  80–100 fl  Bilirubin  20 μmol/l  3–17 μmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  205 u/l  30–150 u/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  25 u/l  7–55 u/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  265 u/l  5–35 u/l  Albumin  32 g/l  35–55 g/l  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.2  1.13  What further investigation is most likely to contribute towards making a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Hepatitis C ribonucleic acid  The most likely diagnosis in this patient is chronic hepatitis C infection. This patient had mild haemophilia,  which was diagnosed following prolonged bleeding following an appendicectomy. It is likely that he received a  blood transfusion at the time and may have been infected with hepatitis C. Blood transfusions were not  routinely screened for hepatitis C before 1990–1992. Patients with chronic hepatitis C infection may remain  largely asymptomatic, but within 15–25 years of infection, cirrhosis may develop. Hepatitis C antibodies and  hepatitis C ribonucleic acid should be checked, with ribonucleic acid being the diagnostic test of choice (as  antibodies alone will only indicate previous exposure).  A  Creatine kinase levels  Creatine kinase levels may be used to identify myositis due to statin therapy. However, there is nothing in the  scenario to suggest that this may be an issue, as the patient does not report any muscle pain or tenderness.  B  Liver ultrasound  Liver ultrasound may indicate the degree of cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C infection; however, this is not the  best test to reveal the diagnosis, as it will only indicate the degree of damage to the liver, not the cause of the  damage.  C  Hepatitis A antibodies  Hepatitis A is spread by the faecal–oral route and is the most common form of viral hepatitis infection  worldwide. It is not spread via blood transfusions.  D  Hepatitis B antibodies  Hepatitis B is an important diagnosis to rule out. It can be spread in the same ways as hepatitis C, via  intravenous injection (drug use/transfusion) or via intercourse. However, blood transfusions have been screened  for hepatitis B since the 1970s and this man has no other risk factors for hepatitis B spread.  A 56-year-old man presents with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 5/15 after being found on the floor by his  neighbour. The only past medical history available is that he has chronic hepatitis C.  Medication found in his bag includes tramadol, diclofenac and furosemide. His temperature is 38.0 °C.  His BP is 100/60 mmHg, with a heart rate of 120 bpm. Heart sounds are normal. There are coarse crackles at  his right lung base. His abdomen is distended, with shifting dullness. His pupils are equal and reactive and the  plantar responses are flexor. He is transferred to the Intensive Care Unit and receives fluid resuscitation and  broad-spectrum antibiotics for his chest. All his usual medications are stopped.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  130 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  13.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  134 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.4 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  130 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  101 fl  76–98 fl  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.6  < 1.1  Urea  11.0 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Bilirubin  38 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  88 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  235 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Albumin  32 g/l  35–55 g/l  Urinalysis  No blood or protein  Computed tomography scan of the  brain  Cerebral atrophy; no intracerebral  haemorrhage or lesions  Computed tomography scan of the  abdomen  Free fluid in the pelvis; cirrhotic liver  Three days later, he becomes oliguric. Ultrasound scan shows no evidence of ureteric obstruction. He has  become apyrexial.  Repeat renal function tests reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Sodium (Na +)  128 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.2 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  25.0 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  300 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Urinary sodium (Na +)  8.0 mmol/l  Blood culture  Negative  Ascitic tap  Polymorphic neutrophil count 30 cells/mm 3; no organisms  What is the most likely diagnosis for his worsening renal function?  A  Septicaemia  B  Drug-induced acute kidney disease  C  Hepatitis B-related membranous glomerulonephritis  D  Acute tubular necrosis  E  Hepatorenal syndrome  Explanation  E    Hepatorenal syndrome  This is usually a diagnosis of exclusion, after other potential causes of acute kidney disease have been ruled out.  The raised white cell count and initial pyrexia are in keeping with likely chest infection, which has been treated.  Hepatorenal syndrome refers to the development of acute kidney disease in a patient who has advanced liver  disease, due to cirrhosis, and who has no identifiable cause of intrinsic renal disease. It usually represents the  end stage of a sequence of reductions in renal perfusion induced by increasingly severe hepatic injury.  Splanchnic vasodilatation appears to play an important role in the decline in renal function in hepatic disease.  The following definition and diagnostic criteria have been proposed for hepatorenal syndrome:  (a) chronic or acute hepatic disease with advanced hepatic failure and portal hypertension  (b) a plasma creatinine concentration >133 µmol/l that progresses over days to weeks  (c) the absence of any other apparent cause for the renal disease, including shock, active sepsis, current  nephrotoxic drugs and the absence of ultrasonographic evidence of obstruction or parenchymal renal  disease. It is particularly important to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is complicated  with acute kidney disease  (d) a urine sodium concentration <10 meq/l (off diuretics) and protein excretion <500 mg/day  (e) lack of improvement in renal function after volume expansion with 1.5 l of isotonic saline.  C  Hepatitis B-related membranous glomerulonephritis  Urinalysis is negative for urine sediment containing red cells or casts, making glomerulonephritis less likely. He  has also been fully fluid resuscitated and remains oliguric.  A  Septicaemia  The fact that this patient is now apyrexial makes continued septicaemia very unlikely as the cause of his kidney  disease.  B  Drug-induced acute kidney disease  Although both diclofenac and furosemide can exacerbate renal impairment, his chronic liver disease is the much  greater contributor to renal dysfunction seen here.  D  Acute tubular necrosis  Acute tubular necrosis is associated with increased renal sodium excretion; urinary sodium here is 8.0 mmol/l,  which is in the normal range.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is under investigation for recurrent fevers and arthralgia. He has had episodes of fevers over  the last 4 years associated with seronegative non-destructive arthropathies. Episodes have been characterised  by elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and have responded to antibiotics. Blood cultures have been persistently  negative.  On this admission, the patient complains of persistent diarrhoea and weight loss over the last 6 months, as well  as myalgia. His wife has noticed that he has become more forgetful of late.  On examination, he is pale and thin, and auscultation reveals a systolic murmur in the aortic area. Central  nervous system (CNS) examination shows signs of mild ataxia.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  115 g/l  135–175 g/l  White Cell Count (WCC)  10.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  300 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Bilirubin  10 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  16 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  21 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Albumin  29 g/l  35–55 g/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  82 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  76 mm/hour  1–20 mm/hour  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Whipple’s disease  Whipple’s disease is a rare but potentially fatal condition caused by an abnormal host immune response to the  intracellular organism Tropheryma whippeli. Symptoms include seronegative arthropathy (> 70%), weight loss  (> 90%) and diarrhoea (> 70%). Cardiac complications including pericarditis and valvular heart disease occur in  up to 30% of patients, and central nervous system (CNS) manifestations (including ocular disturbances, higherfunction abnormalities and cerebellar symptoms) occur in 15%. Biochemical abnormalities include a systemic  inflammatory response with anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia secondary to malabsorption.  The histological hallmarks of the disease are (1) lipid deposition in the lamina propria of intestinal villi and (2)  the presence of lipid-containing macrophages with sickle-like inclusion bodies that stain with diastase-resistant  Periodic acid Schiff reagent (PAS). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based detection from affected tissues and  body fluids is now possible. Treatment is with protracted courses of antibiotics.  A  Histoplasmosis  Although macrophage infiltration of the small bowel is associated with histoplasmosis, the clinical features  seen in this case are not usually seen with histoplasmosis - a large encapsulated organism that predominantly  affects the respiratory system.  C  Giardiasis  This is a parasitic infection that is spread by contaminated food and water. Infection presents with  gastrointestinal symptoms, usually diarrhoea and bloating, but it is not associated with any extra-intestinal  symptoms, so this option is therefore incorrect.  D  H. pylori infection  This condition would not account for the multitude of symptoms seen in this case. H. pylori is associated with  peptic ulcer disease, anaemia and gastric malignancy, but not fevers or arthralgia as is seen in this case.  E  Sickle cell crisis  Sickle cell crisis is usually associated with painful episodes with a drop in haemoglobin caused by sickling. This  patient’s haemoglobin is still 115 g/l.  A 52-year-old premenopausal woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of  epigastric pain that is occasionally retrosternal which is also worse at night. She has tried over-the-counter  antacid preparations which have achieved no relief. Her weight is steady and her bowel habits are normal. Her  father died from gastric malignancy aged 72.  On examination, the patient is obese and her body mass index is 31 kg/m 2. Her GP has checked her  haemoglobin (Hb) level, which is 137 g/l (normal range 115–155 g/l), and the mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  is in the normal range.  Which of the following is the best management step?  A  Check ferritin and then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy  B  Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and refer for endoscopy if there is no resolution within two  weeks  C  Prescribe a PPI and review symptoms in one month  D  Start a PPI and perform breath test screening for Helicobacter pylori  E  Upper GI endoscopy  Explanation  C    Prescribe a PPI and review symptoms in one month  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that in this age group, dyspepsia,  in the absence of dysphagia or evidence of upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding, should be treated with lifestyle  advice and proton pump inhibitor (PPI) if needed. If after one month, symptoms are not controlled, then testing  for H. pylori (breath test or serology) could be carried out. Alternatively, H. pylori screening could be performed  at the beginning, although there is no strong evidence as to which to do first. There needs to be a 2-week  washout period of the PPI for a urea breath test to be reliable. While there are risk factors for gastric  malignancy, including family history, by virtue of her age (under 55 years) and the absence of dysphagia, this  patient does not satisfy the 2-week wait criterion at this point. In the event that her symptoms do not resolve  after treatment, she should be referred to a Gastroenterologist, and endoscopy considered.  A  Check ferritin and then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy  The Hb level is only just below the lower limit of normal and the MCV is normal. Therefore, significant iron  deficiency is unlikely.  B  Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and refer for endoscopy if there is no resolution within two  weeks  A 2-week trial of therapy is too short to make a decision as to the impact on symptoms so would not be  appropriate for this patient.  D  Start a PPI and perform breath test screening for Helicobacter pylori  H. pylori testing should be conducted after a 2-week washout period off PPI, as use of acid suppression can  make interpretation of the test unreliable.  E  Upper GI endoscopy  There are no alarming symptoms such as weight loss, regurgitation of food or anaemia seen here, and the  patient is under 55 years. Therefore, going straight for endoscopy is not appropriate.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with deep jaundice, drowsiness and confusion. He has  been increasingly unwell for the past 3 months, and an ultrasound of his abdomen from 2 weeks earlier  demonstrated a mass in the head of the pancreas, a degree of biliary obstruction and probable metastases  within the liver substance itself.  On examination, he is drowsy and confused, his temperature is 37.8 °C, his BP is 100/60 mmHg with a pulse of  85/min, there are several scratch marks on his skin, and he is deeply jaundiced. He is tender in the epigastrium,  and you can feel a liver edge.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  101 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  8.2 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  102 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.0 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  130 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  105 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Bilirubin  280 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  485 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Which of the following is the most important intervention here?
options: E. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with stenting
questions.explanation:   Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with stenting  This patient has hepatic obstruction, as evidenced by his deep jaundice and obstructive picture on liver function  testing. ERCP with stenting delivered at the same time is the preferred option here, and is likely to drive an  improvement in symptoms for at least a few months.  B  Percutaneous trans-hepatic cholangiography (PTC) tube  PTC is only indicated in the event that the obstruction cannot be relieved by ERCP alone.  A  Oral ciprofloxacin  Ascending cholangitis is a possibility and antibiotics would be used in combination with ERCP. They are not  likely to be effective used in isolation. Recent advice is also to avoid quinolone antibiotics wherever a suitable  alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating side effects.  C  Choledochojejunostomy  Choledochojejunostomy is a potential alternative to ERCP, although this patient’s advanced disease implies that  even this procedure is not an option.  D  Whipple’s procedure  Surgical resection will not be curative, carries a high operative risk and should be avoided here.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Ward with a 2-day history of fever, abdominal pain  and diarrhoea, with bowel opening up to ten times per day. She has a background of ulcerative colitis and is  treated with intravenous hydrocortisone and broad-spectrum antibiotics.  After 72 hours into admission, she still reports to be feeling unwell and is opening her bowels 7–8 times per  day with watery, bloodstained diarrhoea. On examination, she has a temperature of 38.4 °C, a blood pressure of  105/70 mmHg and a heart rate of 90 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is generally tender, although soft, and she  has active bowel sounds.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  101 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  13.9 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  155 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.5 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  110 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  85 mm/h  1 - 20 mm/h  C-reactive protein (CRP)  180 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Abdominal X-ray  Colon diameter 5.5 cm  What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: B. Referral to General Surgical Team
questions.explanation:   Ciclosporin  Intravenous (IV) ciclosporin has a role in induction of remission in patients with severe or fulminant colitis.  According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, it is usually offered to  patients who are on steroids for 72 hours without any improvement. Therefore, it is an appropriate next step in  this case but is not effective for long-term use. Ciclosporin is given as a continuous IV infusion of 2 mg/kg over  24 hours, which can be adjusted according to the concentration of the drug in the blood and the patient’s  response.  B  Referral to General Surgical Team  A referral would be necessary if a colectomy is indicated. A colectomy is indicated in patients with fulminant  colitis and who fail to respond to ciclosporin (due to either failure to respond or relapse) within 4–7 days and in  those with toxic megacolon (diameter ≥ 6 cm or caecum > 9 cm and systemic toxicity) who do not respond to  therapy within 72 hours. Surgery is also indicated if the patient experiences frequent flare-ups and whose  quality of life is adversely affected by the condition.  A  Azathioprine  Azathioprine is recommended in patients with corticosteroid-dependent ulcerative colitis and is an effective  agent for relapse prevention. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest  that if aminosalicylate does not work well in preventing flare-ups, then azathioprine or mercaptopurine can be  used.  D  Infliximab infusion  The NICE guidelines recommend that infliximab is used in the treatment of acute exacerbations of ulcerative  colitis in patients in whom ciclosporin is contraindicated or clinically inappropriate. This is not the case for this  patient, and therefore, ciclosporin should be tried initially.  E  Rectal mesalazine  Mesalazine (5-aminosalicylic acid) is the standard first-line therapy for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis. It is  also used in the maintenance of remission and prevention of relapse of ulcerative colitis. However, it has little  role in cases of fulminant ulcerative colitis or flare-ups.  A 58-year-old man is referred for investigation of dysphagia. This had been gradually worsening over the last  year, but was intermittent in nature and was for both solids and liquids. He also described the frequent  regurgitation of old food several hours after eating.  Recently, he had been experiencing occasional episodes of severe retrosternal chest pain. He denied weight  loss and heartburn. He had no significant past medical history and was on no regular medication. He was a  non-smoker and rarely drank alcohol.  A full clinical examination was entirely normal, as was his full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver  function tests. His CXR was normal, and barium swallow is shown below:    Which one of the following investigations should be performed next?  A  Oesophageal manometry  B  CT scan of the abdomen  C  Endoscopic ultrasound scan  D  Double-contrast barium meal  E  24 hour intraluminal oesophageal pH monitoring  Explanation  A    Oesophageal manometry  The diagnosis is achalasia, where a range of investigations including endoscopy may be normal. The barium  swallow, showing dilatation in the upper portion of the oesophagus with tapering at the lower end (bird beak  appearance), is suggestive of achalasia and the definitive diagnostic test is oesophageal manometry, which will  confirm a high oesophageal resting tone, weak or absent peristalsis and a non-relaxing lower oesophageal  sphincter. Treatment options include endoscopic pneumatic dilation of the LOS (successful in 80% of cases),  intra-sphincteric botulinum toxin injection and surgical division of the LOS (Heller’s cardiomyotomy). There is an  increased risk of carcinoma of the oesophagus in patients with achalasia.  Achalasia has an incidence of 1 per 100 000 per year and is defined as reduced or absent peristalsis and failure  of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) to relax when swallowing. It is due to the degeneration of ganglionic  cells in the nerve plexi of the oesophageal wall. It can present at any age with intermittent dysphagia to both  solids and liquids, regurgitation, severe retrosternal chest pain and aspiration pneumonia.  Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acha.JPG  (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acha.JPG)  D  Double-contrast barium meal  A double-contrast barium meal wouldn’t add further information to that already known about this patient’s  oesophageal dysmotility, and is therefore not useful here.  B  CT scan of the abdomen  Given the barium swallow points towards achalasia and endoscopy has ruled out oesophageal malignancy, the  next important step is manometry. CT of the abdomen is more useful for investigation of intra-abdominal  masses.  C  Endoscopic ultrasound scan  Endoscopic ultrasound of the oesophagus may be of value in investigating underlying oesophageal carcinoma,  but doesn’t have a role here.  E  24 hour intraluminal oesophageal pH monitoring  Intraluminal pH monitoring is most useful when oesophageal reflux is suspected, particularly when it occurs at  night, but the endoscopy examination is equivocal.

questions.question: 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of recently worsening indigestion. He  also complains of fatigue, weight loss and recent night sweats.  Clinical examination shows a BP of 147/86 mmHg, pulse of 70/min and regular and a BMI of 26. He is mildly  tender in the epigastrium. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a suspicious area of mucosa in the stomach  with particularly rigid folds. Biopsy reveals large numbers of lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and  abundant cytoplasm.  Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:   Gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALToma)  MALT is characterised by large numbers of immunocompetent cells in the lamina propria. MALTomas are B-cell  lymphomas comprising large numbers of lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and abundant cytoplasm.  Higher-grade lymphomas show clusters or sheets of blast-like cells. Up to 75% of small low-grade lymphomas  may regress completely after antibiotic therapy for helicobacter eradication. Where treatment fails, surgical  therapy or combinations with radio- and chemotherapy may be considered. In addition, Rituxamab has recently  shown success in achieving remission in this condition.  E  Helicobacter infection  H pylori infection presents with lymphocytic invasion on biopsy but the abnormal lymphocyte morphology seen  here is not present.  A  Gastric carcinoma  Gastric carcinomas can be tubular, mucinous, poorly cohesive or unclassified in histology. A hallmark on  histology is submucosal invasion.  B  Gastric adenoma  Gastric adenomas are rare in Western populations, and rather than showing growth without evidence of  invasion, histology normally reveals at least some evidence of carcinomatous transformation.  D  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma  High grade mature B cell lymphomas in a Western population often present with symptoms of CNS lymphoma  or mediastinal lymphadenopathy picked up with other symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss over a  period of time.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman has chronic autoimmune hepatitis. She is managed on prednisolone and azathioprine.  You review her in the clinic and notice that she has worsening of her jaundice with a rising bilirubin and  increasing ascites.  You admit her; the nurses call you to see her urgently the following morning as she has become increasingly  drowsy. Her blood pressure is 100/50 mmHg, with pyrexia of 38.2 °C.  Which investigation is most likely to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: E. Peritoneal tap for microscopy and culture
questions.explanation:   Peritoneal tap for microscopy and culture  Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in around 8% of cirrhotic patients with ascites, infecting organisms  probably gaining access to the peritoneum via haematological spread. Most frequent infecting organisms are  Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and enterococci. Pain and pyrexia may frequently be absent. A raised neutrophil  count alone in ascitic fluid is enough to commence treatment. Mortality is high, at up to 25%, and recurs in 70%  of patients within one year. Oral quinolones may be used as prophylaxis  A  Computed tomography (CT) head  CT head would be a useful investigation in confusion during which an intracranial cause is suspected or needs  to be excluded. This can be considered in, for example, subdural haematomas (worsening pain and confusion),  subarachnoid haemorrhage (sudden occipital severe headache) or abscess (recent sinusitis or other infection,  headache and fever). In this patient there is a clear cause for confusion – acute decompensation of the liver.  B  Electroencephalograpm (EEG)  EEG can demonstrate encephalopathy, but it is unlikely to be of significant aid in decision making as there is  sufficient evidence of liver decompensation clinically.  C  Blood culture  Blood culture should be taken in this patient to help guide antibiotic therapy, but is unlikely to be very specific in  making the diagnosis. It can demonstrate bowel organisms in this setting, but may not give much help  regarding the exact origin, nor would it provide an answer in a timely fashion.  D  Lumbar puncture  A lumbar puncture is a useful investigation in a confused patient with fever, but the clinical picture already  suggests a clear cause of this. If he had symptoms of meningitis as well, such as photophobia or neck stiffness,  then it would be a diagnostic investigation.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man who has a 20-year history of ulcerative colitis (UC) presents to the gastroenterology clinic  for review. His UC is relatively quiescent, although most recently he has begun to suffer from tiredness, itching  and vague right upper quadrant pain.  On examination, you can feel two fingers’-breadth hepatomegaly. His only medication is salazopyrine.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  121 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  6.0 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  320 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  420 u/l  30 - 150 u/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  74 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Which of the following is the most effective therapy for his underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Liver transplantation    Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for patients with decompensated cirrhosis with a background of  PSC. Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase and a positive history of ulcerative colitis make PSC a likely  diagnosis. Complications of this condition include advanced-stage liver disease with hepatic decompensation.  Around 70% of patients diagnosed with PSC are men, with an average age of around 40 years. Up to 90% of  patients diagnosed with PSC have co-existent inflammatory bowel disease, normally ulcerative colitis.  Cholangiocarcinoma is also an established complication of PSC. Indications for liver transplantation in patients  with PSC do not differ from those with other forms of chronic liver disease, which primarily relate to  complications of portal hypertension, chronic liver failure and impaired quality of life. Moreover, patients with  PSC have specific indications for liver transplant, which include recurrent bacterial cholangitis, intractable  pruritis and cholangiocarcinoma.  B  Penicillamine  As described in a systemic review by Klingenberg et al., there is insufficient evidence to refute or support the  use of penicillamine for patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).  Reference: Klingenberg, S.L. and Chen, W. (2006). D-penicillamine for primary sclerosing cholangitis. Cochrane  Database Syst Rev. Jan 25(1):CD004182.  A  Cholestyramine  Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant, is used to treat hyperlipidaemia and for the pruritus of biliary  obstruction and chronic liver disease.  D  Prednisolone  Corticosteroids, e.g. prednisolone, have not demonstrated any improvement in disease activity or outcome of  PSC patients, as evident in a systemic review by Giljaca et al.  Reference: Giljaca, V., Poropat, G., Stimac, D. et al. (2010). Glucocorticosteroids for primary sclerosing  cholangitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. Jan 20(1):CD004036  E  Azathioprine  Many immunosuppressive agents are used in the management of patients with PSC, However, there no  substantial evidence for its role in prognosis of patients with PSC is noted. A review study by Goode et al.  mentioned controversial evidence underlying the usage of immunosuppressive therapy and other prospective  agents that may bring new hope regarding the treatment of PSC in the 21st century.  Reference: Goode, E.C. and Rushbrook, S.M. (2016). A review of the medical treatment of primary sclerosing  cholangitis in the 21st century. Therapeutic Advances in Chronic Disease, 7(1), 68–85.  http://doi.org/10.1177/2040622315605821  A 50-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a 5-month history of tiredness. He has no previous  medical history and takes no medication. There is no history of weight loss or fever. He eats a regular healthy  diet and has no urinary or bowel symptoms. His examination is unremarkable.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  115 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.0 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  300 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  70 fl  80 - 100 fl  Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH)  20 pg  27 - 33 pg  Ferritin  10 µg/l  24 - 355 µg/l (male)  Vitamin B 12  500 ng/l  160 - 760 ng/l  Folate  9 μg/l  2.0 - 11.0 μg/l  Urinalysis: negative.  Which investigation should be performed next?  A  Capsule endoscopy  B  Faecal occult blood testing  C  Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD)  D  Outpatient colonoscopy  E  Urgent referral to Colorectal Services under 2-week wait  Explanation  B    Faecal occult blood testing  Faecal occult blood testing is appropriate in this patient. Indications for faecal occult blood testing include:  An abdominal mass  Change in bowel habit  Iron-deficiency anaemia  ≥40 years and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain  ≥50 years with rectal bleeding and either:  Abdominal pain  Weight loss.  ≥Aged 50 years with any of the following unexplained symptoms:  Rectal bleeding  Abdominal pain  Weight loss.  ≥60 years with any anaemia.  As this patient is 50 years old and has iron deficiency anaemia, a faecal occult blood sample is recommended.  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) as the  primary method of testing. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies and urinalysis would also be appropriate  investigations here.  A  Capsule endoscopy  This investigation is usually reserved for patients who have a normal OGD and colonoscopy but remain  anaemic despite iron replacement therapy. This investigation is then performed to rule out a small bowel cause  for their anaemia such as Crohn’s disease or angiodysplasia. It is not a first-line investigation.  C  Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD)  In all men, post-menopausal women and women aged over 50 years, mandatory investigations for iron  deficiency anaemia include an OGD. However, more simple non-invasive investigations, such as a faecal occult  blood sample, would be considered first.  D  Outpatient colonoscopy  This would be indicated, particularly to exclude malignancy as a cause for this patient’s anaemia. However, it  would not be the next test performed as it is an invasive procedure.  E  Urgent referral to Colorectal Services under 2-week wait  Urgent referral under the 2-week wait is not appropriate here. Criteria for a 2-week wait referral for colorectal  cancer investigation include:  patients aged ≥ 40 years with weight loss and abdominal pain  patients aged ≥ 50 years with unexplained rectal bleeding  patients aged ≥ 60 years with iron deficiency anaemia or change in bowel habit  positive faecal occult blood  anal or rectal mass on examination  abdominal mass on examination  patients aged < 50 years with rectal bleeding and any:  abdominal pain  change in bowel habit  weight loss  iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.question: A 54-year-old businessman presents with a 12-month history of intermittent lower back and right knee pain  and diarrhoea. He has previously undergone investigations for diarrhoea when a gastroscopy and colonoscopy  performed 8 months ago revealed a small area of non-specific inflammation in the ascending colon, but  investigations were otherwise normal.  He has lost approximately 3 kg in weight over the last 18 months. He takes no regular medication, drinks  occasional alcohol and smokes 10 cigarettes per day.  Cardiovascular and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Examination of his spine reveals tenderness over  the sacroiliac joints but no restriction in movement. He has a small right knee effusion.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  120 g/l  135–175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  108 fl  76–98 fl  White cell count (WCC)  5.6 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  206 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  38 mm/hour  1–20 mm/hour  Sodium (Na +)  136 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.8 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  5.3 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  84 µmol/l  50–120 mol/l  Albumin  40 g/l  35–55 g/l  Bilirubin  12 µmol/l  2–17 mol/l  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Whipple’s disease  Whipple’s disease is caused by infection with Tropheryma whippelii. The organism can be identified by PAS  staining of a jejunal biopsy. It is an uncommon condition classically affecting men aged 40–60 years.  Gastrointestinal symptoms of diarrhoea, malabsorption and steatorrhoea are often preceded by arthropathy. In  the past, various antibiotic regimens (including penicillins) were used on an empirical basis. Tetracycline  treatment seems to be associated with a high frequency of relapse, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole  (160/800 mg orally twice daily) or long-term ampicillin given for around a year is now recommended.  A  Chronic pancreatitis  Chronic pancreatitis is a syndrome involving progressive inflammatory changes in the pancreas that result in  permanent structural damage, which can lead to impairment of exocrine and endocrine function. Chronic  pancreatitis may be asymptomatic over long periods of time, can present with a fibrotic mass or there may be  symptoms of pancreatic insufficiency without pain. The serum amylase and lipase concentrations tend to be  normal in patients with chronic pancreatitis, but are almost always elevated with acute disease.  Morphologically, chronic pancreatitis is a patchy focal disease characterised by a mononuclear infiltrate and  fibrosis. There are no joint symptoms associated with chronic pancreatitis.  B  Coeliac disease  Coeliac disease is a common and underdiagnosed condition, which may present at any age. It is a  hypersensitivity to gluten found in wheat, rye and barley. The gliadin fraction of the protein provokes an  inflammatory response causing subtotal or total villous atrophy of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption.  It classically presents with a history of diarrhoea, weight loss, oral ulceration, lethargy and anaemia (folate, B 12  or iron-deficient). There is an association with dermatitis herpetiformis, a very pruritic polymorphic skin rash,  and an increased risk of developing gastrointestinal malignancy. Treatment is by maintaining a strict diet  avoiding foods containing wheat, rye, oats or barley. The clinical picture in this scenario is not consistent with  Coeliac disease.  D  Increased plasma renin activity  Patients with renin-secreting tumours are typically young (average age 22 years) and have severe hypertension  and hypokalaemia. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) appears to be the diagnostic procedure of  choice, since false-negative results occur with arteriography or renal vein renin sampling. Surgical removal of  the tumour cures the disease. The clinical picture in this scenario is not consistent with increased plasma renin  levels.  E  Ulcerative colitis  Ulcerative colitis is characterised by recurring episodes of inflammation limited to the mucosal layer of the  colon. It commonly involves the rectum and may extend in a proximal and continuous fashion to involve other  parts of the colon. Patients with ulcerative colitis usually present with diarrhoea, which may be associated with  blood. Bowel movements are frequent and small in volume as a result of rectal inflammation. Associated  symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, urgency, tenesmus and incontinence. Patients with mainly distal  disease may have constipation accompanied by frequent discharge of blood and mucus. The endoscopic  findings in patients with ulcerative colitis include loss of vascular markings due to engorgement of the mucosa,  giving it an erythematous appearance. In addition, granularity of the mucosa, petechiae, exudates, oedema,  erosions, touch friability and spontaneous bleeding may be present. More severe cases may be associated with  macro-ulcerations, profuse bleeding and copious exudates. The endoscopic findings in this scenario are not  consistent with ulcerative colitis.

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department in the early hours of the morning after  vomiting blood. Her blood pressure is 125/85 mmHg, with a pulse of 89/min, you arrange routine bloods.  Around 30 min after arrival, she has a further small (100 ml) haematemesis. Her daughter is briefly questioned  and reports that her mother has been previously well apart from mild indigestion and occasional angina.  She has not been taking any medication, has no history of gastrointestinal (GI) or liver disease and does not  drink alcohol.  She is taken into the resuscitation room and her initial assessment is outlined below.  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Bilirubin  10 µmol/l  1 - 22 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  21 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Albumin  40 g/l  35 - 55 g/l  Haemoglobin (Hb)  80 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  300 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Prothrombin time (PT)  12 s  11 - 14 s  Pulse  125 bpm  Blood pressure  80/40 mmHg  Respiratory rate  38/min  Which of the following would you instigate immediately?
options: A. Triple lumen central line placement
C. 0.9% normal saline via peripheral cannula
D. High dose intravenous (IV) proton pump inhibitor
questions.explanation:   0.9% normal saline via peripheral cannula  The initial step in the management of upper GI haemorrhage is the assessment of hemodynamic state. A  systolic blood pressure of 80mmHg identifies the patient as ‘High risk’ with severe acute bleeding. 0.9% saline  via peripheral cannula is given immediately to stabilize the patient, making it the best answer. Urgent GI  endoscopy is indicated as soon as possible in this patient after adequate resuscitation as there is increased risk  of death due to bleeding in this patient in view of his age, blood pressure reading and history of ischemic heart  disease.  A  Triple lumen central line placement  Triple lumen Central line is desirable in conditions of significant cardiac overload, but it should not interfere with  rapid volume resuscitation via large bore peripheral cannula.  B  O negative (uncrossed) transfusion  Patients with evidence of hemodynamic compromised state are given IV fluids and cross-matched for 2-4 units  of red blood cells. However, it is rarely required to administer type specific or O-negative transfusion. Blood loss  seen in this patient should be replaced with crystalloid initially, followed by typed and cross-matched blood.  Unmatched blood should only be used in patients with uncontrolled blood loss who are unresponsive to other  fluid resuscitation.  D  High dose intravenous (IV) proton pump inhibitor  High dose IV proton pump inhibitors have been shown to be of benefit in upper GI haemorrhage but only to  prevent re-bleeding, and do not form an integral part of initial resuscitation attempts.  E  IV Terlipressin  According to British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage , it is  important to exclude variceal haemorrhage due to liver disease in any patient with significant hematemesis.  Normal liver function tests and lack of history makes ‘oesophageal varices’ highly unlikely. Thus IV terlipressin is  not recommended in this case. Teripressin is preferred in reducing bleeding, as it reduces blood flow in  splanchnic circulation and decreases portal blood pressure.  A 51-year-old Chinese man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with hepatitis B. He is teetotal.  Investigations:  Investigation  Hepatitis B surface antigen  Hepatitis B e antigen  Hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) level  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  Result  Positive  Negative  2100 copies/ml  96 U/l  Normal value  Negative  Negative  Negative  5–30 IU/l  Similar results were observed when these tests are repeated three months later and the liver biopsy shows  early cirrhosis.  Which of the following is the most appropriate management?  A  Close monitoring of liver function test  B  Repeat biopsy in two years  C  Start pegylated interferon  D  Start pegylated interferon and ribavirin  E  Start lamivudine  Explanation  C    Start pegylated interferon  The patient has e antigen-negative (eAg) chronic hepatitis B. The eAg negativity indicates there is no active  viral replication; however, raised alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels and high viral titres indicate chronic  active infection, which is confirmed on biopsy, thereby necessitating treatment. The National Institute for Health  and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines now recommend treatment in patients who meet the following criteria:  adults aged > 30 years with Hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) > 2000 IU/ml and  abnormal ALT (> 30 IU/ml in men; > 19 IU/ml in women) on two consecutive tests, three months apart  adults aged < 30 years with HBV DNA > 2000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (> 30 IU/ml in men; > 19 IU/ml in  women) on two consecutive tests, three months apart, if there is evidence of necro-inflammation or  fibrosis on liver biopsy or a transient elastography score > 6 kPa  adults who have HBV DNA > 20 000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (> 30 IU/ml in men; > 19 IU/ml in women)  on two consecutive tests conducted three months apart, regardless of age or the extent of liver disease.  patients without a liver biopsy with a transient elastography score > 11 kPa.  The NICE guidelines recommend first-line treatment with pegylated interferon alfa-2a in patients with  compensated liver disease for 48 weeks. Entecavir and tenofovir are offered as second-line treatments where  pegylated interferon therapy has failed or is not tolerated.  D  Start pegylated interferon and ribavirin  This is offered as first-line therapy for patients with hepatitis C. However, NICE has recently recommended new  antivirals for hepatitis C, eg sofosbuvir–velpatasvir (Epclusa®), and patients are being selected based on clinical  need. Therefore, patients may elect to defer treatment with interferon–ribavirin due to its side-effect profile and  opt to wait for the newer, better-tolerated antivirals.  A  Close monitoring of liver function test  The patient has chronic hepatitis B with histological evidence of early cirrhosis, making treatment imperative to  avoid progression to further fibrosis and to reduce hepatocellular carcinoma risk.  B  Repeat biopsy in two years  Having established that the patient has early cirrhosis, it is clear that he requires treatment. Indications for a  further biopsy would be in cases of suspected hepatocellular carcinoma or failure to respond to treatment and  therefore exclude an alternative diagnosis. Transient elastography (FibroScan), as an assessment of liver  stiffness and as a surrogate marker of cirrhosis, has reduced the number of biopsies performed before  commencing antiviral therapy.  E  Start lamivudine  Lamivudine is only indicated as an adjunct in patients who are hepatitis B e antigen-positive and with  compensated liver disease and who, despite 96 weeks of tenofovir, still have detectable hepatitis B DNA or in  patients who are likely to be immunocompromised for six months with hepatitis B DNA < 2000 IU/ml.

questions.question: A 42-year-old pre-menopausal woman presented to her general practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of  epigastric pain, occasionally retrosternal and worse at night. She had tried over-the-counter antacid  preparations but had achieved no relief. Her weight was steady and bowel habit normal. There was no history  of gastric malignancy in the family.  Examination was unremarkable except for obesity. Full blood count is normal.  Which of the following describes the next best management step?
options: A. Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and review symptoms in one month
C. Start a PPI and perform a Carbon 13 urea breath test. If this is positive, prescribe pylori eradication therapy
D. Check repeat haemoglobin in three months. If low, then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy.
E. Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on a proton pump inhibitor
questions.explanation:   Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and review symptoms in one month  NICE guidelines state in this age group that dyspepsia, in the absence of alarm symptoms, should be treated  with lifestyle advice and PPI if needed. In the event that symptoms of indigestion have not been relieved, H.  pylori testing or upper GI endoscopy can then be considered.  D  Check repeat haemoglobin in three months. If low, then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI)  endoscopy.  This is the appropriate course of action where there are alarm features, these including weight loss, persistent  vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass.  B  Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy  A routine endoscopy would be considered where symptoms don’t improve after 1 month of empirical PPI  treatment.  C  Start a PPI and perform a Carbon 13 urea breath test. If this is positive, prescribe pylori eradication  therapy  Urea breath testing for H. pylori should ideally be conducted off PPI for a period of at least 2 weeks.  E  Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on a proton  pump inhibitor  This time period is too short to assess response to PPI therapy. At least four weeks of therapy to assess  response is required.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male patient presents with non-bloody diarrhoea with mucus and 1-stone weight loss over six  weeks. He has had no recent travel except to France for a holiday one year ago. All his family and friends are  well but his uncle has diarrhoea for which he has to take tablets.  On examination, he looks unwell, his BMI is 21, BP is 110/70 mmHg, heart rate is 75/min and regular. His  abdomen is soft but there is mild tenderness. You suspect inflammatory bowel disease and perform a  sigmoidoscopy and biopsy.  Which one of the following findings would most favour a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis over Crohn’s  disease?
questions.explanation:   Crypt abscesses  Ulcerative colitis is inflammation confined to the mucosa and lamina propria with crypt abscesses. The mucosal  appearance is characterized by erosions, mucopus, and edema with a diffused involvement of large intestine  D  Non-caseating granulomas  Non-caseating granuloma are present in less than 25 % of patients but highly suggestive of crohn’s disease.  B  Ileitis  One third of crohn’s disease cases involve the small intestine (especially the terminal ileum) causing ileitis.  C  Skip lesions  Skip lesions are seen characteristically in crohn’s disease, which are areas of normal appearing mucosa adjacent  to inflamed mucosa.  E  Large joint arthritis  Arthritis of large joints is associated with crohn’s disease, along with other conditions such as ankylosing  spondylitis, conjunctivitis, episcleritis, sacroilitis.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic after presenting to his General Practitioner with a 1year history of tiredness. He has no previous medical history and takes no regular medication. He denies weight  loss or a change in bowel habits. He has a varied diet, including red meat. There is nothing to find on  examination.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal Values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  115 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.0 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  300 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  70 fl  80 - 100 fl  Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH)  20 pg  27 - 33 pg  Ferritin  10 µg/l  24 - 355 µg/l (male)  Vitamin B 12  500 ng/l  160 - 760 ng/l  Folate  9 μg/l  2.0 - 11.0 μg/l  Which of the following investigations should be performed next?
questions.explanation:   Urinalysis  In the developed world, iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) has a prevalence of 2–5% among adult men and postmenopausal women. The British Society of Gastroenterology published guidelines on the investigation of such  patients. For the investigation of IDA, urinalysis for blood is recommended, as an estimated 1% of patients with  IDA will have renal tract malignancy caused by haematuria and haemosiderin deposition in the tumour. This is a  non-invasive test and, therefore, should be performed next on this patient. A faecal occult blood test is also  indicated.  C  Colonoscopy  This would be indicated, particularly to exclude malignancy as a cause for this patient’s anaemia. However, it  would not be the next test that is performed, as it is an invasive procedure.  B  Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy  In all men, post-menopausal women and women aged over 50 years, mandatory investigations for IDA include  an oesophageal-gastro-duodenoscopy, looking for a source of occult bleeding. However, this would not be the  next test you would perform.  D  Iron studies  Iron studies in this patient would reveal a low iron level and high total iron binding capacity. This does nothing  but confirm the iron deficiency anaemia we know exists. Iron studies might be useful in cases where iron  deficiency is suspected but ferritin is high due to a presumed inflammatory response or in iron overload.  E  Capsule endoscopy  This investigation is usually reserved for patients who have a normal OGD and colonoscopy but remain  anaemic despite iron replacement therapy. This investigation is then performed to rule out a small bowel cause  for their anaemia such as Crohn’s disease or angiodysplasia.

questions.question: A 59-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an acute upper GI bleed. He admits to having  had symptoms of indigestion for the past 6 months, he smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks 30 units of  alcohol per week. Most recently he has been taking ibuprofen for a back injury.  On examination, is blood pressure (BP) is 110/70 mmHg, with a pulse of 90/min; on moving from lying to  sitting, his systolic falls to 90 mmHg and his pulse increases to 105/min. He is acutely tender in the epigastrium  and vomits up a mix of fresh and altered blood after the consultation.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin  87 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.2 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets  152 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  138 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine  110 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Urea  18.2 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Albumin  38 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  24 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Upper GI endoscopy  Large bleeding DU,  injected during the procedure  Which of the following further interventions has been shown to positively impact on prognosis?
questions.explanation:   IV omeprazole  IV omeprazole has been proven in a number of meta-analyses to impact positively on mortality when used in  addition to optimal endoscopic therapy. The aim of IV PPI therapy is to increase the pH in the stomach to  promote coagulation. Oral PPI has also been shown to reduce the length of hospital stay and re-bleeding rates.  B  Oral lactulose  Lactulose is used to reduce absorption and production of ammonia from a blood meal in patients with liver  failure who have had a significant GI bleed.  A  Oral propranolol  Oral propranolol is used as a chronic treatment in patients with proven portal hypertension and varices.  D  Oral famotidine  Oral H2 receptor antagonists have not been shown to reduce the risk of ulcer re-bleeding.  E  IV terlipressin  Terlipressin is an acute treatment that has a role in the management of variceal bleeding. This patient has risk  factors and history suggestive of peptic ulcer disease, and a bleeding duodenal ulcer is found on upper GI  endoscopy.  Leontiadis GI, Sreedharan A, Dorward S, et al. Systematic reviews of the clinical effectiveness and costeffectiveness of proton pump inhibitors in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Health Technol Assess. Dec  2007;11(51):iii-iv, 1-164.

questions.question: You are asked to review a 65-year-old retired politician in the Coronary Care Unit who was admitted 6 days ago  with a non ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).  On admission, he was haemodynamically stable and apyrexial. He developed atrial fibrillation 24 h after  admission and was commenced on intravenous digoxin.  On questioning, he complains of severe abdominal pain, which is initially dull in nature but has now become  sharp and radiates to his back. This pain is precipitated by meals and he finds it worse after food. He has never  had similar symptoms previously and denies any chest pain. His drug chart shows that he is currently on  aspirin, clopidogrel, digoxin, low molecular weight heparin, atorvastatin, omeprazole and regular salbutamol  inhalers.  He was diagnosed with non-insulin-dependent diabetes 6 years ago, and had an inferior myocardial infarction 2  years after that. There is a strong family history of ischaemic heart disease. He is also hypertensive and has mild  chronic obstructive airway disease. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks a glass of brandy in the  evening.  On examination, he looks pale and unwell. He has xanthelasma. His heart rate is 120 beats/min and regular  and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. His temperature is 37.5 °C and saturation is 98% on 2 l oxygen. The jugular  venous pressure is not visible and there is a soft systolic murmur at the apex. He has a left carotid bruit. There  are sparse bibasal crackles on chest examination. His abdomen is tender in the epigastric and umbilical area.  There is no palpable aortic aneurysm or ascites. Scanty bowel sounds are audible.  Investigations are as below:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  110 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  14.2 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  220 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  93 fl  80 - 100 fl  International normalized ratio (INR) 1.3  < 1.1  Sodium (Na +)  141 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  5.3 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Urea  14.0 mmol/l  2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  147 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Bicarbonate (HCO 3-)  15 mmol/l  22 - 29 mmol/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  34 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Liver function tests  Normal  Amylase  380 u/l  Electrocardiogram  Sinus tachycardia and Q waves on inferior leads  Chest and abdominal radiographs  Normal  23 - 85 u/l  Which of the following is likely to be the most useful next investigation?
options: E. CT scan of the abdomen with angiography
questions.explanation:   CT scan of the abdomen with angiography  CT scan of the abdomen with angiography. The combination of acute abdominal pain 15-30 min post-meal,  relative hypotension (note normal hypertensive) and acidosis all point towards acute mesenteric ischaemia. The  condition is often associated with modest elevations in amylase. He is diabetic, a long-term smoker and has had  a cardiac event in the past. All these favour atherosclerosis, making the diagnosis of intestinal ischaemia more  likely in this situation, although other differential diagnosis includes acute or chronic pancreatitis. Carcinoma of  the pancreas normally has a more insidious onset. Increased intestinal motility after a meal exacerbates  ischaemia, causing pain. Mesenteric ischaemia is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion. In this situation a  computed tomography (CT) scan will help exclude necrosis of the pancreas, and mesenteric angiography would  help validate the clinical suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia. The patient will probably need a laparotomy, which  will be high risk in view of recent coronary event, but mortality is extremely high without surgery. An arterial  blood gas will no doubt show a metabolic acidosis, and amylase can be normal in chronic pancreatitis.  A  Blood cultures  Blood cultures may reveal evidence of bowel pathogens, but they won’t reveal the underlying cause of this  patient’s acute presentation.  B  Urgent digoxin level  Given there is tachycardia, and no signs of digoxin toxicity such as yellow vision, nausea or vomiting, digoxin  toxicity is very unlikely.  C  Creatine kinase  There are no specific pointers towards a further myocardial infarction or towards rhabdomyolysis.  D  Re-check troponin  The presentation with abdominal pain and hypotension is much more consistent with a primary abdominal  cause rather than an acute myocardial infarction.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intermittent jaundice and right upper quadrant pain.  She drinks minimal alcohol and is a non-smoker. She had an emergency surgery many years ago when she  presented with diarrhoea and abdominal pain.  On examination, she is mildly icteric. There is no lymphadenopathy. There is a visible scar on the abdomen.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Bilirubin  101 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  54 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  370 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)  240 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  What is the most likely operation she has had in the past?
options: A. Partial gastrectomy for gastric ulcer
B. Ileal resection for Crohn’s disease
C. Right hemicolectomy for caecal carcinoma
D. Left lobectomy of the liver for carcinoid tumour
E. Jejunal resection for gastrointestinal lymphoma
questions.explanation:   Ileal resection for Crohn’s disease  Her predominantly cholestatic liver function tests and abdominal pain would be consistent with biliary  calculi/choledocolithiasis. Ileal resection reduces the reabsorption of bile salts and as a result, a reduction in the  enterohepatic circulation of bile salts. This, in turn increases the risk of cholesterol stone formation.  C  Right hemicolectomy for caecal carcinoma  Although part of the ileum may be resected in a right hemicolectomy (and thus lead to bile salt malabsorption),  this is not guaranteed whereas ileal resection for Crohn’s disease is much more likely to lead to this side effect.  A  Partial gastrectomy for gastric ulcer  This is associated with an increased frequency of iron deficiency anaemia and B 12 deficiency (due to the reduced  acidic environment required to convert Fe3+ to the more absorbable Fe2+ and the reduction in parietal cells to  produce intrinsic factor).  D  Left lobectomy of the liver for carcinoid tumour  Left liver lobectomy is not associated with the formation of gallstones. Indeed, depending on the position of the  tumour the gall bladder may need to be resected as well.  E  Jejunal resection for gastrointestinal lymphoma  Depending on the length resected, small bowel resection may result in short bowel syndrome characterised by  malabsorption, maldigestion and malnutrition and frequently diarrhoea. However, it is not associated with the  formation of gallstones.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her husband, complaining of upper  abdominal and lower chest pain radiating to the back. As part of their fortieth wedding anniversary  celebrations, they had been out for a large meal, at which they had consumed more alcohol than they were  normally used to.  On returning home, she had become nauseated and had vomited three times, and developed sudden-onset  upper abdominal and lower chest pain and, subsequently shortness of breath.  On examination, she is tachycardic with a heart rate of 105 bpm, and tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 25  breaths per minute and oxygen saturations of 94% on air, and has a temperature of 37.8 °C. On abdominal  examination, there is firmness in the upper abdomen.
