options: A. CXR is completed and is shown below:  By Jto410 (In my work as a radiologist) [GFDL (http://www.gnu.org/copyleft/fdl.html) or CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia Commons Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Boerhaave syndrome    Boerhaave syndrome is defined as a spontaneous (as opposed to an iatrogenic) oesophageal rupture. It is  classically associated with violent vomiting and is more common in men than in women. It most commonly  occurs in the distal oesophagus and typically affects the left posterior wall. Unlike in Mallory–Weiss syndrome  (in which a partial-thickness tear occurs), haematemesis is uncommon in Boerhaave syndrome.  Instead, the classic presentation is vomiting, followed by sudden onset of severe retrosternal chest pain/upper  abdominal pain. Other symptoms may include shortness of breath, odynophagia and pleuritic pain.  Clinical findings include surgical emphysema, pleural effusions (normally left-sided, as this is where the  perforation tends to be) and – depending upon the interval between onset and presentation – features of  mediastinitis.  A CXR may be normal early in the disease process but can demonstrate pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax,  subcutaneous emphysema and pleural effusions as the condition progresses. The X-ray shows streaky linear  opacities tracking down the mediastinum, which indicates subcutaneous emphysemam and, therefore,  pneumomediastinum.  CT scans may confirm the diagnosis and demonstrate any associated collections. In contrast, the pattern of  contrast extravasation on a water-soluble contrast swallow helps to define the anatomy and extent of the leak.  Definitive management of the condition is surgical.  E  Spontaneous pneumothorax  The radiological findings make a spontaneous pneumothorax very unlikely to be the unifying diagnosis. Severe  coughing and vomiting can precipitate a spontaneous pneumothorax. However, the history and clinical features  are more suggestive of Boerhaave syndrome.  A  Aspiration pneumonitis  Although vomiting, particularly while intoxicated or with a reduced GCS score, may predispose patients to  aspiration pneumonitis, the presence of severe lower chest and abdominal pain makes pneumonitis less likely.  The CXR findings show a pneumomediastinum, more likely to be secondary to oesophageal rupture from  vomiting.  C  Mallory–Weiss tear  A Mallory–Weiss tear is unlikely here, given the lack of haematemesis and the systemic response following the  vomiting.  D  Perforated peptic ulcer  A perforated peptic ulcer could explain the vomiting and abdominal discomfort but would not explain the CXR  findings.

questions.question: A 49-year-old woman is referred to the Cardiology Clinic with a heart murmur and symptoms of flushing,  especially when she drinks alcohol. She has a history of atrial fibrillation and thyroid disease.  An echocardiogram and ultrasound scan are arranged, but she misses her appointments and defaults to followup.  Nine months later, she re-presents to the Emergency Department with widespread pigmentation on her face  and neck, confusion and diarrhoea.  What is the cause for her new symptoms?
questions.explanation:   Pellagra  Pellagra is characterised by the ‘4Ds’, which are dementia, diarrhoea, dermatitis and death. The rash is  photosensitive and normally affects the face, neck and forearm. It is rare and can be either primary or secondary.  Primary causes include niacin or tryptophan (precursor of niacin) deficiency. Secondary causes include carcinoid  syndrome, which is what this woman has. Patients with carcinoid get pellagra as the tumour cells convert  tryptophan to serotonin, thereby reducing endogenous niacin production. It can also present in patients with  anorexia nervosa, chronic alcoholism, gastrointestinal tuberculosis and human immunodeficiency virus. In  carcinoid syndrome, patients develop right-sided valvular disease and, if she has attended for her  echocardiogram, the possible findings are tricuspid incompetence or pulmonary stenosis.  C  Cerebral abscess  A cerebral abscess is a focal collection within the brain parenchyma. It can occur either through direct spread  from the ears, sinuses or oropharynx, or by haematogenous spread. It presents with headache, changes in  mental state and fever. The absence of high fever and headache, and the presence of diarrhoea and rash, makes  this a less likely diagnosis.  A  Cerebral systemic lupus erythematosus  SLE is an idiopathic chronic inflammatory disease which is characterised by the presence of antinuclear  antibodies. Presentation is varied as SLE can affect virtually any organ. In some patients the presentation can be  neuropsychiatric, causing a broad range of neurological deficits which could explain this patient’s confusion.  However, the skin involvement in SLE is usually in the form of a butterfly rash or discoid lesions, rather than the  type of pigmentation this patient has, which is why this is a less likely diagnosis. In addition, SLE is not a good  explanation for diarrhoea.  B  Cerebral tuberculosis  TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which can cause infection in almost any organ. In 1% of TB cases  the presentation is with tuberculous meningitis. This presents with a subacute febrile illness preceded by an  insidious headache and malaise, then characterised by meningismus, vomiting and confusion. It can proceed to  coma as well. It is of much higher risk in the presence of HIV. Whilst this could be an explanation for her  confusion, the absence of meningism and headache makes this a less likely diagnosis, which also could not  explain her rash.  D  Amiodarone toxicity  Amiodarone is an anti-arrhythmic drug which can cause multiple side effects. In the lungs it can cause  interstitial pneumonitis, in the thyroid it can cause both hyper- and hypothyroidism, and it also causes AV block,  photosensitivity rash and gastrointestinal upset. Whilst it could explain many of the patient’s symptoms,  including a rash which could be photosensitive in nature, it would not explain the confusion or the previous  murmur.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to Outpatients after noticing the whites of her eyes changing colour. She is 36  weeks’ pregnant with her first child. She feels well in herself and has no relevant past medical history other  than a transient episode of jaundice in her late teens, and takes no medication. There is no history of recent  travel.  Clinical examination reveals icteric sclerae and excoriations on the upper arms.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Bilirubin  150 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  150 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  600 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Albumin  40 g/l  35–55 g/l  Urinalysis  Bilirubin +++  Haemoglobin (Hb)  110 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  5.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  350 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Prothrombin time (PT)  17 s  10.6–14.9 s  What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets)
E. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
questions.explanation:   Cholestasis of pregnancy  Cholestasis of pregnancy is by far the most likely diagnosis. This condition is caused by a bile acid transporter  defect and usually manifests in the last trimester. It is not associated with significant constitutional symptoms  for the mother, although the risk of stillbirth and postpartum haemorrhage is slightly increased. Milder episodes  may have occurred earlier in life associated with hormonal contraception, and it recurs in subsequent  pregnancies. Prothrombin time may be prolonged in any cholestatic process due to deficiency of vitamin K.  Pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome and acute fatty liver of pregnancy form a spectrum of disease known as  toxaemias of pregnancy. All are associated with constitutional symptoms and are potentially life-threatening.  A  Pre-eclampsia  Pre-eclampsia is defined as pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria. There can also be oedema, but  this is not essential for a diagnosis. It can become life-threatening and any organ can be affected. Blood  pressure would by greater than 160/100 mmHg and proteinuria should be greater than 0.3 g/24 h. Eclampsia is  evidenced by convulsions following features of pre-eclampsia. The patient may present with severe headache,  new oedema, RUQ tenderness or visual disturbances, and examination can show oedema, clonus and  papilloedema. Pre-eclampsia is associated with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) in 20% of cases, but  jaundice is unusual in all but severe cases and proteinuria would be expected.  B  HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets)  The vast majority of cases occur with pre-eclampsia and this has similar clinical features, but with the addition  of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets. The absence of a low platelet count excludes HELP.  D  Hepatitis E  Hepatitis E is an enterically spread RNA virus, the epidemic form of which has a high (10–20%) mortality in  pregnant women in developing countries. It is especially common in India, but in the absence of any travel  history this is a very unlikely diagnosis.  E  Acute fatty liver of pregnancy  This is a rare condition which tends to occur late in pregnancy and is associated with first pregnancy and preeclampsia. It is associated with nausea, vomiting, fever, headache and pruritis and can present with jaundice on  examination. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is associated with abnormalities of synthetic function, and therefore  serum albumin would be expected to be low. The absence of clinical symptoms as well makes this unlikely.  A 38-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of feeling unwell and very lethargic. He is a known  hypertensive. His wife tells you he has been rather stressed at work recently and is drinking fairly heavily.  As a child, he was found to have an abnormality in the structure of his heart though she is not sure what this is,  but she does know that he has had problems with palpitations.  In Accident and Emergency, he has two generalised tonic-clonic seizures, which are treated with intravenous  lorazepam.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  134 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  12 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  122 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Neutrophils  8.4 × 10 9/l  2.5–7.58 × 10 9/l  Bilirubin  44 µmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Cholesterol  6.0 mmol/l  < 5.2 mmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  647 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  110 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Gamma-glutamyl-transferase (γGT)  540 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  C-reactive Protein (CRP)  84 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Total Protein  50 g/l  60–80 g/l  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.4  < 1.0  Albumin  28 g/l  35–55 g/l  Which of the following drugs is the best choice for the long-term treatment of his seizures?  A  Sodium valproate  B  Lamotrigine  C  Gabapentin  D  Vigabatrin  E  Carbamazepine  Explanation  B    Lamotrigine  The most important intervention is for this patient to stop drinking, although this should take place under cover  of a reducing course of benzodiazepines. Lamotrigine is an appropriate first-line intervention for seizures: it has  the advantage of not being a CYP450 enzyme inducer or inhibitor, and has data suggesting it may reduce longterm alcohol dependence.  A  Sodium valproate  Sodium valproate should not be used in patients with hepatic dysfunction, because it is a CYP450 inhibitor.  Additionally, MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests  that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate unless two consultants agree that there  is no suitable alternative treatment.  C  Gabapentin  Gabapentin is a normal adjunctive therapy for patients with persistent seizures despite starting a first-line  agent; as such, it’s not the appropriate choice here.  D  Vigabatrin  Vigabatrin is associated with peripheral visual field defects in up to 1/3 of users. It is also associated with  suicidal ideation, and is therefore not an ideal option in a patient with alcoholism.  E  Carbamazepine  Carbamazepine is a potent CYP450 enzyme inducer, and it may also be associated with AV conduction defects  and is therefore not ideal in a patient with congenital heart disease.  A 42-year-old premenopausal woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of  epigastric pain that is occasionally retrosternal and worse at night. She has tried over-the-counter antacid  preparations and esomeprazole which have achieved no relief. Her weight is steady and her bowel habits are  normal. There is no history of gastric malignancy in the family.  The examination is unremarkable, except for the fact that the patient is obese. The full blood count is normal.  Which of the following describes the next best management step?  A  Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy  B  Arrange upper GI endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on an alternative proton pump  inhibitor (PPI)  C  Check repeat haemoglobin level in three months; if low, refer for upper GI endoscopy  D  Start an alternative PPI and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test; if positive, prescribe Helicobacter  pylori eradication therapy  E  Stop esomeprazole and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test after two weeks  Explanation  E    Stop esomeprazole and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test after two weeks  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that in this age group, dyspepsia,  in the absence of alarm symptoms, should be treated with lifestyle advice and a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) if  needed. In the event that symptoms of indigestion have not been relieved, H. pylori testing or upper  gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy can then be considered. However, PPI therapy needs to have been stopped for  two weeks before H. pylori testing, due to the risk of a false-negative result.  D  Start an alternative PPI and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test; if positive, prescribe Helicobacter  pylori eradication therapy  Urea breath testing for H. pylori should ideally be conducted off PPI therapy for a period of at least two weeks.  A  Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy  A routine endoscopy would be considered where symptoms do not improve after one month of empirical proton  pump inhibitor (PPI) treatment.  B  Arrange upper GI endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on an alternative proton pump  inhibitor (PPI)  Patients with dyspepsia without any alarm features should ideally be tested for H. pylori infection before more  invasive endoscopy is considered.  C  Check repeat haemoglobin level in three months; if low, refer for upper GI endoscopy  This is the appropriate course of action where there are alarm features, including weight loss, persistent  vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening abdominal distension, severe  epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. She was previously fit and well with no significant past medical history  and the only medication she took was the oral contraceptive pill. There was no relevant family history. She  smoked 10 cigarettes per day and drank approximately 12 units of alcohol per week.  On examination, she was unwell, drowsy and deeply jaundiced. She was apyrexial. Her heart sounds were  normal, her chest was clear to auscultation and she had peripheral oedema. Her abdomen was distended with  shifting dullness and tender hepatomegaly. There were no focal neurological signs.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  130 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  13.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  200 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  132 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.8 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  120 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  82 fl  76–98 fl  Urea  7.2 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Bilirubin  120 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  410 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  900 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Gamma-glutamyl-transferase (γGT)  850 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Albumin  29 g/l  35–55 g/l  Prothrombin time (PT)  30 s  10.6–14.9 s  Ascitic fluid analysis reveals the following:  Investigation  Result  Protein  17 g/l  Neutrophils  80 cells/mm 3  Gram stain  No organisms seen  Amylase  100 IU/l  Which investigation should be performed next?
options: B. Colour flow Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature
questions.explanation:   Colour flow Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature  The diagnosis is Budd–Chiari syndrome. Doppler ultrasound will show obliteration of the hepatic veins and  abnormalities of the direction of blood flow in the remainder of the hepatic vasculature. Budd-Chiari syndrome  is defined as the obstruction of venous outflow from the liver caused by hepatic vein occlusion. The most  common cause is thrombosis, usually in association with a hypercoagulable state, in conditions such as primary  polycythaemia, thombophilias and leukaemia. There is also an association with the oral contraceptive pill. Other  causes include malignancy (especially hepatocellular, renal and adrenal), radiotherapy, trauma and congenital  venous webs. The cause is unknown in one-third of cases. It can present either acutely or chronically. In the  acute from, there is abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, ascites, tender hepatomegaly and sometimes  fulminant hepatic failure. The chronic form presents more insidiously, with signs of cirrhosis and portal  hypertension. Ascitic fluid analysis will show a high serum ascitic albumin gradient (SAAG= serum albumin –  ascitic fluid albumin) and is classified as a transudate. . An enlarged caudate lobe may be seen on  ultrasound/computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the liver. Liver biopsy usually  shows centrilobular congestion with fibrosis. Management includes treating the underlying cause, portocaval  shunts and TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunt). Treatment with streptokinase and  subsequent anticoagulation may be attempted if the thrombus is known to be of recent onset. Liver  transplantation is the only option in the acute presentation, which has a very poor prognosis, with two-thirds of  patients dead within 1 year.  A  Serum alpha-fetoprotein  A rising alpha-fetoprotein may be seen in hepatocellular carcinoma, known to be associated with Budd-Chiari  syndrome, but isn’t specific for the condition itself.  C  Liver biopsy  Liver biopsy usually shows centrilobular congestion with fibrosis which is related to pressure and flow changes  within the liver, but this isn’t the next investigation here.  D  Anti-mitochondrial antibodies  Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive in primary biliary cholangitis, a disease of insidious onset, which  usually presents with tiredness, lethargy and itching, rather than the acute deterioration seen here.  E  Serum caeruloplasmin  This is an investigation for Wilson’s disease, which presents with abnormal transaminases either picked up  incidentally or associated with neuropsychiatric features, rather than the acute deterioration seen here.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of abdominal pain and distension for the past 7 days.  On examination, she is found to have jaundice, a smooth, 5 cm hepatomegaly and ascites. There are no  stigmata of chronic liver disease and she does not take any regular medication.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  150 g/l  115–155 g/l  White Cell Count (WCC)  11.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  200 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  140 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.7 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  200 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Urea  20 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT)  50 s  23.0–35.0 s  Prothrombin Test (PT)  13 s  10.6–14.9 s  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Budd–Chiari syndrome  The prolonged APTT in the presence of a normal PT is suggestive of lupus anticoagulant, which would be  consistent with anti-phospholipid syndrome, well recognised as a cause of Budd–Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari  syndrome commonly presents with a triad of abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites. It is a rare condition  caused by occlusion to the hepatic vein. Treatment is with anticoagulation, surgery or a transjugular intrahepatic  portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure.  C  Glomerulonephritis  This would not explain the hepatomegaly and jaundice.  A  Alcoholic liver disease  Although this could account for her presentation, there is no mention of excessive alcohol intake in the history  and her presentation is far more typical of Budd-Chiari syndrome.  B  Right heart failure  Although this might cause an engorged liver and ascites, it would not explain her clotting abnormalities.  E  Metastatic liver disease  You would not expect to feel a smooth liver in this case, and the ascitic fluid tap is more likely to be exudative in  malignancy rather than transudative.

questions.question:   Which of the following should be the next step?
options: A. Colonoscopy and removal of the object
C. Laparotomy and removal of the object
D. Monitor with weekly X-rays to ensure passage through the GI tract
E. Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and removal of the object
questions.explanation:   Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and removal of the object  While most ingested foreign objects will pass through the GI tract without complication, there are certain  instances where intervention is required.  The presence of large objects that are unlikely to negotiate the duodenum, sharp objects, batteries and multiple  magnets are indications for intervention. After four hours, these swallowed foreign bodies are still located  proximally, which suggests that they cannot pass through the pyloric sphincter to the duodenum. Furthermore,  the close contact of the two objects is suspicious for magnet ingestion. Urgent endoscopic intervention is  required to remove these objects.  (Of note, narcotic packages should probably not be removed endoscopically, because of the risk of accidental  rupture.)  C  Laparotomy and removal of the object  This is not the optimal course of action for this situation. Currently the object is easily accessible via endoscopy,  given its proximal location.  A  Colonoscopy and removal of the object  Colonoscopy is usually not indicated, as once the foreign object has passed distally, it is likely to pass naturally  with a bowel motion. Furthermore, colonoscopy would only be indicated for a more distally located foreign  body, which is not seen here.  B  Gastrointestinal stimulation with metoclopramide  Because of where the object appears to be lodged, advising metoclopramide or other GI stimulants runs the risk  of significant pain and potentially even oesophageal rupture.  D  Monitor with weekly X-rays to ensure passage through the GI tract  Where endoscopic removal is not possible or is contraindicated, an alternative strategy is for daily X-rays to  monitor the progress of more distal objects, and for surgery to be considered for objects that do not move for 72  hours and/or people in whom symptoms develop. This would be the alternative strategy if the patient was  deemed to have capacity and refused endoscopy.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of shortness of breath and  tiredness. She recently started oral steroids prescribed by her General Practitioner for an intensely itchy,  vesicular rash on the elbows, knees, buttocks and back. She also gives a history of mild diarrhoea and  abdominal bloating and has lost a stone in weight.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal Values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  56 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  90 fl  80 - 100 fl  White cell count (WCC)  5.8 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  387 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Red cell distribution width (RDW)  11.8 - 14.5 %  Sodium (Na +)  138 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.4 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Urea  4.4 mmol/l  2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  99 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  Albumin  3.2 g/dl  3.4 - 5.4 g/dl  Corrected calcium (Ca 2+)  2.0 mmol/l  2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l  Bilirubin  25 µmol/l  1 - 22 µmol/l  Which of the following is most likely to be contributing to her anaemia?
options: D. Iron deficiency due to malabsorption
questions.explanation:   Iron deficiency due to malabsorption  The constellation of anaemia, weight loss, diarrhoea and bloating – together with a pruritic rash on the extensor  surfaces – is highly suggestive of this patient having coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis.  Coeliac disease may present in various ways, but iron deficiency anaemia is not an infrequent presentation. In  contrast, folate deficiency may also occur in the condition; B12 deficiency is less common, as this vitamin is  absorbed in the terminal ileum. Hypocalcaemia may also occur due to malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D.  Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely pruritic, vesicular rash that typically affects the elbows, scalp and  extensor surfaces of the forearms and buttocks. It is more common in men and may occur at any age, although it  tends to present in young adulthood. It is normally – if not exclusively – associated with gluten-sensitive  enteropathy.  Treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis includes strict adherence to a gluten-free diet. Dapsone may be effective  in controlling the rash but is often associated with mild, dose-related haemolytic anaemia. Haemolysis can,  however, be dramatic in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Monitoring of  liver function tests and a full blood count is advised, as dapsone may also rarely cause liver dysfunction and  aplastic anaemia. Drug treatment can often be withdrawn after a period of adherence to a gluten-free diet.  A  Anaemia of chronic disease  Anaemia of chronic disease is associated with normochromic normocytic anaemia but would only be  entertained as a diagnosis once other causes of anaemia, including iron deficiency, have been ruled out.  B  Autoimmune haemolysis  The clinical presentation here is much more consistent with coeliac disease, which is not associated with  haemolysis. Although dapsone, occasionally prescribed for dermatitis herpetiformis, may lead to haemolysis,  this is not seen with corticosteroids.  C  Bone marrow failure  Bone marrow failure is unlikely in the context of an isolated anaemia. It would be more likely to be bone marrow  failure if there were associated thrombocytopenia and leukopenia.  E  Pernicious anaemia  Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune disorder characterised by atrophic gastritis and a reduction of parietal  cells in the gastric mucosa, leading to vitamin B12 malabsorption. The MCV here is inconsistent with isolated  B12 deficiency. The MCV of 90, together with increased RDW and symptoms of coeliac disease, is more  consistent with a mixed picture of iron and B12 vitamin deficiencies.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man is admitted from the clinic with dysphagia and weight loss. Over the last few months, he  has found that it has been progressively harder to swallow solids. He was able to swallow them but he had to  regurgitate them about 30 minutes later.  Over the last few weeks, he has been having increasing difficulty with fluids. He has previously been in good  health and never smoked. He drinks half a bottle of wine at weekends and the only other history of note has  been long-term dyspepsia for which he uses antacids.  On examination, there is nothing to find except some mild tenderness on palpation in the epigastric area.  Barium swallow – oesophagus appears dilated and the distal oesophagus is narrowed. Oesophageal  manometry – incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter in response to swallowing with high  resting pressure. Absent oesophageal peristalsis.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Achalasia  Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder characterised by failure of a hypertensive lower  oesophageal sphincter to relax and the absence of normal oesophageal peristalsis. Oesophageal manometry  will demonstrate findings as for our patient. An OGD should be carried out to make sure there is no cancer.  The goal of therapy for achalasia is to relieve symptoms by eliminating the outflow resistance caused by the  hypertensive and non-relaxing sphincter. This can be accomplished by mechanical disruption of the muscle  fibres of the lower oesophageal sphincter (e.g. pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy or per-oral endoscopic    myotomy) or by pharmacological reduction of oesophageal sphincter pressure (e.g. injection of botulinum toxin,  oral nitrates or calcium channel blockers).  C  Plummer–Vinson syndrome  Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a triad of iron deficiency anaemia, dysphagia and a cervical oesophageal web. It is  more common in women, and may be associated with glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, splenomegaly, an  enlarged thyroid and symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia. Oesophageal webs characteristically cause  intermittent solid food dysphagia. These typically arise from the anterior wall, or are circumferential, and are  best seen on barium swallow as they are more easily missed on endoscopy due to their proximal nature. The  barium swallow report for this patient is not consistent with an oesophageal web.  B  Oesophageal cancer  The dysphagia is usually for solids, with the possibility of difficulty swallowing liquids in advanced disease.  Barium swallow would show obstruction by the tumour, rather than the characteristic ‘bird’s beak’ appearance  of achalasia, as described in this case.  D  Oesophageal candidiasis  Oesophageal candidiasis is more likely to cause retrosternal odynophagia rather than a progressive dysphagia.  Patients usually have a history of immunosuppression, of which there is no suggestion in this case. In severe  cases, barium swallow may reveal an irregular, ‘shaggy’ appearance to the oesophagus due to pseudomembrane formation.  E  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease  This patient has reported dyspepsia, suggesting possible gastro-oesophgeal reflux. While barium swallow  studies could reveal obstruction from a peptic stricture in the context of long-standing gastro-oesophageal  reflux, the oesophageal dilation and abnormal manometry findings would not be present in simple gastrooesophageal reflux disease.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis comes to the Emergency Department with an  exacerbation. She is opening her bowels some ten times per day with bloody diarrhoea. She tells you that she  stopped taking oral mesalazine some eight weeks ago after she found out she is pregnant with her first child.  She is now 16 weeks pregnant. On examination, her BP is 105/70 mmHg and his heart rate 88 bpm and  regular. Her abdomen is soft but generally tender. She has active bowel sounds.  Investigations;  Investigations  Results  Normal Values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  98 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  12.2 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  387 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  75 mm/1 sthour  0–10 mm in the 1 sthour  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine  100 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  31 g/l  35–55 g/l  Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her exacerbation?
options: C. Oral Mesalazine and oral Prednisolone
E. Rectal Mesalazine and Predsol enemas
questions.explanation:   Oral Mesalazine and oral Prednisolone  While no randomised controlled trials of 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) compounds exist specifically in  pregnant women, they are generally thought to be safe, with animal studies revealing no evidence of  teratogenicity. As such, it is most appropriate to restart oral mesalazine and to add oral prednisolone to gain  control of the exacerbation.  A  Azathioprine and Prednisolone  Research suggests that azathioprine is less effective than mesalazine in controlling symptoms, although it is  also an appropriate option from the point of view of safety for use in pregnancy.  B  Mycophenolate mofetil  Mycophenolate mofetil use during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk for malformations and firsttrimester pregnancy loss. The most frequent malformations include external ear and other facial malformations  such as cleft palate and lip. As we know that there are safer options in this case, mycophenolate mofetil should  be avoided.  D  Prednisolone  Prednisolone would be a reasonable option to control the exacerbation, but it should be done in conjunction  with restarting mesalazine.  E  Rectal Mesalazine and Predsol enemas  The generalised abdominal tenderness raises the possibility of more than just rectal disease. For this reason,  rectal mesalazine and prednisolone are unlikely to be effective.

questions.question: A 29-year-old sales assistant undergoes upper endoscopy for symptoms of dyspepsia. The OGD demonstrates  a duodenal lesion and biopsies have returned showing a MALT lymphoma.  What would be the best initial therapeutic strategy?
options: E. Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation:   Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori  A MALT lymphoma is a B-cell tumour caused by an immune response to chronic H. pylori (HP) infection. The  first therapeutic strategy in treating a GI MALT lymphoma is to eradicate HP with a regimen of standard  antibiotics and PPI, which leads to remission in 75% of cases. HP eradication regimens are usually given to all  patients, due to the possibility of negative HP results. Patients should undergo a Carbon-13 urea breath test  (UBT) approximately ≥6 weeks after eradication therapy and ≥2 weeks after PPI withdrawal, to confirm  eradication.  The carbon-13 UBT is based on the detection of the products created when urea is split by the organism.  Patients are asked to drink urea (usually with a beverage) labelled with a carbon isotope (carbon-13 or -14).  After a certain duration, the concentration of the labelled carbon is measured on the breath. The concentration  is high only when urease is present in the stomach. Because the human stomach does not produce urease, such  a reaction is possible only with HP infection. Problems include negative results due to infection with coccoid  forms of HP that do not produce as much urease; and intake of antibiotics, bismuth, histamine-2 (H2) blockers,  or proton pump inhibitors.  In the minority of patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, irradiation and  systemic oncological therapies should be considered, depending on the stage of disease.  A  Duodenal stent insertion  There is no suggestion from the history that the patient is suffering from symptoms of upper gastrointestinal  tract or gastric outlet obstruction.  B  Radiotherapy  In patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, radiotherapy with curative  intent might be the preferred option for localised-stage disease. However, this is not an initial treatment  strategy for this patient.  C  Chemotherapy  In patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, chemo-immunotherapy with  cyclophosphamide or chlorambucil may play a role in management, but this would not be an initial treatment  strategy for this patient.  D  Laparoscopic resection  Endoscopic mucosal resection and resectional surgery are rarely needed. In such instances, this would follow  failure of initial medical therapies.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic alcoholism presents to the clinic with increased abdominal  swelling. She has noticed increasing abdominal girth over the past 4-6 months.  On examination, there are signs of chronic liver disease, including spider naevi and ascites, and she also has  jaundiced sclerae. Her BP is 100/65 mmHg.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal Values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  105 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  107 fL  80 - 100 fl  White cell count (WCC)  5.6 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  202 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  136 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.9 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  85 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  CA-125  65 u/ml  < 35 u/ml  What is the most likely cause for the increased CA-125?
questions.explanation:   Cirrhosis  The patient has clinical features of chronic liver disease and the alcohol history makes cirrhosis the most likely  option. Cirrhosis with ascites is a well recognised cause of a false positive CA125.  C  Colonic carcinoma  Colon cancer can produce a falsely positive CA-125. However, this patient clearly has signs of chronic liver  disease.  A  Hepatitis B  Hepatitis B infection is not strongly associated with an elevated CA-125.  B  Ovarian carcinoma  A patient presenting with ascites and a raised CA-125 raises the suspicion of ovarian cancer, however, there is  a clear alcohol history and the patient has features of chronic liver disease. Although CA-125 is often used to  screen for ovarian cancer there are multiple conditions that also result in an elevated CA-125 (including  cirrhosis and ascites, other intra-abdominal cancers, endometriosis, PID, fibroids, pancreatitis and heart failure  amongst others).  If ovarian cancer is suspected, NICE recommend using the “Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI)”, which combines  transvaginal US, menopausal status and CA-125 level to assess the risk. All women with a score >250 should  be referred for specialist assessment.  In women where there is a family history of ovarian carcinoma, genetic screening for BRCA1/2 is recommended  as the preferred method for assessing future ovarian carcinoma risk.  D  Hepatocellular carcinoma  HCC is not associated with a rise in CA-125 (although it may be elevated in a patient with HCC as HCC occurs  as a consequence of cirrhosis). Alfa-fetoprotein can be elevated in HCC.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman who has undergone multiple small bowel resections comes to the clinic for review. She  is finding it virtually impossible to maintain her weight and suffers from chronic diarrhoea. On examination, her  blood pressure is 103/80 mmHg; her pulse is 80 bpm and regular. She has a healed laparotomy scar on her  abdomen. Her body mass index is 19. She was tried with total parenteral nutrition but unable to be weaned  from it.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  87 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  5.9 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  162 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  138 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.4 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  85 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  11 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Albumin  22 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  39 U/l  7–55 U/l  Bilirubin  12 µmol/l  1–22 µmol/l  Which of the following is the most effective next intervention?
questions.explanation:   Teduglutide  The answer is Teduglutide.  Teduglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 2 agonist, which promotes small bowel mucosal growth; therefore, it is  of value in the treatment of short bowel syndrome caused by multiple resections for Crohn’s disease. Six  months after commencing therapy, patients with short bowel syndrome requiring total parenteral nutrition  (TPN) top-ups achieved a reduction in their TPN requirements between 20 and 100%.  A  Codeine phosphate  Codeine phosphate is incorrect. Although codeine phosphate may slow gastrointestinal transit and have an  impact on the symptoms of diarrhoea, it is not likely to have a significant impact on the symptoms of  malabsorption.  B  Liraglutide  Liraglutide is incorrect. Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 1 agonist used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes;  it has no significant impact on small intestinal mucosal growth.  C  Loperamide hydrochloride  Loperamide hydrochloride is incorrect. Like codeine phosphate, loperamide hydrochloride may improve the  symptoms of diarrhoea, but it is not likely to improve the symptoms associated with malabsorption.  E  Vildagliptin  Vildagliptin is incorrect. Vildagliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor used in the treatment of type 2  diabetes.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presented with an attack of acute upper abdominal pain associated with vomiting.  On examination, he had epigastric tenderness and guarding. Serum amylase was 1300 IU/l. He was treated  with intravenous antibiotics, fluids and analgesia. His pain settled and he made a good recovery and was  discharged from hospital several days later.  Eight weeks later, he was readmitted with malaise and persistent abdominal pain.  On examination, he had low-grade pyrexia and there was a tender mass palpable in the upper abdomen. His  heart rate is 96 bpm and his blood pressure is 124/81 mmHg.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  112 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  14 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  390 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  82 fl  76–98 fl  C-reactive protein (CRP)  200 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Sodium (Na +)  137 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K+)  4.3 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  4.8 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  120 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+)  2.50 mmol/l  2.20–2.60 mmol/l  Bilirubin  22 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  160 IU/l  30–130 IU/l  Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)  78 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  42 IU/l  10–40 IU/l  Amylase  1000 U/l  < 200 U/l  What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: D. Recurrent attack of acute pancreatitis
questions.explanation:   Pancreatic pseudocyst  Pancreatic pseudocysts are an uncommon complication of acute pancreatitis, and are localised collections of  pancreatic fluid and debris, usually in the lesser sac. They are initially contained within a fragile wall of  granulation tissue which eventually forms a fibrous capsule. They cannot be diagnosed until more than 6 weeks  after the acute attack, and may present with abdominal pain or a mass, fever and persistently raised amylase  and liver function tests. Small pseudocysts usually resolve on their own, but those that are greater than 6 cm in  diameter seldom disappear spontaneously and may lead to complications such as haemorrhage and infection.  They are usually managed by endoscopic or percutanous drainage or surgical intervention.  B  Pyogenic liver abscess  Liver abscesses mostly occur following peritonitis due to leaking of bowel content with spread to the liver by  portal circulation. Alternatively, there can be direct spread from the biliary system or haematogenous seeding  from systemic infection. Liver abcesses commonly cause fever and abdominal pain, whilst patients can also  have anorexia, vomiting and weight loss. The low-grade, as opposed to a high-grade, fever, as well as the very  delayed timing, makes this an unlikely diagnosis.  C  Chronic pancreatitis  Chronic pancreatitis occurs with progressive inflammatory changes causing permanent structural damage,  which results in impaired exocrine and endocrine function. It can present as chronic epigastric pain with nausea  and vomiting which radiates to the back, or with pancreatic insufficiency causing malabsorption and steatorrhea.  The acute abdominal signs and elevated amylase make this a less likely differential.  D  Recurrent attack of acute pancreatitis  Recurrent acute pancreatitis can occur, and in some patients this becomes a regular problem necessitating  surgery if very severe. The presence of a tender and palpable mass makes this a less likely diagnosis.  E  Pancreatic carcinoma  Pancreatic carcinoma is a cause of a painless epigastric mass and progressively worsening jaundice. The  presence of pain and tenderness reduces the likelihood of this diagnosis, as does the absence of jaundice. 6743

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with a history of type I diabetes presents with a 3-month history of nausea, early satiety,  bloating and intermittent vomiting, particularly after meals. She reports poor glycaemic control and frequently  experiences hypoglycaemic episodes after eating. Physical examination is unremarkable. She has tried antacids  and proton pump inhibitors, with no improvement in her symptoms.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  130 g/l  135–175 g/l  Platelets (PLT)  300 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Fasting blood glucose  8.0 mmol/l  4.0–6.0 mmol/l  HbA1c  9.5%  Less than 7%  Creatinine (Cr)  85 µmol/l  60–120 µmol/l  What is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Gastric emptying scintigraphy  Gastric emptying scintigraphy is the gold standard for diagnosing gastroparesis, as it quantitatively assesses  the rate of gastric emptying. In gastroparesis, delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction is a key  feature, especially in patients with a history of diabetes.  A  Abdominal ultrasound  While abdominal ultrasound can be helpful in ruling out other causes of abdominal pain, such as gallstones or  biliary pathology, it does not assess gastric emptying function. This patient’s symptoms and history are  suggestive of delayed gastric emptying, making gastric emptying scintigraphy more appropriate.  C  Upper GI endoscopy  While an endoscopy can help to identify structural abnormalities, it cannot evaluate gastric emptying.  Endoscopy may be helpful to rule out other causes of this patient's symptoms if gastroparesis is not confirmed,  but it is not the primary diagnostic tool for delayed gastric emptying.  D  CT of the abdomen  A CT scan is useful for evaluating intra-abdominal pathology but does not provide information on gastric  motility. It may help to exclude other causes but is not diagnostic for gastroparesis.  E  Hydrogen breath test  The hydrogen breath test is used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or carbohydrate  malabsorption disorders, which can cause bloating and discomfort but would not confirm gastroparesis. 74428

questions.question: A 27-year-old office worker presents with a 3-year history of epigastric pain, especially 30 min after eating.  This is associated with nausea and belching. She also describes constipation with occasional explosive  diarrhoea. The stools are normally hard with mucus and she needs to strain with every motion.  Abdominal pain is relieved after defecation but abdominal bloating persists. She wakes up an hour earlier each  morning to finish her breakfast in order to prevent vomiting. She has missed work on a few occasions and feels  that her weight has fluctuated.  Past medical history includes scarlet fever. She is not on any regular medications except intermittent laxatives  over the counter. Abdominal examination is normal. Rectal examination reveals an anal fissure.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  131 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  6.0 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  180 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  87 fl  76–98 fl  International normalised ratio (INR)  1.0  < 1.1  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  1.1 mm/hour  1–20 mm/hour  Sodium (Na +)  136 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  3.9 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Urea  3.7 mmol/l  2.5–6.5 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  70 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Albumin  39 g/l  35–55 g/l  Liver function tests (LFTs)  Normal  Anti-endomysial antibody  Negative  Thyroid function tests (TFTs)  Normal  Gastroscopy  Normal  Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy  Normal  Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound scan  Normal  What is the most likely diagnosis to account for her symptoms?
options: A. Overlap irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia
B. Diarrhoea pre-dominant irritable bowel syndrome
D. Malabsorption sydrome and non-ulcer dyspepsia
questions.explanation:   Overlap irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia  This lady has signs of irritable bowel syndrome, especially in light of all the normal investigation results. It is  the result of complex interactions between psychosocial factors, disordered bowel motility and altered  intestinal sensations. This disorder is commonly associated with functional dyspepsia and patients are more  likely to get chronic fatigue syndrome and globus hystericus.  Diagnostic criteria have been developed, most notably the ‘Rome criteria’. These include symptoms of  abdominal pain relieved by defecation that is associated with a change in stool frequency and consistency,  abdominal bloating and passing mucus per rectum.  B  Diarrhoea pre-dominant irritable bowel syndrome  Although she does report occasional diarrhoea, her more predominant symptom is constipation.  C  Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction  The classical symptoms of Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction are of recurrent biliary-type epigastric / right upper  quadrant pain, which last from 30 minutes to several hours, and is not relieved by bowel movements. It is not  typically associated with diarrhoea, or a change in stool consistency. For diagnosis, the patient must have biliary  pain, and imaging must reveal the absence of bile duct stones or other structural abnormalities, and elevated  liver enzymes or dilated bile duct, but not both.  D  Malabsorption sydrome and non-ulcer dyspepsia  There is no supporting evidence in the history of a malabsorption syndrome: no sustained weight loss, albumin  is normal, and coeliac antibodies are negative.  E  Globus hystericus  Globus sensation is a functional oesophageal disorder characterized by a sensation of a lump, retained food  bolus, or tightness in the throat that is not due to an underlying structural lesion, gastroesophageal reflux  disease, mucosal abnormality, or an esophageal motility disorder. This is not the presentation of this patient.

questions.question:   A 59-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She was referred by her General  Practitioner with cramping abdominal pain and frequent episodes of diarrhoea. On further questioning, she  denies indigestion. There is no significant past medical history, apart from hypertension which is controlled with  bendroflumethiazide. She drinks two bottles of wine per week.  Examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/72 mmHg and a heart rate of 75 bpm and regular. She has pale  conjunctivae. There are no abnormal findings, and her body mass index is 24 kg/m 2.  Investigations:  Investigations  Haemoglobin (Hb)  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  Ferritin  White cell count (WCC)  Platelets (PLT)  Sodium (Na +)  Potassium (K +)  Creatinine  Albumin  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  Amylase  Results  91 g/l  78 fl  18 µg/l  8.1 × 10 9/l  201 × 10 9/l  137 mmol/l  4.3 mmol/l  85 μmol/l  30 g/l  44 IU/l  50 U/l  Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
options: E. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy Normal value 115–155 g/l 76–98 fl 10–120 µg/l 4–11 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l 135–145 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 35–55 g/l 5–30 IU/l 70–300 U/l
questions.explanation:   Tissue transglutaminase  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend coeliac screening for any patient  who presents with iron deficiency anaemia before beginning specific investigations. This is because of the  recognition that underlying coeliac disease may present without the classical symptoms of abdominal bloating  and diarrhoea. In this case, the low albumin level hints at chronic malabsorption, which may be due to an  underlying small bowel disease. Following coeliac antibody testing, the patient should be referred for both  upper and lower gastrointestinal investigations, with colonoscopy being a more definitive option (when  preparation is adequate), compared to barium enema.  A  Ultrasound abdomen  An abdominal ultrasound scan would be an appropriate first-line investigation in patients with deranged liver  function tests or abdominal pain. In this case, the patient importantly has no symptoms to suggest this and  there are no data indicating significantly deranged liver function tests.  B  Colonoscopy  Colonoscopy is an important investigation to consider. However, importantly, in this case, there are no red flag  symptoms (eg weight loss or change in bowel habit). Therefore, it would be reasonable to screen the patient for  coeliac disease before referring them for a colonoscopy. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence  guidelines state that all patients over the age of 60 with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia should be  referred for a colonoscopy on the 2-week wait rule.  C  Faecal elastase  Faecal elastase is a test of the exocrine function of the pancreas, particularly for patients with chronic  pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis is commonly caused by alcohol excess and symptoms include abdominal pain  and steatorrhoea. Amylase levels are often elevated, but not always. However, chronic pancreatitis does not  explain this patient’s anaemia and the lack of a history of acute pancreatitis makes the diagnosis even less  likely.  E  Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy  This would be an investigation that could be considered if the patient had a normal colonoscopy and a normal  coeliac screen.  A 42-year-old former intravenous drug abuser presents to the Hepatology Clinic for review. He has just  completed a 48-week course of Peg-interferon alpha-2a for hepatitis B infection. On examination, his  observations are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft, with no obvious stigmata of liver disease.  On review in the clinic, his results are as follows:  Investigation  HBsAg  HBeAg  Anti-HBc IgG  Result  Positive  Positive  Positive  Anti-HBs IgG  Anti-HCV IgG  HCV RNA  Negative  Negative  Negative  Investigation  Albumin  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  Bilirubin  Result  27 g/l  122 u/l  148 u/l  24 µmol/l  Normal value  35–55 g/l  7–55 u/l  30–150 u/l  1–22 µmol/l  Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?  A  Continue interferon  B  Switch to tenofovir  C  Switch to lamivudine  D  Reassurance and stop treatment  E  Switch to ribavirin  Explanation  B  Switch to tenofovir    This patient still shows signs of hepatitis B infection, given positive HBsAg and HBeAg. A positive anti-HBc IgG  suggests chronic infectivity. Management of hepatitis B and C has been revolutionised over recent years by the  introduction of novel antiviral agents. In this situation, tenofovir is a logical next step and is recommended by  the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase  inhibitor which inhibits hepatitis B deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) replication.  A  Continue interferon  Given that interferon has failed to achieve clearance of hepatitis B, alternative therapy is required.  C  Switch to lamivudine  Lamivudine is less effective, compared to modern agents such as entecavir or tenofovir. It does, however, carry a  lower acquisition cost, compared to more modern agents.  D  Reassurance and stop treatment  This patient still shows signs of active infection with positive HBsAg and HBeAg. Therefore, additional  treatment is needed.  E  Switch to ribavirin  Ribavirin is used in combination with interferon for the treatment of hepatitis C. However, the combination is  less effective than more modern agents, such as boceprevir, and has therefore been largely superseded. 70041

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She undergoes  emergency laparotomy, which is normal.  On further questioning, she reveals a family history of an aunt who has a light-sensitive rash and a diagnosis of  porphyria.  On examination, she is hypertensive, with generalised rebound tenderness. She responds to analgesia and once  she is stabilised a porphyrin screen is sent.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal Values  Sodium (Na +)  125 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.0 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Glucose  5.0 mmol/l  3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l  Full blood count (FBC)  Normal  CT abdomen  Normal  Urinary porphobilinogen (PBG)  300 µmol/dl  Faecal porphyrins  Normal (co-proporphyrins and protoporphyrins)  Plasma porphyrins  Markedly increased  What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Acute intermittent porphyria  Attacks of acute porphyria are often mistaken for surgical abdomens. Family histories may be misleading, as  porphyria may be misdiagnosed or may not be manifest in other family members. Acute intermittent porphyria  is correct as it fits the clinical symptoms of gastrointestinal upset with abdominal pain and cramp with nausea  and vomiting. Urinary porphyrins are raised in all three acute porphyrias (acute intermittent porphyria,  hereditary co-proporpyria and variegate porphyria), so these can often be impossible to distinguish clinically.  Faecal porphyrins can be useful to differentiate the conditions, because they are elevated in coproporphyria and  variegate porphyria.  B  Variegate porphyria  Variegate porphyria is an autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutation of protoporphyrinogen oxide. It is  characterised by symptoms of neurovisceral crises similar to those in a patient with AIP, but is also associated  with a classic photosensitive skin disorder which this patient did not have.  C  Hereditary coproporphyria  Similarly, hereditary co-proporphyria is also incorrect as it is associated with a blistering skin rash, particularly in  sun-exposed areas.  D  Porphyria cutanea tarda  Although it is the most common of all porphyrias, it is purely a skin disease, resulting from a deficiency of the  enzyme uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.  E  Lead poisoning  This does not cause increase in urinary porphyrins. Lead poisoning predominantly affects the nervous system,  with symptoms such as delirium, tremor and convulsions.

questions.question: A 52-year-old truck driver has been referred by his general practitioner (GP) to the rapid access upper  gastrointestinal (GI) clinic with a 10-day history of intermittent epigastric pain and nausea.  He has been prescribed a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which he started taking 4 days ago with some relief. He  has taken regular co-codamol for years for chronic back pain but otherwise has no previous medical history. His  weight is stable and clinical examination is unremarkable.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal Value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  147 g/l  135–175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  3.6 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  212 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  86 fl  76–98 fl  Which is the most appropriate next step in management according to available evidence?
options: D. Refer for routine upper GI endscopy and give symptomatic antacids in first instance
E. Add metoclopramide 10 mg tds and review in 2 weeks
questions.explanation:   Continue proton pump inhibitor  This gentleman is <55 years old without ‘alarm’ features – weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia – and  does not take non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). He is not anaemic and has no epigastric mass  on examination. As he has gained some relief from the PPI it’s therefore appropriate to continue the medication.  A  Urgent upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy  Alarm features that prompt urgent referral for endoscopy include weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia,  anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass on physical examination.  B  pylori eradication therapy  H. pylori testing is useful, particularly where there is a limited response to PPI, although a 2-week wash-out  should be accomplished if possible before breath testing is instituted.  D  Refer for routine upper GI endscopy and give symptomatic antacids in first instance  Before referral for routine endoscopy, a trial of PPI and/or H pylori breath testing should first take place.  E  Add metoclopramide 10 mg tds and review in 2 weeks  Although metoclopramide is a pro-kinetic and may improve nausea, its use is now discouraged because of  dopamine antagonist-related adverse effects of therapy.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with an upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. He is a non-smoker and drinks  only occasional wine. On further questioning, he admits to problems with indigestion over the past few months,  for which he has tried over-the-counter Ranitidine tablets, and increasing diarrhoea.  Upper GI endoscopy reveals multiple small gastric ulcers and helicobacter testing is negative. He is willing to  have a short period off Ranitidine to be properly investigated.  Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation in this case?
options: B. Fasting gastrin on three different days
questions.explanation:   Fasting gastrin on three different days  There is a suspicion that this patient may have Zollinger–Ellison syndrome as a result of a gastrinoma. The best  initial screen is a fasting gastrin level on three separate days, as the secretion of gastrin is pulsatile. Three  samples in the normal range make a gastrinoma unlikely. This is usually followed by basal acid output  estimation and a secretin stimulation test. After this, patients usually move on to imaging studies. In the  absence of metastases, surgical resection is advised. Octreotide, interferon and chemotherapy may be useful in  non-surgically resectable lesions.  D  Secretin stimulation test  Like basal acid output estimation, secretin stimulation test is an investigation which follows the three gastrin  measurements.  A  Single fasting gastrin level  Gastrin has a short half-life and release is cyclical, hence re-measuring on 3 separate days is recommended.  C  Basal acid output estimation  Basal acid output estimation is a subsequent test after elevated gastrin has been established.  E  Protein meal test  An arginine stimulation test is used in the evaluation of growth hormone deficiency.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with liver failure. She drinks no alcohol but over the  past few months has suffered from increasing tiredness, upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, anorexia and  itching. Most recently, she has noticed markedly increased bruising if she takes a knock on something.  On examination, her blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. You notice signs of chronic liver disease including scratch  marks on her skin, spider naevi and evidence of mild jaundice. She also has extensive bruising on her limbs.  Hepatomegaly is also present.  Investigations reveal the following:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin (Hb)  105 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  5.5 × 10 9/l  4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  110 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  134 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.2 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  90 µmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Prothrombin time (PT)  27.3 s  10.6–14.9 s  Albumin  22 g/l  35–55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  765 IU/l  5–30 IU/l  Bilirubin  100 μmol/l  2–17 µmol/l  Anti-soluble liver antigen antibody  +  Gamma-globulins  Increased  Liver biopsy  Hepatic cirrhosis  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:   Autoimmune hepatitis Type 3  This patient has an autoantibody pattern consistent with autoimmune hepatitis type 3, and features of cirrhosis  which are said to occur in around 75% of patients with the condition. It is commonest in those of the 30–50year group, the vast majority being women. The prolonged PT is likely to be as the result of severe hepatic  dysfunction. Corticosteroids achieve remission in around 2/3 of patients, although the relapse rate is as high as  80% after steroid withdrawal. Azathioprine is the main steroid-sparing agent used in the treatment of the  condition.  A comparison between subtypes of autoimmune hepatitis is listed below:  Clinical Features  Type 1  ASMA  Diagnostic autoantibodies  ANA  Anti-actin  Type 2  Anti-LKM  Type 3  P-450 IID6  Soluble liver-kidney  antigen  Synthetic core motif peptides 254271  Cytokeratins 8 and 18  Paediatric (2-14y)  Age  10y - elderly  Women (%)  Concurrent immune disease  Gamma globulin elevation  +++  +  ++  Low IgA  No  Occasional  No  HLA association  B8, DR3,  DR4  B14, DR3, C4AQO  Uncertain  Steroid response  ++  ++  +++  Progression to cirrhosis  Rare in adults  Adults (30-50y)  A  Wilson’s disease  Wilson’s disease presents at an earlier age and is usually associated with an asymptomatic rise in  transaminases, psychiatric symptoms or a movement disorder.  B  Haemochromatosis  Haemochromatosis presents later in women because of the natural blood loss afforded by the regular  menstrual cycle. It also presents with other features such as diabetes and chondrocalcinosis, which aren’t seen  here.  C  Autoimmune hepatitis Type 1  This is associated with anti-smooth muscle antibodies rather than the soluble liver–kidney antigen antibodies  seen here.  D  Primary biliary cholangitis  Primary biliary cholangitis presents with itching and lethargy and is associated with an obstructive picture on  liver function testing.

questions.question: A 35-year-old alcoholic is admitted after an upper GI haemorrhage. An endoscopy is performed soon after  admission with variceal banding, but you are asked to see him the following morning as he is drowsy and  confused.  On examination, his BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular and his temperature is 36.5°C. He is  mildly tender in the epigastrium and there is evidence of ascites. He is very drowsy and appears confused when  you wake him from sleep. PR reveals melaena.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal values  Haemoglobin (Hb)  91 g/l  135 - 175 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  10.5 × 10 9/l  4.0 - 11.0 × 10 9/l  Platelets (PLT)  131 × 10 9/l  150 - 400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  128 mmol/l  135 - 145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  5.1 mmol/l  3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine (Cr)  122 µmol/l  50 - 120 µmol/l  C-reactive protein (CRP)  17 mg/l  < 10 mg/l  Albumin  23 g/l  35 - 55 g/l  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)  231 u/l  7 - 55 u/l  Glucose  5.9 mmol/l  3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l  Which of the following is most likely to reveal the cause of his confusion?
questions.explanation:   Serum ammonia  The fact that the increased confusion has occurred following the upper GI bleed is suggestive that blood  ingestion has led to increased ammonia production by the bacteria within the GI tract. Strategies to reduce  bacterial ammonia production include use of rifaximin and lactulose.  B  Ascitic tap  Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is potentially one of the differential diagnoses in a case of confusion in a  patient with decompensated alcoholic liver disease; in the current situation, however, the onset of confusion  soon after the GI bleed points towards the blood ingestion and ammonia production as the likeliest cause.  C  Blood cultures  Sepsis is a potential cause of confusion, but in this scenario there is no evidence for it, either from the physical  examination/observations or from the blood results.  D  CT head  A subdural haematoma could be another cause for confusion, but in our case there is no history of fall or head  injury.  E  Lumbar puncture  Neither the history nor the blood results support the diagnosis of meningitis/encephalitis.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic complaining of long periods of constipation  interspersed with short episodes of diarrhoea. She has not lost any weight over the past year and continues to  eat a varied diet.  On examination, her BP is 122/82, her heart rate is 67 and regular and her BMI is 22.5 kg/m 2. Full blood count  and viscosity are normal. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is unremarkable.  What is the next most appropriate management step?
questions.explanation: Soluble fibre supplementation  Normal clinical examination, stable weight and normal routine bloods make a sinister diagnosis unlikely.  Irritable bowel syndrome is, therefore, the most likely cause of her symptoms. Psyllium or ispahula  supplementation is of value in patients like this who have predominant constipation symptoms.  A  Colonoscopy  Given the normal findings so far, there is little value in progressing to colonoscopy in this patient. Committing  her to further investigation will only serve to increase anxiety.  B  Barium enema  Like colonoscopy, progressing to barium enema would be considered over-investigation in this situation.    C  Lactose-free diet  A lactose-free diet may be effective in reducing bloating associated with irritable bowel syndrome, but has  limited impact on constipation.  E  Wheat-free diet  There is no evidence this patient has coeliac disease. Some patients with bloating benefit from reducing their  wheat intake, although greater benefit is usually found from lactose exclusion.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man presents complaining of diarrhoea for the past 2 days. It is watery and he has opened his  bowels three times already today. He feels concerned as he thinks there was a small amount of blood mixed in  with the stool on the most recent occasion. He does not feel too unwell and has been drinking plenty of fluids.  He has not eaten anything unusual or been travelling abroad in the last 6 months. He had an infected boil on  his back, for which he received flucloxicillin 2 weeks ago for one week in total. No one else in the household  feels unwell.  He has no past medical history and takes no medications. BP is 105/80 mmHg with a postural drop of 20  mmHg on standing.  What would be the most appropriate next management step?
questions.explanation:   Oral rehydration salts  NICE suggest that acute diarrhoea should be assessed for cause and the severity of dehydration should be  established. The Table below is based on NICE guidelines to help divide the different features.  Mild dehydration  Moderate dehydration  Severe dehydration  Lassitude  Apathy/tiredness  Profound apathy  Anorexia/nausea  Dizziness  Weakness  Light-headedness  Muscle cramps  Confusion  Postural hypotension  Pinched face  Shock  Dry tongue or sunken eyes  Tachycarida  Reduced skin elasticity  Peripheral vasoconstriction  Postural hypotension  Hypotension  Tachycardia  Oliguria or anuria  Oliguria  As his only feature dehydration is postural hypotension he can be managed for mild dehydration with oral  rehydration.  C  Loperamide  Whilst infection has not been proven, it is suspected, especially as there is an element of PR bleeding.  Loperamide should be avoided if infective diarrhoea is suspected.  A  Oral antibiotics  According to guidance, antibiotics should be reserved for when a patient has a positive stool culture or is  extremely unwell. This patient is very stable. He has noticed a small amount of blood on passing stool so it is  definitely worth sending a stool culture. His short course of flucloxicillin is very unlikely to have precipitated  Clostridium difficile infection in an otherwise healthy young man.  B  IV antibiotics  As with the previous option there is no indication to treat with antibiotics, IV or oral, unless there is a specific  pathogen identified or there is evidence of severe infection. This patient is well and no samples suggesting  infection have yet been returned.  D  Sigmoidoscopy  Endoscopic examination would be necessary if inflammatory bowel disease was suspected to be the  underlying cause. There is not very much in the history or examination to support such a suspicion; absence of  fever, chronic history, abdominal pain and systemic features. Should such features develop or his diarrhoea not  settle then this could be a reasonable choice.

questions.question: A 28-year-old teacher presents to his General Practitioner with bloating, abdominal pain and weight loss. He  also reports diarrhoea, which is very difficult to flush away and tends to float on the toilet pan.  On examination, his blood pressure is 115/72 mmHg and he looks pale. His BMI is 21 kg/m 2 and his abdomen  is soft and non-tender. Results of blood tests show iron deficiency anaemia and an elevated alkaline  phosphatase (ALP) level; his albumin level is low at 30 g/l.  Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following associated complications will have the best response to  treatment?
questions.explanation:   Osteopenia  The symptoms and iron deficiency anaemia in this scenario are suggestive of coeliac disease. Coeliac disease  can be associated with deranged liver function tests. Serological tests for coeliac disease include  immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies to tissue transglutaminase (TTG) (preferred and most widely available),  anti-endomysial antibodies and gliadin antigen. The ‘gold standard’ for diagnosis remains a duodenal or jejunal  biopsy. There are many recognised complications of untreated or undertreated coeliac disease in adults  including depression, anxiety and eating disorders like nutritional deficiencies and anaemia due to  malabsorption, reduced bone mineral density, hyposplenism malignancy and dermatitis herpetiformis. Some  renal diseases, including IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy and chronic kidney disease, are  associated with coeliac disease; however, this does not include renal cystic disease.  A  Dermatitis herpetiformis  Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin manifestation of active coeliac disease. Episodes can recur, even on a strict  gluten-free diet, making it inappropriate here. In recurrence, treatment with dapsone, in conjunction with a  gluten-free diet, may be helpful.  B  Infection with encapsulated organisms  Hyposplenism and splenic atrophy are closely associated with the development of other complications and  autoimmune diseases in patients with coeliac disease. This increases patients’ risk of infection with  encapsulated bacteria and sepsis. Studies have shown that treatment with a gluten-free diet can reverse  functional hyposplenism, but not splenic atrophy, making it inappropriate for this patient.  D  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma  People with coeliac disease are at increased risk of cancer, including an estimated 2- to 4-fold risk of nonHodgkin’s lymphoma. Increased risk of malignancy in coeliac disease has been shown to normalise following a  few years of a gluten-free diet. As this risk takes longer to normalise, compared to osteopenia, it is not  appropriate here.  E  Small bowel cancer  Those with coeliac disease are at increased risk of cancer, including an estimated 30-fold risk of small bowel  cancer. As the increased risk of malignancy in coeliac has been shown to normalise after a few years of a  gluten-free diet, compared to osteopenia, this risk takes longer to normalise and is not appropriate here. 2277

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of shortness of breath and cough. There is a long past  medical history of indigestion, worse when she lies flat on the bed, with occasional acid regurgitation. She may  even wake at night occasionally with acid in her mouth and paroxysms of coughing.  On examination, her body mass index (BMI) is 31, she is pyrexial with a temperature of 39 °C, there is an area of  bronchial breathing over the right lung and a suggestion of increased shadowing on the chest X-ray at the right  base.  Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause for this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:   Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)  This woman has a long history of indigestion, particularly worse when lying flat, and acid regurgitation,  complicated by a chronic nocturnal cough. It is likely that an episode of regurgitation has led to right-sided  lower respiratory tract infection. She is obese, which may well contribute to her symptoms. Other predisposing  factors which increase the likelihood of GORD include smoking; hiatus hernia; medications which relax the  lower oesophageal sphincter such as calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers; pregnancy; and foods such  as chocolate and peppermint. Weight reduction would be the mainstay of management in this case, with the  addition of proton pump inhibitors.  D  Benign oesophageal stricture  Benign oesophageal stricture leads to regurgitation of food, often a mix of both solid and liquid meals, rather  than the progressive dysphagia seen with oesophageal Ca.  A  Bronchiectasis  Bronchiectasis is associated with longer-term shortness of breath and recurrent episodes of lower respiratory  tract infection.  B  Exacerbation of asthma  Given the long history of water brash and associated coughing, reflux is the more likely primary cause of her  symptoms, and the CXR changes, rather than asthma alone.  C  Oesophageal carcinoma  The long history of indigestion without progression to dysphagia and lack of weight loss doesn’t fit with a  diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman has been referred to the clinic by her GP who suspects she may have irritable bowel  syndrome. She suffers intermittent bouts of diarrhoea, problems with bloating, and flatulence. On further  questioning, it transpires that she has been feeling a little tired over the past few months.  On examination, her BP is 125/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. She looks a little pale, her BMI is 22.  Abdominal examination is unremarkable.  Investigations:  Investigation  Result  Normal value  Haemoglobin  105 g/l  115–155 g/l  White cell count (WCC)  5.4 × 10 9/l  4–11 × 10 9/l  Platelets  201 × 10 9/l  150–400 × 10 9/l  Sodium (Na +)  139 mmol/l  135–145 mmol/l  Potassium (K +)  4.1 mmol/l  3.5–5.0 mmol/l  Creatinine  110 μmol/l  50–120 µmol/l  Small bowel biopsy  villous atrophy, increased epithelial lymphocytes  Which of the following represents the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:   Gluten free diet  This patient has symptoms consistent with coeliac disease. She is also anaemic, which likely reflects iron  deficiency from malabsorption. Her small bowel biopsy shows increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and villous  atrophy, which is characteristic of the condition. As such the most appropriate therapy is a trial of gluten free  diet.  Coeliac disease is caused by an immune response to gluten exposure causing a small bowel enteropathy in  patients with a genetic predisposition. It is associate with HLA-DR3 + DQ2. Diagnosis is made on the basis of  serology (IgA for endomysial or tissue transglutaminase (EMA/TTG) and duodenal biopsy. NB there is an  association with IgA deficiency. In these cases patients should be tested for IgG to tissue transglutaminase.  (TG2).
